author: @amanshukla8758
text: I think whether you liked the movie or not depends upon your understanding of Physics and the relation between gravitational force and time. This movie explores the Theory of General Relativity very well. The use of Gravity Time Dilation, in the way the astronauts don't age, as time becomes slower for them due to the increasing gravitational force of the planets, is incredible. The working of a Wormhole is also beautifully and accurately shown. The depiction of how a Black Hole looks from the outside is accurate as hell and a sight to behold. The use of Centrifugal Force to produce 1 g so that the astronauts can walk inside the spacecraft normally, is clever. The use of Consevation of Momentum to provide gravitational assist to the spacecraft to escape the Black Hole, that's all real Physics. I was so much invested in the movie, because right now I'm pursuing a master's degree in Theoretical Physics, and to see a movie depict all of those complex concepts of physics so fluidly and beautifully was more than enough for making me love the movie. Now, about the end of the movie. We still don't know for sure what's inside a Black Hole. What we do know is that Black Holes (the rotating ones) might act as some sort of "teleporting devices" by bending the curvature of space-time, so that could explain how he managed to reach back to our solar system. However, we know that a person would never be able to survive the journey to the centre of the Black Hole, since the enormous gravitational force would squeeze him like a spaghetti. But still no one hasen't gone into a Black Hole so we don't know for sure what happens inside it, that's why I'm fine with what they showed at the end of the film. Because although we don't know what will happen if we go inside a Black Hole, it is generally accepted among physicists that whatever happens inside it, it's bizarre as hell. Nevertheless, this film is a treat to watch because seeing all these complex and mysterious phenomena on the big screen, and that too, so accurately depicted, along with the great cast, realistic acting, astounding visual effects, mesmerising music and awesome direction is more than enough for me to call this movie a masterpiece.

author: @riderule4944
text: Interstellar (2014) Ending Explained: Part - 6 1. Kya Gravity Equation Solve Karne ke liye Singularity Se Data Zaroori Tha? 🔹 Dr. Brand (Professor) ne Gravity Equation pe kaam kiya tha, लेकिन उसका एक हिस्सा missing था—Singularity ke andar ka Quantum Gravity Data. 🔹 Ye Quantum Data tabhi mil sakta tha jab koi event horizon cross karke singularity ke andar jaye aur wahan se gravitational fluctuations ko measure kare. 🔹 TARS (robot) ne ye kaam kiya—usne Singularity ke andar jaake data collect kiya aur Cooper ne us data ko Tesseract se Murph tak reach karaya. ✅ To haan, Singularity ka data zaroori tha, bina uske Gravity Equation complete nahi hoti. --- 2. Cooper Singulariy me gaya tha kya? Kya uska bachna loophole hai? Ye sabse bada sawaal hai! Kyunki Black hole me girne ka matlab hai—spaghettification (death!). Fir bhi Cooper kaise bacha? 🔹 Jab Cooper Gargantua ke andar girta hai, to wo Tesseract me pahunchta hai. 🔹 Tesseract ek higher-dimensional space hai, jo Bulk Beings ne artificially create kiya tha. 🔹 Cooper physically singularity tak nahi pahucha, balki usse pehle hi Bulk Beings ne usko Tesseract me place kar diya. 🔹 Matlab uska bachna loophole nahi hai, balki usse Bachaya gaya tha! 🚀 Kip Thorne (Nobel Prize Winner, Physicist) ne bataya tha ki real-life me koi Black Hole ke andar nahi bach sakta, lekin agar higher-dimensional beings exist karein, to wo kisi ko singularity tak pahunchne se pehle hi save kar sakte hain. --- 3. Nolan Sahab Ne Science Ko Kitna Accurate Rakha? 👏 Nolan ki film 95% tak real physics pe based hai! ✔ Gargantua Black Hole ka depiction ekdum scientific hai (Kip Thorne ne hi model banaya). ✔ Time Dilation theory real hai (Miller’s Planet ka time dilation correct hai). ✔ Black Hole ke andar direct jane se bachna possible nahi, lekin Higher Beings ke concept se ye justify ho jata hai. ⏩ Bas ek chhota loophole yahi hai ki "Bulk Beings" ka proof nahi hai, lekin theoretical physics me Higher Dimensions ka possibility hai. --- Final Answer ✅ Gravity Equation ke liye Singulariy ka Data zaroori tha, kyunki bina uske Quantum Gravity ke laws nahi samajh aate. ✅ Cooper technically Singulariy me nahi gaya, balki usse pehle hi Higher Beings ne usko Tesseract me shift kar diya. ✅ Nolan ne Science ko 95% accurate rakha, bas Higher Beings ka concept ek Fictional Element hai jo loophole cover karta hai.

author: @JamesJohnson-lg1iz
text: I ageee, guy is smart.... but the examples only allow the average person to accept the fact that "this is how it works and no matter how weird it is, I accept it now." I like to think about it this way-- Imagine a closed spherical tank of water that is completely full, about to burst. Now imagine opening up the top and shoving a 2 liter empty pop can, top down, in to the tank, then closing it back up, leaving the bottle in the tank. We can easily imagine that no water gets in the bottle. If we think of space time as "the water" in this example, we can not exist inside the pop bottle, because there is no water inside of it, and no way for us to allow water in to it. Even if we force a jet of water directly at the opening of the bottle, it may displace the empty space inside the bottle slightly, but we can't TURN the space in the bottle in to water, no matter what we do. You can do this if you have a pool or a hot tub. If the return jet is on, do like I said and push an empty bottle, top off, in to the water upside down, and hold it with both hands so that the return jet is forcing water toward the opening. If you play with it a little bit you will get the idea pretty quickly. This is, I believe anyway, a better way to talk about extra dimensional zones of space and/or spacetime that are inaccessible to us at least for now.

author: @Michaelonyoutub
text: While you got it, you are still missing much of the answer. Amelia Brand's love argument is completely correct, though she does a terrible job of explaining why it is worth listening to. The key to why "Love" is the answer is the fact "They" exist in this universe. In their universe, "They" left a wormhole for them. "They" can create gravitational anomalies to affect things in their reality. "They" are likely 5 dimensional beings, able to travel through time as easily as walking up a hill. Why would "They" ever care about humanity? Why would "They" ever go out of their way to help us? The answer to that question is the answer Brand comes to, it is "Love", and love is the solution to their quest. If they followed Brand's argument then they would have went to Edmunds's planet instead of Mann's. They would have found the habitable planet much sooner, not been betrayed by Mann, Romily would be alive, and heck if they followed Brand's love and went to Edmunds's instead of Miller's planet first, then Doyle would be alive too, decades wouldn't be lost, so Cooper can likely spend more time with his kids. That seems random and unscientific to go off a gut feeling like that, but it isn't necessarily random when "They" exist and are helping humanity. "They" don't communicate with us and give us the answers, but "They" could have left clues for us to reach the answer as painlessly as possible. "They" with their view of all possible timelines laid out in front of them, could see where they could tip the balance through gravitational manipulation to rig it so Edmunds got the only habitable planet. Just think about it, what are the chances that Edmunds not only was assigned one of the 3 candidate planets out of the original 12, but also has the only true habitable one? Solving the riddle of why "They" are helping us, leads to the path of least pain, the likely answer left for humanity by "Them". That argument could fall apart since then there is little reason for Cooper to enter the blackhole to get the data to save humanity, but following the love argument, you might ask, why would they take us to a system with a big blackhole? Why not a star? Brand herself even argues before the love argument that around a blackhole there is not enough opportunity for things to happen for life to accidentally occur and evolve. There are likely billions of star systems with habitable planets. If "They" can travel through time so easily, space likely isn't much of an issue so they could probably put that wormhole wherever they want. Why would they take us to such a hostile environment? The answer is that it is necessary for solving the gravity equation and saving all of humanity, "They" wouldn't have taken them there otherwise. They thus need to study it, and after Romily hits his head against a wall for a decade, he would probably want to try to go in like he suggested on Mann's planet. Cooper would likely be bored feeling useless, similar to how uncomfortable he was as a farmer, rotting in the dirt, unable to save his kids, and volunteers to pilot the ship in. If all else fails, eventually Murph is going to send that video messages talking about how it was all a scam, which likely would also push Cooper to do it.

author: @TheManCybo
text: There's a big problem with time. It doesn't exist, it's a human construct to make it easier comprehend our memories. A clock, atomic or mechanical isn't a prove time exist. About relativity where fast moving objects are slower in time, measured with a clock, it can be explained: For this to work, the speed of the moving object must be very high. In experiments with satellites which have atomic clocks synchronized with the same ones on earth, they showed to be slower for a few seconds in a period of an year. The measurement of the clocks are no prove time exist, it proves only a difference between the two of them. Why? Gravity and speed. All objects moving with high speed are getting inert. But earths gravity is pulling the material structure of the clock on the satellite while it's traveling ca. 20 km per second. this is what slowing material down. This applies also for very high speed, linear traveling trough the universe, gravity is everywhere. Ever rotating on a playground on those round platforms with handles? With enough speed you couldn't even move your hand to the center of the platform - the kinetic energy of the spinning is pulling you away from the center, so material is getting inert, lazy. The satellite is also spinning around earth, plus the gravity of it: 2 forces - centrifugal and gravity pulling from earth. Imagine how it works with stars and galaxies. But time doesn't exist. If time would exist, science would find a way to catch it, to establish a timeline. Imagine our present moment makes a never ending imprint in something like timeline, of course, no future yet - it simply didn't happened yet. So, science must be able to enter this timeline at any past point in it, like with a time machine. But if it would be possible, they would jump in a point of the timeline which is frozen till the moment they jump in. At this point, they should move forward in the timeline. It's practically in every movie. Does this means, all past timeline is frozen, until time travelers enter? Or is every moment (what is a moment, how long is it?) in constant loop? The problem with this movie is, mankind could never get to the future without installing the wormhole. The wormhole is allegedly the reason that mankind exist in the future. So, for mankind to get to its future, it would have to preinstall the wormhole in the present to get to the future. One could say, they got away from earth with the missing data about anti gravity and got to the 3 planets. Still, how could they install the wormhole to get to those planets, since the future is established only with the existing of the wormhole? There is simply now way to get to future without setting the wormhole in the present. And this couldn't be done by humanity, this future never happened.

author: @danielklein5732
text: Great analysis here! I have a theory about the end of the film which also introduces the element of sacrificing one’s life to save their loved ones across galaxies and time. I actually think the entire ending sequence only takes place in Coop’s mind as he floats in space after he gives the message to Murph from the Tesseract right before he dies. Mann told him earlier in the film he would see his children flash before his eyes before dying. Why would there be a baseball game right outside his hospital room which distorted his earth memories when he awakens? And a whole space station that only served as a museum to his life? Because those are the only possibilities he could conceive for the future that could still reunite him with his daughter in space while maintaining his only semblance of memory from Earth. Notice the framing of the shot when he is sitting out on the old house porch with TARS, and he sees a white circle of light in the sky with his old power line sticking out from a darker foreground. It seems like he is viewing his old universe from the other side of a black hole right when he says “I don’t care for this pretending to be back where we started…” before we jump cut to a completely different setting. Doesn’t this feel like a dream someone would have from a black hole? Coop tells Murph in their reunion scene “I’m here now,” and she first replied plainly “No,” before clarifying after a pause that line about parents seeing their children die, which didn’t make much sense based off what he originally said. Why would she even mention Dr. Brand and know so many details about her plight if she hasn’t been saved and still needs Coops help? The other family in the room only serve as window dressing since they don’t matter to Coop now,as he is only focused on Murph. The minor characters he talks to use phrases it’s easy to imagine Coop using, like when the doc tells him he’s not a “spring chicken” anymore. Finally, he entered a black hole directly, not a wormhole like in the first sequence. Even with the advanced technology of the Tesseract, matter cannot typically escape the event horizon of a black hole without going faster than the speed of light. And the last image we see of the Tesseract is it disintegrating around him in a flash of white light. Earlier in the film when they discuss sending TARS only, it’s clear they are only needing the data it will transmit back, understanding it can likely never return. Coop dying at the end would have been bad for most audience expectations, so I think this ending is deliberately ambiguous. It pleases most casual fans with a happy ending, but I think they def build in this other interpretation too. Thus, Coop was the one most willing to risk even certain death in order to have a chance to send a message that could save his daughter and thus humanity. Since matter cannot exit a black hole, this is theoretically the only way to learn the quantum revelations: transmitting the data across dimensions through the power of love and family intuition.

text: One of my all-time favourite EVER films. That's saying A LOT, because I LOVE films, most genres, old & new. The first time I watched Interstellar, I was blown away. For me, it confirmed a theory about where we are now, how our energy manifests/ communicates/ is received & where we go to when we die. Our bodies are just electricity & goo, bit of bone, a soul cage. When the cage expires the energy is freed. Vivid memories of astral travelling when I was a child were provoked. The multi-dimensional grid, of time in space that was depicted, that Cooper drifted toward then fell into, within which he is trying to send a message to his daughter, seeing it made me cry. It gives me peace to know in my heart & mind that death is NOT the end; we are such a tiny part of something more vast & mysterious than most of our 3-4 dimensional minds can ever comprehend. Christopher Nolan is a true visionary, I'm such a fan of his work. I want to say here & now that I feel Interstellar is his best work. It is one of those films that with each watch, it makes more & more sense, in that way, it gives it more & more meaning - that's an interstellar talent at work & makes it so much more enjoyable than a film that gives you nothing more than everything at first watch. I so desperately want a sequel to this, a prequel even would do, but mostly I really want to know what happened after Cooper went to find Brand.

Its like stretching a spring, by having one end remain stationary, while the other is pulled away. A reduction in energy (amplitude) would instead look like the entire spring was being shrunk instead of stretched.

author: @globnomulous
text: Thanks for this. It's full of really striking insight, which led me to realize something: books' prominence in the film is another clever nod to time. We can digest them only as three dimensional beings moving through time, but the book itself relates to time more in the manner of the fictional five-dimensional beings, because the book itself has no past, present, or future. The parts we experience as individual moments all exist simultaneously. Imagine the book as a kind of three-dimensional shape sphere. Humans experience it exactly as the two-dimensional beings of Flatland experience the three-dimensional shape passing through their universe. So it's perfectly appropriate that the contents of the tesseract, representating different moments in time, showing the changing state of Murphy and her room, even as the books themselves remain stable and unchanging -- because that's exaclty how the content of a book relates to time. In a way, this makes the film a lovely reflection on literacy, writing, and books. I'm a former humanist who now works as an engineer. I miss my own life in the world of books and grieve for the apparent loss of multiple forms of book-base literacy in our culture -- and their replacement with 'media' literacy. If I'm right, Interstellar is a rather clever, sentimental love letter to book and their sort of metaphysical and epistemological superiority to forms of media that, like video, are more temporally limited. Books are timeless, in contrast to the forms of technology and media that have become so prominent -- which are all temporary, changing, and disposable. So if we're to survive as a species, we'll do so only because we somehow meet to the challenges that our best literature and writers ask us to meet. This gives the film a rather unexpected Manichaean, gnostic, even Platonic flavor. It's hardly the case that Nolan wants us to think of the physical realm as somehow evil or suspect (the idea of looking up rather than down also figures prominently in a famous early passage of the Roman historian Sallust), but the film does clearly communicate that it's a good thing for us to look and aim 'higher,' both metaphorically in ourselves and physically/cosmically in teh univers.

text: Wow, this video is really great. I'm so happy to find people who actually understand de meaning of this film. Let me add something from my understanding: Matthew Mcconaughey' caracter, Joseph Cooper (JC), as you said, is an anallogy to Jesus Christ (JC); Do you remember what Jesus said about love?: “A new command I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you must love one another. By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another.” John 13: 34-35 NIV. Fun facts: There are 12 astronauts being led by him (Cooper is the pilot), he "dies" when he enters the black hole just to try to save us all and he comes back to live, just as JC did. Continuing about love: Don't you think that if we really loved one another, leaving evil, envy and selfishness aside, we would advance more as humanity? Don't you think that if we recognize ourselves within a group, that of being human, and truly love ourselves, without distinctions of races or flags, we will be able to survive in spite of everything? Maybe Cooper is being guided by the love of his daughter and Amelia is being guided by the love of her lover, but Romilly, Doyle and the other astronauts, who have no family or ties, are being guided by another type of love: love for humanity. So, Christopher Nolan is making us a statement of the importance of love in the advancement and survival of humanity, an idea that departs from religion. But on the other hand, it clearly shows us another atheistic / agnostic reasoning: Humanity does not need that a God come to solve our problems and save us but that it is we, humanity, who are going to save ourselves ("them"=future beings= we, mankind). In conclusion, Christopher Nolan is using religious and non-religious discourses to explain the path that humanity must follow to achieve survival throughout eternity. So yes, I believe that Interstellar is a masterpiece, that it does not have an inch of foolishness (just as some "flim crisitcs" say) and that in fact it is one of the deepest films that have been ever made. text: I love all the mathematical and astrophysical concepts used to create this exceptional film. Unfortunately, there are several problems with their narrative, and yours by extension. The time dilation is present regardless if you land on the planet surrounding Gargantua or not. The time dilation will get more severe the closer you get to the black hole, to the point of stopping once you reach the event horizon of Gargantua. Even if you're orbiting Miller’s Planet, you will still be subject to the 7:1 time dilation; the only problem with landing on the planet will be the extreme gravitational stresses. The gravity of Miller’s Planet will be compounded by the gravity of Gargantua once you land. So the problem we have is that the time dilation will not show its effect until they leave the gravitational influence of Gargantua. They would not be able to receive the messages as they showed in the movie; again, those would only be accessible once they leave the frame reference of Gargantua. I'm sure Kip Thorne explained all this to the filmmakers, and we need to suspend our disbelief for this film’s premise to work. As Einstein stated in his seminal Theory of Relativity, it's all relative.

It's so strongly profound in it's own unique way, it really left me with the feeling that it's an absolute masterpiece, much like Inception did. The visuals are second to none, the physics is astounding, and the conceptualization of what lies beyond the event horizon is facinating to say the least. Not to mention the goosebumps you get when Coop sees Murph for the 1st time again... Also, it takes one hell of a movie to make me think of Michael Caine's character as an asshole. If that isn't groundbreaking, I don't know what is. 😂 It most certainly isn't a film for everyone, but I'm thankful Nolan and his team produced this wonderful bit of cinema. I hope this inspires people to keep pushing boundaries and to look up and be a little more curious about what lies out there.

text: Coming home after the 2020 pandemic was definitely that intrinsically personal experience: time did pass, no the world and home didn’t freeze, and it was an experience likely shared by billions. We are beings constantly experiencing time, albeit, subtly sometimes but passing nonetheless.

text: The title of this video makes me feel vindicated at calling this film the 2001: A Space Odyssey of this generation. I can remember when this movie came out it was mostly well received but there were certain corners of this platform that seemed nonchalant about Interstellar and picked it apart poor point by plot point (Cinema Sins, Nerdwriter, Doug Walker, Honest Trailers etc.). If people don’t like this movie that’s fine but I sensed a cinephile’s equivalent of a music fan reviewing a new album by a famous musician with “I liked their early work better.” There was an enormous amount of anticipation surrounding Christopher Nolan’s science fiction epic. At this point in his filmmaking career he had reinvented the Batman franchise (and possibly the whole comic book movie franchise) had multiple academy award nominations and was easily considered an A list director in Hollywood. I feel that when a new film comes out by an established director cinephiles have a tendency to think more about the director and their previous works rather than the film right in front of them. It can also appear smart and sophisticated to be critical of a director’s latest work. Upon its release Jurassic Park, while favourably reviewed by Roger Ebert, was criticized in his review for showing too much of the dinosaurs (unlike Jaws which at this in 1993 was considered a classic). I suppose my rambling point is this: a film is not always a masterpiece in its own time. Pauline Kael didn’t like the aforementioned 2001: A Space Odyssey or Star Wars (1977) for that matter! Click bait reviews nit-picking reviews upon a film’s release do not tell the entire story of its reception. Interstellar is my favourite movie of the 2010’s!

text: 2001 A Space Odyssey is looked at more as a piece of art. Interstellar is going to be remembered as an experience. Literally every aspect of this movie, whether its the acting, direction, cinematography, the editing, the sound design, THE MUSIC, set design, and writing(debatable)...is firing on all cylinders. It represents the peak of filmmaking. It also has 2 scenes that I think will go down in history as some of the greatest scenes put on film; watching his children’s messages scene and the docking sequence. I remember seeing this movie in IMAX on the first day of release, planned it perfectly to make sure i got there early to get center seats and not too close to the screen. Right after Cooper pleads to Dr. Mann not to dock and then Mann blew himself up, Cooper accelerates towards the Endurance and Dr. Brandt then asks Cooper what he's doing, and he just says..."docking" (Cue Hanz Zimmer's score). I lost my shit in the theater, I got goosebumps and literally leaned forward and audibly said pretty loudly "what...the...fuck!?!". As the scene went on I remember thinking, Nolan... you crazy bastard , you just cranked the intensity up to a 10. Then the music tipped it over to an 11. That moment, that sequence with that music and the sound just blasting. Sensory Overload...I will never forget the experience. Seriously, if you sat down and really thought about "what" this movie is about, like really thought about all its themes, all its layers of depth and what its trying to say, your gonna come to only one conclusion. Its about Everything.

text: Over the years there have been lots of films that were filmmakers' love letters to Kubrick's 2001, and this one is probably the most invested in shamelessly showing it. Likely because Nolan was fresh off of a film where he borrowed some of 2001's "Fuck Gravity" filming techniques, Inception. First is the placement of the wormhole near Saturn, which was where it was originally scripted in 2001 before Douglas Trumbull couldn't come up with convincing Saturn VFX on Kubrick's schedule (though he kept at the problem after wrap, which is how we got Silent Running). Second is TARS & CASE echoing the shape of the Monolith. Third, you have an artificial being killing, but only because of how they were programmed by man. Fourth, there's Lithgow's commentary on baseball hotdogs, echoing a similar conversation he had in 2010. But most importantly there's the "you may want to be chemically elevated for this" final act. Doug Trumbull's V'Ger visuals in Star Trek: The Motion Picture may have been stunning, but they drag on too long, and they're not close enough to the end to count as a proper homage. Cameron's descent into the underwater alien city in The Abyss hits closer to the mark, but it's lacking the brainfuckery. As for Interstellar? It nails it.

author: @double00spy
text: Prof. Thorne says he calculated the time dilation using the equation for a rotating black hole. However, I used an equation for a non-rotating one, and got the same answer. An hour spent on the planet was worth 7 years on earth. I would think that most black holes rotate. This pulls space time around with the massive object, and the equations are way beyond me. Since the planet is revolving around the hole, and, is close, it must be at a very high velocity. I began to wonder what the time dilation would be on the planet with its high orbital velocity. Turns out that the planet would have to orbit at about 75% of the speed of light for a stable orbit. That velocity effect only amounted to 1.5 hr vs the 7 years for the gravity effect for 1 hr on the planet.

author: @Godsen5
text: Christopher Nolan is like me in early high school. Side note: in Italy we have several high schools (lyceums, technical schools, professional schools) they all share few single universal subjects, the most important of which is Italian (language and literature) and the main test is the "Tema" (a sort of free essay, a sub-genre of which is the proper "essay"). Now, in early high school I discovered the "Ringkomposition" the idea of suggesting an idea at the beginning just to come back there for a poetic, emphatic or rhetoric conclusion. Christopher Nolan f*cking loves Ringkomposition (no wonder its one of the central compositive tools of the homeric poems, one of which has a movie coming out later this year, guess by who?). Interstellar is a movie about "time" as "circular" (Endurance is literally a spinning clock), the idea that the beginning is the end. The same idea present in Memento, Insomnia and The Prestige. Here the beginning is the end. The Saturn's wormhole is Gargantua and Gargantua is the other end of the wormhole. And so on and so forth the whole movie is about how to make it so the beginning is the end. And every major movement in the film is a rotation, a wave, a circular motion. Ringkomposition, baby! It's a cheap trick, but it'll get you far .... and then back to the beginning.

author: @QFTenthusiast
text: Interstellar will always be, in my opinion, amongst the greatest si-fi movies ever made. There is an immense amount to reflect on and comprehend after the movie finishes. Sure, the actual astrophysics and what not are a bit confusing to the average layman, though you can EASILY educate yourself about the subjects in one easy internet search and 20-30 minutes of reading, but that really is not the core of the movie. This movie is about the consequences of our actions as individuals and as a race, and the moral dilemmas behind how far we will go as individuals to save ourselves/families over the entire population, and much more. This movie is, as cliché as this sound, very deep, and if you treat it like a lame, surface level, marvel movie, you are an idiot and will likely wrongfully dislike this masterpiece. This movie REQUIRES your full attention at all times, and it really rewards you if you stay attentive. This is hands down, with out a shred of a doubt, Nolan's greatest work. One common complaint is that this movie is unnecessarily slow, and that it feels like a steady grind until the last half an hour or so. First off, its 2 hours and 40+ fking minutes, so, no sht its long sherlock. However, more importantly, if you have this opinion, please, i beg of you, carve out 3+ hours one night and totally focus your full attention on this movie during its entire length. Dont check your phone, though if you are paying attention, you will be FAR too engrossed in the movie to do so, and just stay focused on making sense of the movie and following the plot. After the movie is finished, please take 15+ minutes to think back on what everything meant and what some deeper meanings throughout the movie were, because I promise you will enjoy the movie so much more if you notice the little nuances and moral debates that are throughout the film. It is really best if you are doing this throughout the film, but just after the film works for beginners. Actually, the entire process I just recommended you do, you should really do for every movie you watch. You will get so much more out of film, both skill-wise and academically, and watching moveis will be a much more memorable experience. if you made it to the end... luv u baby.

author: @Dr_Ohm
text: Despite the fact that Interstellar is partly based on scientific theories such as General Relativity, many things are actually inaccurate and even wrong (not even talking about the scenario's countless absurdities). To take just the example of Miller's planet : if an orbiting planet around the black hole should experience such an insane time dilation (factor x 61,362 !!!) it has to be so close to the event horizon that even for a supermassive black hole, the tidal forces would rip it apart. Second point : for such a huge time dilation, the black hole must be spinning at very nearly the critical value (the speed of light). As it drags space-time, the zone near to the event horizon called the ergosphere is drawn by the rotation of the black hole, which makes it even harder for any object the size of a planet to have a stable orbit and not to be torn apart there. And of course as this black hole has an accretion disk (which was absolutely not accurately rendered in the film because you have huge Doppler effects, one side of the disk should be very bright, while the other is red shifted), the inner rings would be at a such a high temperature due to friction they would produce very energetic radiation such as X-rays. No need to mention this environnement would burn you and kill you in seconds. And now about one of the biggest absurdity of the scenario : why choosing to explore such an extreme planet in the first place when its enormous time dilation leaves you plenty of time (!) to explore the others? Actually, aside from horror films, I haven't seen such stupid and dull characters in a so-called Science-Fiction film !

translated_text: Using Sanskrit possibly will not just be for hacking. There are many time travelers mentioned in Indian Sanskrit texts, talking about the universe's timeline. The Bhagavad Gita says energy cannot be destroyed, it can only be transformed. That formula E=MC² was also mentioned by Christopher Nolan in the Oppenheimer movie along with verses from the Bhagavad Gita. It says there is no time in the 5th dimension, which Krishna tells Arjuna in the Bhagavad Gita that when you reach the Brahmaloka, there is no death or birth, there is neither the beginning nor the end, so this Brahmaloka could be another dimension. author: @mattgriffinreal
text: Now, Paul, you already know that I'm about to write a whole essay... (Cracks fingers.) Okay. So, Interstellar is my favorite Christopher Nolan film over Memento, The Dark Knight, and Tenet. I think that the best part about Interstellar is the accuracy pertaining to time dilation and the time dimension in general. Interstellar does the best job visually explaining the effects of time on reality. There are hundreds of other stories that depict other aspects of time, such as Groundhog's Day and Avengers Endgame, but even those examples have their flaws. As stated by Bruce Banner, "Changing the past doesn't change the future." So, obviously, films like Back to the Future do not make any logic sense because, as Dr. Amelia Brand stated, "Time is relative." That means that time is not the same for all observers. For instance, a time traveler can only interpret time moving from present to the future. The past is just something that was recorded for reference. So, if a time traveler travels to the "past," that past is recorded AFTER the present, not before. (You would have to know the trajectory of every single particle in the entire universe of that exact moment in the true past that you choose as the arrival point. It's just extremely difficult to calculate...) Anyway, storytellers often make that mistake when dealing with features of time, especially time travel. Interstellar does not make that mistake and, instead, corrects it by describing a complex scientific and mathematical phenomenon in the simplest way possible for audiences. When you're floating around in empty space, time speeds back up because you don't have that gravity slowing you down - slowing your senses and, thus, how your brain interprets reality. Gravity slows time down, and that is what happened when Cooper, Brand, and Doyle were on that planet that was just off the edge of the black hole. Because they were so close to that extremely dense gravitational pull, time slowed down exponentially. This is where Nolan hooks people in because Cooper stopped aging as fast as he was aging when he was on Earth. Now his daughter is the same age as he is because of the effects of gravity on time, and the audience is suddenly drawn into this story emotionally because of the mechanics of the actual universe that they are all in. It's just absolutely brilliant how Nolan was able to bring the world of science and human emotion together like that.

text: Black holes represent one of the most intriguing phenomena in astrophysics, combining extreme gravity, spacetime distortion, and untapped cosmic potential. Their event horizons offer a glimpse into the limits of our understanding of physics, where Einstein's general relativity and quantum mechanics seem to collide. For interstellar time travel, black holes could serve as both obstacles and opportunities. The intense warping of spacetime near a black hole might theoretically enable phenomena like time dilation, as depicted in Interstellar, where seconds near a black hole translate to years elsewhere. This tantalizing possibility opens a window into the future of cosmic exploration and perhaps even human survival beyond Earth. Harnessing such extreme environments for time travel or wormhole navigation requires breakthroughs in physics, particularly in unifying general relativity with quantum mechanics. Yet, black holes remain a double-edged sword; they are both cosmic wonders and formidable threats. Their study not only pushes the boundaries of scientific inquiry but also challenges us to imagine new frontiers of human potential, where interstellar journeys and even glimpses into the past or future could one day be reality. The key lies in advancing our understanding of spacetime and developing the technology to safely approach and utilize these cosmic powerhouses.

text: While seemingly complex, the ending of Interstellar always struck me as actually VERY simple to explain. The fact that the protagonist actually TELLS you precisely what is happening is the key. The fact that a species who has evolved beyond the normal limitations of Space-Time and is trying to communicate with a Human is the explanation. Its all a matter of perspective and in order to achieve a state of control within a 3 dimensional frame of reference that he could understand required them to forcibly "simplify" it to ensure that he can understand. This is precisely why (and its even explained by he himself) they limited his "interface" with them to a very small 3 dimensional set of coordinates but extrapolated over the duration of time. Now admittedly this is where the movie goes off the rails a bit because it has fallen into an "oversimplification trap" as it regards Time which is often the error in any movie in which Time is being manipulated, traversed or made flexible. Time is NOT, I repeat NOT, a "dimension" let alone a "4th dimension". Dimensions are STRICTLY defined by physical parameters and what has to be understood is that Time is a component of that Space that is intrinsically linked. Space and Time (or more accurately Spacetime because they cannot be separated) are bound inextricably and while they do function mathematically as a 4 dimensional manifold its less about actual dimensionality and more about a dimension in the sense of just another variable to be considered in what would otherwise be a strictly x, y, z system. In the case of this movie the species which is communicating with him (or rather allow HIM to communicate with his daughter using their technology) is able to traverse "time" because he is manipulating Gravity. Its already known that Gravity and its influence on Time is very well defined. For example, the best know relationship is such that at faster velocities (and thus greater and greater Gravity) time literally slows down within that frame of reference as it relates to other frames of reference. The fact that everyone has heard the very basic example of "as you travel near the speed of light time appears to stop for the traveler but only from outside their reference as observed by someone NOT travelling at the speed of light" but the correlary to this situation is that to the person who is moving at light speed the outside universe would appear to be on "Fast Forward" compared to them. The ONLY reason this occurs is NOT because you are traveling fast its because by doing so you are also increasing the force of gravity and thus warping the flow of time because you literally gain Mass the faster you go. More Mass, more Gravity. More Gravity, Slower Time. At the core of a Black Hole for instance you would have the unenviable experience to be being pulled apart at the atomic level and also stretched for what would essentially be the end of the Universe. THESE Beings (whether they are really Us or just Helpful Aliens, it doesn't matter) allow him to manipulate Gravity to allow him to communicate by figuring it out within his own context. They are limited in their interactions with him because it would be like having a Human try to communicate and empower a 2-dimensional "flat" lifeform to exist within an infinite number of planes that extend along Time. We are not able to just "lower our dimensionality" whenever we want to be able to somehow magically become 2-dimensional to have a nice little chat with such a being, so in much the same way these Beings can't do that with him, though if they could it would be soooo much easier.

text: I am suggesting that Plan B might have been the initial step that eventually enabled the success of Plan A through a complex interplay of timelines. Let’s delve into this idea further. Analysis of Interstellar’s Timelines and Plans Initial Setup and Problem • Earth’s Imminent Demise: Humanity faces extinction due to deteriorating environmental conditions on Earth. • Two Plans for Survival: • Plan A: Solve the gravity problem to enable the construction of large space stations to transport Earth’s population. • Plan B: Send embryos to another habitable planet to ensure the continuation of the human species, albeit through a new, isolated branch of humanity. The Role of Cooper and the Tesseract • Cooper’s Journey: Cooper’s journey through the wormhole ultimately leads him to the tesseract, a construct made by future beings. • Communication Across Time: Inside the tesseract, Cooper can communicate with his daughter, Murph, across time by manipulating gravity through the fifth dimension. Plausible Scenario for Plan B Leading to Plan A Plan B as the Initial Survival Mechanism 1. Plan B Colonization: • The initial Plan B missions successfully establish human colonies on habitable planets. • These colonies evolve, develop advanced technologies, and eventually create a civilization that survives for millions of years. 2. Evolution of Future Humans: • These future humans evolve to a point where they can manipulate higher dimensions (time and space). • They understand that their own existence and the preservation of essential human qualities, such as love, depend on helping their ancestors. Ensuring the Success of Plan A 3. Creation of the Wormhole and Tesseract: • Future humans create a wormhole near Saturn and the tesseract within the black hole. • Their goal is to enable Cooper to provide Murph with the quantum data needed to solve the gravity equation. 4. Murph Solves the Gravity Equation: • With the quantum data provided by Cooper, Murph successfully solves the gravity equation. • This allows the construction of massive space stations, enabling Earth’s population to migrate and survive in space. Temporal Interplay • Interconnected Timelines: The intervention of future humans (descendants of Plan B) ensures the success of Plan A, creating a loop where both plans are essential for humanity’s ultimate survival. • Plan B as a Catalyst: Plan B’s success over millions of years leads to the evolution of future humans who can manipulate time and space, thereby ensuring Plan A’s success by aiding their ancestors. Conclusion My interpretation aligns well with the film’s themes and narrative structure. Plan B provides the initial means of survival, allowing humanity to evolve into advanced beings capable of influencing the past. These future humans ensure Plan A’s success, creating a temporal loop where both plans are interconnected and essential for the survival of the human species. By this logic, Plan B can be seen as the actual solution that, over millions of years and through different temporal timelines, leads to the eventual success of Plan A as depicted in the movie. This interplay of timelines and plans underlines the film’s exploration of time, survival, and the transcendence of human qualities such as love.

author: @cesarjom
text: 8:40 You are missing the point (source) of the gravitational time dilation effect here. It is not the gravity of Miller's planet that creates the time dilation that the crew undergoes, but rather it from the supermassive black hole (BH) that the planet is orbiting. The BH has an effect on the spacetime (curvature) around its horizon that is slowing down time as you get closer to the horizon (where time would come to stop at the actual BH horizon). You can calculate the mass and radius from the BH horizon from Einstein's GR field equations, using... (time near BH)/(time on Earth) = sqrt( 1 - 2GM/(rc^2) ) note: this is the familiar gravitational time dilation equation where M is mass of BH and for the movie, we can approximate r as the distance from BH to Miller's planet. Also c is speed of light and G is gravitational constant. Then, 3600s/(2.21x10^8s) = sqrt( 1 - 2GM/(rc^2) ) ... using the 7 yr on Earth to 1 hr on Miller's planet (near massive BH) M/r = (c^2/2G)*(1 - ( 3600/(2.21x10^8) )^2 )*(SolarMass/(2x10^30 kg)*(10^6m/RadiusEarth) ... using conversions to solar mass and earth radius. M/r = 337 * (SolarMass/RadiusEarth) ... after doing the calculation using the usual constants. One type of intermediate BH would have a typical ratio of M/R = 1000 * (SolarMass/RadiusEarth), where M is BH mass and R is Schwarzschild radius (ie, event horizon of BH). Therefore, for the example in the film, dividing this typical M/R ratio by M/r (we calc above) gives... r/R = 1000/337 r = 3*R ... this would show the distance between Miller's planet and BH at three times the size of BH (event horizon) in order that the gravitational time dilation effects from film to hold true.

author: @wealthelife
text: The crop burning motivation was not as you stated IMHO. The brother's crop wasn't the sole remaining one to sustain humanity (where was that stated in the movie?), just another blighted field of monoculture that would eventually be burned to stop the spread of the blight, without causing a significant impact on humanity. Murph didn't just burn it as a distraction, but mostly to destroy the farm so that her brother would finally see reason and leave the farm and get medical attention for his family at NASA (he was insisting on staying on the farm, even though it was killing his family, due to resenting his father leaving and abandoning the farm and his family). If Murph had only needed time to decode the watch, she could have just stopped arguing with her brother and gone to her old room to quietly work on the watch code. It also wasn't that Dr Brand snr. didn't "plan on solving the equation" and simply chose to do plan B all along, but that he had realized years ago that the equation couldn't be solved (without data about gravity that was impossible to access, as no information can escape a black hole), so he simply wanted his daughter to survive the extinction of the human race via plan B. author: @randm4246
text: Excellent job breakdown. The one plot contrivance that I haven't heard anyone look into or mention is the wormhole paradox: In the film, humans could not have survived the destruction of Earth without the wormhole, but how did humans evolve past the great filter to get to the point that they were able to construct the wormhole without the wormhole? We can mess with the relativity of space time all we want, but without the wormhole we wouldn't have survived and evolved to create the wormhole. It's a catch 22. I understand that you hypothesize that it was AI that was able to place the wormhole for us, but we wouldn't have gotten to the point where we could have fallen into the black hole to bridge that gap without the wormhole being there in the first place. What I think happened is that a race of humans from either another planet that has existed for far longer than we have had found Earth and decided to help us, or more likely it was another race of humans from a parallel universe's Earth that placed the wormhole to assist humanity in our universe.

text: I think what needs to be clarified is that time dilation refers to only the perception or realization of time being slower. Time itself is not what is able to decelerate. This is all about gravity’s affect on matter. “Dilation” is just the phenomenon of light itself being slowed down. Redshifts are certainly fascinating and hard enough to comprehend. The only way you can stand behind dilation is by saying we can time travel. That can’t reasonably be argued beyond a theoretical level. Remember, time is not what’s malleable: only our perception of it is. Also, don’t misinterpret what it means for clocks to tick slower or faster. Atomic clocks rely on a specific measure of gravity to give us the common “second”. At varying gravities, the frequency of the atomic radiation and be faster or slower. I’m as fascinated by the time dilation enigma just as much as anybody else, but we can’t romanticize it to a point where we accept nonsensical concepts that are not proven. Also, the GPS clock argument is the most shallow argument. They simply tick slower. The satellites themselves do not experience time slower.

author: @angelamartzen7499
text: I can see how some people didn't like the "love" aspect of this movie because on the surface it sounds corny and contrived. But if you set aside the urge to roll your eyes at any and every utterance of the word love, you would see that Brand's speech makes sense. If Cooper did not have a family that he cared about, a daughter that he so desperately wanted to get back to, then he would not have tried as hard as he could to complete their mission. Doing something for the good of all humanity is honestly too big for most people. He never even wanted to go on this mission in the first place. You can tell that by the time they get to Gargantua, Cooper is really only thinking about his daughter... if he ends up saving the rest of humanity then that's a bonus, but his real goal was to get back to his daughter. It's not selfish, it's human. We have the instinct to protect ourselves and our young. It's unrealistic to think that in a time of desperation and survival, that we would be taking every single other person into account. We prioritize what's most important to us. If your child was trapped in a burning building with several other random people, who would you save first? Your own child of course. If you could then help save others then maybe you would, but your goal is to save yourself and your loved ones first. Even heroes are not textbook perfect individuals. Brand was determined to get to Edmunds planet because she loved him and yes she made some poor decisions based on this feeling, but that just shows how love itself is a driving force to motivate someone to do something, good or bad. If you listen to Brand speaking about love, she openly points out how love can be nonsensical when you try to break it down logically, "We love people who have died. Where's the social utility in that?" and "I'm drawn across the universe to someone I haven't seen in a decade, who I know is probably dead." She is just acknowledging the undeniable fact that love compels us and it's bigger than what we believe it to be.

text: Interstellar (2014) Ending Explained: Part - 2 Interstellar me Cooper Gargantua Black Hole ke andar girta hai aur singularity ke paas pahunchta hai. Kaise Pahucha? 1. Tesseract Scene: Jab Cooper aur TARS Gargantua ke accretion disk me enter karte hain, tab extreme gravity aur time dilation ke wajah se wo singularity ki taraf accelerate hote hain. Normally, Black Hole me girne wale kisi bhi object ka spaghettification ho jata hai (matlab, wo infinite stretch ho jata hai). Par movie me Cooper spaghettification se bach jata hai kyunki usse fifth-dimensional beings (bulk beings) bacha lete hain. 2. Fifth-Dimensional Tesseract: Ye beings higher-dimensional entities hain jo time ko ek physical dimension ki tarah dekh sakte hain. Unhone Cooper ke liye ek Tesseract structure banaya, jisme uska consciousness 5D spacetime me freely move kar sakta hai. Wahan Cooper apni beti Murph se contact karta hai through gravitational signals (watch ke second hand ke motion se). Kya Ye Scientifically Possible Hai? Agar Cooper directly singularity me girta, to Quantum Mechanics ke rules ke mutabik uska existence collapse ho jata. Kip Thorne (physicist, jo movie ke scientific advisor the) ne kaha ki Singularity tak koi bhi survive nahi kar sakta. Par movie me extra-dimensional intervention dikhaya gaya hai, jo theoretically higher dimensions aur brane-world physics me possible ho sakta hai. Matlab, Cooper singularity tak physically nahi pahucha, balki higher-dimensional beings ne usse ek safe 5D space (Tesseract) me place kar diya, jisse usne past me interact kiya aur Murph ko Gravity Equation ka hint diya.

text: This is of only 3 films I give a 10/10. I am VERY harsh when reviewing and critiquing movies but this one was a 10/10 for me. The only other films I give a 10/10 are (and in order) Interstellar, The Dark Knight, and 2001 A Space Odyssey. Yes, I am a bit partial to space movies but something like Gravity I would give a 5/10 at most. Nolan is my favorite director of all time (with Kubrick at second and maybe Speilberg or Tarantino at 3rd/4th). Interstellar hits every single criterion perfectly. I thought Matthew McConaughey and Anne Hathaway's performances were a 10/10. Obviously, the visuals were a 10/10, the plot was a 10/10, and who could forget possibly the greatest 10/10 score of all time. I mean there isn't a single lacking point in this entire movie. Nolan is a fucking genius and what's so special about this movie particularly, was that it wasn't just another space movie. This movie LITERALLY revolutionized how we think about space, Nolan brought on the greatest living Astro Physiscts for this movie and REVOLUTIONIZED how we think about space, black holes, and gravity. If you haven't read up on the real-life implications of this movie, I highly recommend it. This movie actually changed what we think about relativity and the black hole scene in particular actually revised our understanding of black holes. Like how can you argue this movie isn't anything other than perfection? It was not only a 10/10 film-wise, but literally changed how we looked at space, relatively, gravity, and black holes. What other film did that?

text: This is the best analysis of Interstellar there is. It mirrors my thoughts that I've had on the film perfectly, thoughts that I've had to argue with people about constantly. There are so many people, including film critics, who claim to be smart and look down on Interstellar who deride the film as rubbish. Their criticism often includes making fun of the film for supposedly claiming that "love is the fifth dimension" which shows a complete lack of understanding of what the film was trying to say. Time and time again I have said to people that the film isn't saying that love is the fifth dimension or anything like that, it's saying that the bulk beings have no way of communicating their important message because they have access to infinite time and they need the connection between Cooper and his daughter to communicate that message in order to save the human race. THAT is why love is important in the film. It's nice to see that at least one other person ACTUALLY understands what's happening in the film. Great video.

author: @burstofsanity
text: I still feel that this film is middling at best. The entire premise is non-sensical. It's the same old, the Earth is dying so let's go somewhere else. Every planet they visit is orders of magnitude worse than Mars for habitability and even if they found the perfect planet to rebuild humanity on the "space station" solution was never an option even though the movie says otherwise. If you can't keep the blight from infecting everything on Earth, how are you going to ensure the space station is free of it? Logically, the whole movie is a non-sensical mess not just the ending. The Wheeler's delayed choice experiment segment sounds like a "quantum frequency of water" level of misunderstanding of what the experiment actually shows. **Time travel is not possible** and claiming this experiment in anyway gives hope that one day it may be possible, or that it could somehow justify the magic black hole in the movie is disappointing. This movie has just about the same amount of science in it as Signs and just about as much magic, just slightly less biblical. Just accept that the movie is fiction with the aesthetics of science. I would be far less interested in people's take on this movie if it was treated more like Star Wars than like Cosmos.

text: I think it is possible that two planets have a difference of gravity as strong, therefore of time dilation as in the movie but not in this way. The difference in time dilation does not only depend on the mass and therefore on the gravitational force of the planet in question but on everything else! If two planets have exactly the same mass, but one is next to a black hole in the center of a galaxy, and the second planet is at the border of the galaxy, so much further away than the black hole, then there will be a real time dilation even if these two planets have the same mass. Because the first planet will be affected by the gravitational force of the black hole. So if two planets have more or less the same mass and therefore the same gravitational force, but if one is next to a black hole and the other one is not, then I think that it is possible that there is a real time dilation to the point that one hour on the world close to the black hole represents 7 years in the world that has no black hole next to it I believe that this is what happened in the movie because there was the black hole Gargantua next to this watery planet. But I don't claim to be right. It's just that I find it logical that for time dilation, the fact that one planet is next to a black hole and the other one is not has an impact even if both planets have the same mass.

This however, is not the case for Edmund's planet, it continues to run on its own time. Eventually, humans evolve into 5D beings on Edmund's planet and create the tesseract, once the tesseract was created, again, time is infinite and inconsequential as explained previously, allowing these 5D humans to manipulate time to their favour and interact with Cooper in different timelines (past and future, that's why there were 2 Coopers). Why did they choose Cooper to be the key person to enter the tesseract? Because Brand was the kickstarter of the human species on Edmund's planet and she must have relayed the information about Cooper's existence to the humans there before they evolved. Cooper then entered the tesseract, manipulated time to contact Murphy and pass the quantum data to her allowing her to solve the gravity equation, eventually saving the humans on Earth. Thus, to conclude, Cooper, by making the decision to go into the black hole and abandoning Brand to Edmund's planet, allowed the human species to restart and evolve on Edmund's planet, then the humans on Edmund's planet, made the decision to save Earth by manipulating time

author: @kaisokusekkendou1498
text: The ending "solution" inside the black hole makes sense to me in a certain way... I'd once watched a video on the physics of a black hole, explaining how it's essentially a flip on how our own reality works. We exist in a spatial dimension that is locked on a single course through time. However, once in a black hole, you are instead locked on a single course in spatial dimensions... and the math indicates that shifting your perspective, you'd be able to observe all time in the same way we travel freely in space. Note "observe", not interact. Where "love" comes into this is based on the two presumptions the movie makes (where we need to suspend our disbelief): 1. That Cooper and TARS could survive entering a black hole. 2. That something in the human consciousness was able to exert influence over this new form of dimensional experience. If we accept those things, then "love" will drive his sub-conscious to bring him to his daughter, to his one regret.. the moment he left her in that room. So in an infinite reality of time and space, his unique emotional background drove him to precisely where he could do something.. and trigger the final concession: that gravity can be influenced beyond space-time limits like a black hole. Since this is the concession that is basically the macguffin that resolves the main plot too, it's fine I think. Honestly, his going into the black hole and influencing time and space can mean this is a closed time loop scenario. There doesn't even have to be "special future humans" or "aliens"... it was literally Cooper going into the black hole, and his emotional subconscious, that spat out the wormhole and started this whole thing in the first place. His "hand passing through their ship going through the wormhole" at the beginning indicates his influence is in there somewhere. I feel it's a perfect resolution to a story of humanity that deals with hope, fighting in spite of despair, and an "I'll do it myself" gumption of a pioneering man of the land.

author: @quietfolk3920
text: As a movie enthusiast and a huge Nolan fan, I was a little disappointed, but very inspired. I think Nolan succeeded in what he wanted. When I stepped out of the theater, A LOT of people were screaming in amazement. Everyone was just so...touched by it, so awed, and I think that was what really makes the movie. For that reason, I think it should be getting higher praise, maybe not as a movie, but definitely for what its trying to do. However, I don't think many critics and serious movie enthusiasts will get it, because I feel like it was never meant to be the perfect movie we expected, its meant to be a spark to something beyond a movie. We were expecting a cinematic masterpiece, when it was reaching for something else. Don't just think about the movie you saw, think "the future of the human race." That, or Nolan was just not in his game :P I would also like to say that just because you couldn't understand the science in the dialogue, it doesn't make the movie bad. One of the main goals of the movie was to present a scenario with as much accuracy as possible, making its message about humans even more inspiring because its telling us that the amazing things we saw in the movie are very possible.

author: @aairahplays
text: What if Interstellar's "They" aren’t just future humans, but actually the evolved descendants (embryo's) of Brand’s colony on Edmunds’ planet? Think about it: Future humans helped Cooper so Murph could solve the gravity equation, leading to Cooper Station. But why? Because Cooper Station ensures that Cooper reaches Brand. And if Brand’s colony fails, They would never exist. Murph sending Cooper to Brand wasn’t just about love or closure—she knew Brand’s colony had to succeed. Surviving alone on a barren planet with only embryos would be incredibly difficult, and Cooper could be the key to making it work. By going to Brand, Cooper unknowingly ensured the future of humanity. So, They interfered to make sure events unfolded correctly. The entire cycle was about self-preservation. They ensured Earth’s people were saved, not just for survival, but so Cooper would eventually reach Brand and help establish the very civilization that would later intervene. This also means Plan B wasn’t a backup—it was always the real future. The loop is self-sustaining: Future humans exist because they made sure their own ancestors survived.
translated_text: What if Interstellar's "They" aren’t just future humans, but actually the evolved descendants (thembryofs) of Brand’s colony on Edmunds’ planet? Think about it: Future humans helped Cooper so Murph could solve the gravity equation, leading to Cooper Station. But why? Because Cooper Station ensures that Cooper reaches Brand. And if Brand’s colony fails, They would never exist. Murph sending Cooper to Brand wasn’t just about love or closure—she knew Brand’s colony had to succeed. Surviving alone on a barren planet with only thembryos would be incredibly difficult, and Cooper could be the key to making it work. By going to Brand, Cooper unknowingly ensured the future of humanity. So, They interfered to make sure events unfolded correctly. The entire cycle was about self-preservation. They ensured Earth’s people were saved, not just for survival, but so Cooper would eventually reach Brand and help establish the very civilization that would later intervene. This also means Plan B wasn’t a backup—it was always the real future. The loop is self-sustaining: Future humans exist because they made sure their own ancestors survived.

author: @stupor_mundi
text: Good video, good points! I thought it very thought-provoking how Nolan introduced love as a kind of powerful force with unique properties that trancends time and space. I recall other two movies that essentially brought forward the exact same idea in different ways: one is of course Contact, the other is The Village. Contact is somewhat comparable to Interstellar in more obvious ways than The Village, so there's no point going into it, but The Village [warning: spoilers from this point] ends with the ultimate conclusion that love is a powerful guiding and supporting force that should be trusted. We explicitly see that in the scene when Ivy's father justifies letting her leave the village to get life-saving medicine for Lucius, whom she loves, when he says "She's more capable than most of us... And she is led by love. The world moves for love, it kneels before it in awe." He's basically saying that despite her disability they should trust that love - as a powerful driving force and source of strength - would open the path for her success. And it did, against all odds. I know The Village gets a lot of flak, perhaps in the same way Contact does (or even Interstellar, to some extent) for introducing love into the equation, but to deny the power of love would be like cutting off an essential part of our humanity, the human experience, maybe even the meaning of life. I think Brand in Interstellar is onto something.

text: I remember watching Interstellar in the cinema and truly feeling like I was travelling in space through a wormhole to another system in another galaxy. Such a powerful experience. author: @Mystikan
text: The idea I got from the scenes inside the black hole is this: when you pass the event horizon, all paths lead to the singularity. At no point is it possible to get further away from the singularity, or even to remain at a constant distance from it. This means that the dimension of space in the direction of the singularity becomes timelike, so time as experienced outside the black hole must become spacelike. This means that he can move back and forth through time in the same manner he normally could through a given dimension of space - at least for as long as he has before he becomes spaghettified by proximity to the singularity, which is his inescapable future. So the "library" inside the black hole to me represented universal time as a spacelike dimension in which he could move at will, because his formerly spacelike path to the singularity had become his axis of time. This is what enabled him to travel back in time to his daughter's childhood and leave the message "STAY" on her bookshelf before he was crushed by the singularity.

author: @pjboyle8369
text: Amazing movie, one of my favourites. An aspect I really enjoy is the connection between the fight scene of Mann vs Cooper and the "first handshake". Mann says to Cooper, after the breaking of the helmet and subsequent slow suffocation, "Do you see your children?" - a common held belief that you see those you love as you are about to die; deathbed visions. Cooper, at that moment, is not having any vision because we know he is not dying. Later in the film, during the tesseract scene, when the message is sent to Murphy via the watch, the tesseract then closes. Cooper asks TARS, when the approaching collapse is upon him, "What happens now?" and a bright light surrounds him and gives the impression that his life is over. Of course, he then travels back through the wormhole, passing the Endurance on the way back, and reaches out, and takes Brand's hand. I often wonder why Cooper saw Brand, in his apparent "dying moments", and not another. With the recurring theme of love, I like to think that this is a reference to his love for Brand; an element confirmed in the Murphy and Cooper reunion where she says "You can go" and prompts him to seek Brand.

text: Two things I'd like to add; a fun observation and a theory: 1) The watch that Murph had was a Hamilton Field Khaki MECHANICAL watch. That's important, because if it was a digital watch, as you might expect in the future, there would have been no way for Cooper to relay the data for Murph to find. 2) So, Plan A, and presumably Plan B were both successful. My fun theory is that it WASN'T Murph's Plan A that lead to 4th Dimensional future humanity. Instead it was Plan B with Cooper, Brand, and their embryos. This is an interesting thought because A) it COULD mean that humanity effectively split into two different evolutionary paths, perhaps unbeknownst of each other. If these two humanities developed for 1000, or 10,000 of years separately and eventually found each other again, how different would they be? And B) because it could have meant Murph WASN'T who the future beings were counting on to save them. It was actually Cooper & Brand, contrary to Coopers "revelation" in the tesseract.

author: @michaelzoran
text: QUESTION: On Mann's planet, after Brand has rescued Cooper, we see Mann's base explodes. This apparently kills Dr. Romily and CASE. I have read online this happens because CASE was programmed with the truth about Dr. Mann's planet not being inhabitable, and that the security clearance that was needed from a person had a form of boobytrap that automatically triggered an explosion - which killed Dr. Romily (the person) and CASE (the robot that was boobytrapped by Dr. Mann). If that information is true, it is VERY COMPLEX and NONE OF IT was explained in the movie! ... Why was none of that explained in the movie? How were we supposed to know all of that simply from seeing Dr. Mann attack Cooper? My personal interpretation was nothing like that at all when I saw Dr. Mann attack Cooper. My personal interpretation was that Cooper learned Professor Brand had been lying to him about Plan A. As a result, Cooper planned to return to Earth with the ship in order to see his kids again. My personal interpretation was that Dr. Mann was being unselfish and was not willing to allow Cooper to place his personal selfish desire to see his kids ahead of what was best for the entire human species. My personal interpretation was that Dr. Mann had no choice but to make it seem like Cooper died in an accident, in order to save the entire human species with Plan B on Mann's planet - which Mann said was a healthy planet. My personal interpretation was that Dr. Mann was left with no choice but to attack Cooper, because Cooper's ship was needed on Dr. Mann's planet in order to help Plan B succeed. I cannot find any spot in the movie where it "says" or even "implies" that Dr. Mann "boobytrapped" the CASE robot. The movie does say Dr. Mann "was lying," but that could be about anything. It makes no mention of CASE being boobytrapped. And the movie even talks about how the CASE robot was destroyed, but didn't seem to care that Dr. Romily died, too. All of that was VERY CONFUSING, because it needed a LOT MORE EXPLANATION. ... Considering the movie is 2 Hours 49 Minutes long, the writers definitely SHOULD HAVE included that information. If there are scenes I did not interpret correctly or pieces of information I missed, please share them with me so I understand it better.

text: There are two things in the film that didn't gell for me. Firstly, it sets the beginning as a battle against the blight. Now I know that this was just a pretext to getting the characters into space, however it created a promise about what dilemma would be overcome, and failed to properly address it. Furthermore, what was resolved was the finding of a solution for quantum gravity, but we don't really understand how this solves what is essentially a resource problem. Linked to the resource problem, the whole distopian authoritarianism complete with information control felt like another unresolved problem promise (or perhaps something resolved off screen). These two problems were promptly forgotten about, in favour of a space adventure, with some newly manufactured problems to overcome, like Mann and the two failed planets. Had it started in the new system, these crises wouldn't have felt so manufactured. Secondly, apart from "love", why did Cooper need to go back? To put it another way, why did plan B need to continue? Humanity was already thriving in space back at Sol.

The vast majority of scientists are afraid to say "I do not know" because of peers. author: @chrisalex001
text: I'm sorry, but Interstellar was not a good movie. Encounters of the third kind was, even Inception (as dark as it was). The great acting did not deliver believable characters. That can only happen when the writing is bad. First of all, why would humanity leave its own planet for who knows what's outthere (even despite the accurately depicted dust storms caused by the erosion of the soil and atmospheric destabilization caused by global warming)? The whole tessaract thing was cool and very interesting, but Michael Cain was just not believable as a great scientist, not like Jack Lemmon was as a nuclear physicist in The China Syndrome or Gregory Peck as the director of NASA in Marooned, or Lindsay Crouse as a climate scientist in The Arrival (1996), or Jodie foster in Contact, or Helen Hunt in Twister, or Armand Assante as Odysseus in the 90s Odyssey, or Richard Harris as Dumbledore in Harry Potter and Sulla in 2002 Julius Caesar, or Richard Burton in Where Eagles Dare, or Brad Pitt, Brian Cox, and Peter O'toole in their respective roles in the movie Troy from the 2000s, should I go on? Matthew McConaughey acted very well, yet his savior role just didn't feel believable, not really. The movie felt like an exercise in great acting even if the audience can't truly identify why the strong emotions being felt are actually felt even with Hans Zimmerman's music. It's as if the audience felt strong emotions but does not really know why. Remember the last scene of Artificial Intelligence (Steven Spielberg)? Yeah, that kind of emotion is what I'm talking about. Also, Matt Damon (one of my favorite actors) acted very well, and his role should have been interesting on paper, and yet it wasn't. Anne Hathaway, who was the best character in my opinion, still felt like she was in the wrong movie. The movie remains very watchable because of its scientific accuracy (at least as close as it gets) but not the story. The movie simply did not convey the genuine believable emotions of a good story, not because of bad acting, but because of bad writing (including what most people would consider an exaggerated nitpick: the fact that when Cooper came to see an old Murph, his own family did not recognize him or wanted to know who he was, or the fact that he didn't ask about them. That might seem normal in this culture but extremely dysfunctional and abnormal in most other countries (I know what you'rethinking but actually having Cooper show much more interest in his descendants before being alone with Murph would have given the scene a far richer touch of authenticity. Great directing and writing often involves including the obvious and predictable but in extraordinary ways because genius is nothing more than taking the ordinary subtlyinto the extraordinary.. I just came to say all this. BTW, if you want a movie that transcends time (The Fifth Element)

author: @roddaman7545
text: @4:15: A thought, and I'll risk sounding like a Luddite: Time is merely context, the inevitability that one thing happens after another that orders events from a galactic scale to an atomic one. It is monolithic, unchanging, inflexible, the ultimate objective continuum. It is our experience of time and the measurement of time and the pace of all thing taking place within time, that changed with gravity (4:23) or speed. If time itself slowed, you would not be able to return to the world in the time you left behind. The atomic clock that falls behind could never be reunited with it's faster sibling because it would always be 2 or 3 seconds ahead. Just as I cannot know what is happening in 2 seconds or 2 days, the clock from 2 seconds ahead would not exist in the reality of now. The concept conveyed in Interstellar toys with the idea of a sort of hub of time, where one can enter from one spoke and exit onto another, thereby jumping over those 2 seconds or 2 days mentioned above or the decades conveyed in the film (although they use a library, not a wheel). Cooper uses this hub to send a message from his time/space to his daughter's. However, in our routine observations (like the Atomic clocks) , we only experience a change in the rate of temporal processes, not a slowing of time itself. In the movie when Cooper returns to find his daughter an old woman, it is merely the differences in the processes of time that is experienced. He is there, in THAT time, in that moment so time itself did not slow for him or accelerate for her. If it had, he would be stuck in the time he left or she stuck in the time that would be.
