author: @smakfu1375
text: Your conclusion is incorrect and illustrates a misunderstanding of space/time and General Relativity. The time dilation effect is a result of proximity to the mass of the supermassive blackhole, not the planet. Gravitational tidal forces, near or, theoretically, just beyond the event horizon, do not result in spaghettification or even a noticeable change (this is ONLY true for supermassive blackholes, "regular" mass blackholes have their event horizon's too close to the singularity, thus a stable environment at or near the event horizon is unlikely). It is even thought that there are potentially whole planetary systems that exist, in stable orbits, inside the event horizon. Nothing can escape from that point, back into the broader universe, but within that relatively stable "pocket" of space-time, just inside the event horizon, you could have stable orbits. Understand that on approach to Millers planet, the astronauts and their ship become part of a common orbital topology along with the planet. Their perceived gravity on the planet is a result of the mass of Miller's planet itself (which is more massive than earth), not the gravity of the blackhole. However, the entire orbital trajectory of Miller's planet is a result of the mass of the blackhole, around which it is circling (this is exactly the same mechanics at play with earth and our sun). The correct way to think of the relationship of an object orbiting a more massive body, is to imagine the more massive body deforming space/time in such a fashion that Millers planet is perpetually circling the blackhole, like an object circling a drain, but only infinitesimally inching closer to the object over time - they're, in an orbital fashion, "falling" towards that massive object. However, while the planet, and the astronauts on approach, and with their eventually landing, are all in a "stable" orbit of the super-massive blackhole, all those objects are still being influenced, by the space/time distortion of the blackhole, relative to earth (or their compatriots waiting for them beyond the distortive time-dilation effects of the blackhole). So yes, they got the science correct (though not the representation of the giant wave tidal effects, or the problem of how much energy their spaceship would require for escape velocity from the orbital path of Miller's planet - that's where they used some creative license, as one does not just easily escape that orbital trajectory when circling a supermassive blackhole).

text: This take had never even occurred to me. Thank you. I am a Jewish-raised atheist, so I have little use for traditional notions of "sin." However. I've though a lot about the sin of sloth lately - the only one that negatively impacts society. For sloth is indifference, apathy, cynicism, "not-in-my-backyard," political passivity, "not my problem." It is "my vote does not matter," or "it only encourages them," or "all politicians behave that way," or "I want to fight climate change but I also want cheap gasoline for my SUV I garage in a suburb accessible only by car." It is feeling defeated before your try. It is, oh, sure, one person can make a difference - if that one person has billions of dollars, super powers and/or alien technology. To which I say...horsefeathers! I never understood "snowflake" as a derogatory term, because if you combine enough snowflakes you get an avalanche. Society changes through millions of individual actions. For example, if every person picked up just one (net) piece of trash daily, that is a few billion pieces of trash taken off the streets every day. So, you are absolutely right about what INTERSTELLAR says. Think big. Think bold. Think...period. Do something constructive, however small. The Jewish yin to the "sin" yang is "mitzvah," a kind of Biblically-sanctioned good deed (613 are listed in the Old Testament). One is encouraged not simply not to be bad - that is a low bar - but to be actively good. This is the kind of positive action we need right, and what INTERSTELLAR told us was possible 10 years ago. Thank you, again.

text: I think that people labeling Nolans films as "cold" or lacking emotions maybe are watching them with preconceived ideas of modern films and how they are presented. Especially nowadays. They are used to characters (usually in ridiculous costumes) trauma dumping, or making stupid quips. They expect everything to be presented right up front and obvious. In my opinion, emotion is at the center of several of his biggest films. Grief and guilt is at the core of Inception. Fear and anxiety is the driving force behind Dunkirk. Just because the characters dont sit in front of the camera and talk to an audience as if in a therapy session doesnt mean there is no emotion. Nolan just chooses to write and direct in a different way to demonstrate it. The reactions and critiques of his films I think are more of a reflection of the cookie cutter, bland, predictable junk that the rest of Hollywood churns out seemingly every week. Are all of his films masterpieces? Of course not. But every one is a unique, singular vision by a director who seems intent on charting his own course.

author: @StevenMurray-b1s
text: I rank Interstellar as the third best science fiction movie ever made, behind only Alien and Blade Runner. I love the movie. My own viewing history of Interstellar is an interesting one. I saw it on the Saturday after it came out, which would be abnormal for me for a fall release since I am a Texas Aggie and never miss a football game. As it so happened, the Aggies on that Saturday were in the midst of a rather middling season, and were traveling to play at #3 ranked Auburn. I was 100% certain the Aggies would lose, so I opted to take my wife to the movie instead. I knew upon leaving the theater that early evening that I had just witnessed a truly great movie, but in that AMC theater there was a (alcohol) bar set up with a big screen TV. I saw there was a game on, so I ventured in that direction to see what game - yep, it was A&M at Auburn. The Aggies were winning with roughly 6 minutes to play. There was a literal snap where my attention redirected immediately, and I literally forgot everything about the movie in that moment. While the Aggies did in fact win that game, I had forgotten the movie until months later, when I bought the BluRay disc. Watching it at home, the entire emotion of the movie came back to me. I've watched it many times on TV over the years, and then two years ago when they re-released it for its 10th anniversary, I returned to a theater to see it again. It was a great experience that felt like seeing it for the first time again.

author: @FirstLast-vb1re
text: Though I am not a Bat-person, and do not wish to become one, I have admired Christopher Nolan for his early films and 'Inception', though, with the exception of 'Insomnia', I always regarded them as, in the immortal words of Andrew Sarris 'less than meets the eye'. I do not like to call films pretentious, but with 'Memento' and 'Inception' the word certainly came to mind. They seemed shallow pretending to be deep. Yes, it carries you along for a ride, and yes the special effects are great, and yes, it might give us pause to think what will, in fact, be the destiny of our species. So living on Fuck would probably feel maddening because everything would feel slow, and returning to Earth would feel disorienting as it all feels too fast.

text: I don't believe that time is the fourth dimension…Imagine a one dimensional point displacing in one axis. A two- dimensional being “sees” the point…is aware of what it really is…just a point. The 2D being perceives the point in motion…but cannot sense it’s true trajectory (the point could move diagonal to the 2D observer but the 2D observer can only perceive it’s movement to the left or right). The observer’s 2D existence only empowers him to see the one dimensional creature’s spatial nature or “spatial possibility” (true form) but not his “temporal possibilities” or “true time-line”….he cannot predict the position of the point in space and time. To be able to perceive the one-dimensional creature’s “temporal possibilities” the 2D creature must look the one-dimensional creature from a three-dimensional world or universe. The 2D object could try to “move around” in his 2D world to try to track the trajectory of the 1D creature…but the 2D creature’s own movement will only further distort his perception of the one dimensional creature’s direction and speed. Again…only a creature two dimensions higher (three dimensional) can see it’s true trajectory …predict it’s position in time-space. This can be proven by imaging a point moving in a sheet of paper in one direction…we that live in a 3D world or “universe” can very easily see it’s “time-line”…we see where the point was…where the point is…and where the point will be. Let’s go one dimension higher this time… We in a three-dimensional world look at a 2D creature moving in a 2d plane (for example a triangular creature) …since it is two-dimensional we can obviously perceive his complete “spatial possibilities” or” true complete form” but since it moves in two axes (can turn around… move straight etc.) we cannot perceive it’s full “temporal possibilities” or trajectory in time and space. Again this happens because we are dimensionally limited to perceive it. Only a person living in a fourth dimension…orthogonal to our 3D world… can see the full time-line of the 2D creature (again it needs to be two dimensions higher). Let’s put it in a basic formula or axiom… The “full spatial possibilities” or true form of an X dimensional element can be perceived by an observer living in an 2X dimensional world or “universe” But the “full temporal possibilities” or “true time-line” of X dimensional creatures can only be completely perceived by a creature living in a 3X dimensional world or “universe”. This means that we, as 3D creatures… to be able to see our complete “temporal possibilities” or “time-line” (past, present and future of any person on earth and any part or our 3D universe)… We must be seen from a fifth dimensional world . In purely dimensional terms of course …this could be one of the basic principles….for Time Travel

text: Neil deGrasse Tyson is humoring a movie that he clearly knows is inaccurate. The film suggests that future humans, who have transcended spacetime, are responsible for the events that unfold in this film. A human being who exits his universe into a higher dimension does not gain dimensions. He would still only be able to move in three directions, and he would still see in two dimensions, therefore he could not possibly intervene with our timeline, let alone construct and infinite bookshelf. In simpler words for you pubescent children to understand: if you tear a sticker of a basketball off a sheet of paper, does it become a sphere in your hand? Overall a terrible script carried by incredible acting talent and amazing visual effects, and a memorable attempt at portraying elements of quantum theory.

text: Whoa, whoa, whoa, whoa, wait: “Humans can’t live on space stations forever?” “Water and other resources will run out?” That makes no sense. text: Everything Dr. Tyson says makes perfect sense. But as others have observed Interstellar is a science fiction movie. About the only part of it that I found really fantastic was the scene when Matthew McConoughey is dragged into the black hole and survives. This is a fantasy. I am not a cosmologists so I cannot say whether details about the singularity in the center of a black hole are actually necessary to unify the theories of gravity and quantum mechanics but I suppose it could be. Ultimately I was happy to suspend my disbelief about some aspects of the movie in order to enjoy it. I was not disappointed.

author: @GarrettBodman
text: The only way to research time is look honestly at your direct experience of it... If you do, you must realize that what we call one moment and another do not occur in different times but share the exact same space of NOW. Right now at this precise instant, watch your experience, and try to notice the passage of time... if you're honest, you'll notice that what we call the past is only a memory or snapshot saved in the mind of what this moment looked like. There are no two moments. There is One single Moment, in which objects move and change within space in relation to each other, which creates our experience of linear time. Just like how the light in the movie theater projects upon the screen and creates the appearance of movement and linear sequence. The screen remains untouched and still, while the images dance upon it. It's the same with life... the Now is in fact absolutely timeless and eternally immediate... it has never and will never change... it is the space or consciousness in which this dream of existence arises and passes away. We are like fish in the sea looking for the ocean.... completely blind to the fact that we're being held by the One Moment of Eternity... or the Womb of God... Alpha and Omega.

text: I had a few issues with the movie , especially with their take on time dilation as it relates to what’s actually going on in the movie. For example after the ranger is hit by the giant wave on Millers planet and they can’t start it right away. Brand says that they’re going to lose decades relative to the people back on Earth. And when they finally return to the Endurance Romilly says they’ve been gone 23 years since the day they left for Millers planet. However what actually happens in the scene when they’re on Millers Planet doesn’t depict them being there for more than a half an hour, maybe an hour tops. And I’m not talking about the length of the scene. I’m talking about the events that unfold in the scene. It’s one continuous series of activities. They fly down, they get out, and they walk around for about 3 or 4 minutes before they see the wave coming. After the wave hits the ship Cooper yells at Brand. Then they have a five minute conversation while they’re waiting for the engines to dry out which Case said would take 45 minutes to an hour. Two minutes after that, they figure out a way to spark the engines and fly off. There is never a gap of time that is unaccounted for or something that suggest they were on that planet for more time then what’s portrayed in that scene. So so going by what actually happens in the scene at best they should’ve be gone about 3.5 / 4 years not 23

That moment, that sequence with that music and the sound just blasting. Sensory Overload...I will never forget the experience

author: @EchelonBlueAlt
text: Sarom mentions that the events are closed time loop. Not for those who are in Edmund's colony - their lives continue on. The real thing is that because Cooper and Brand take the risks they took, they make the future possible that occurs. The events that led to the tesseract, the gravity equation, and the wormhole - THOSE events are linear and are set in stone, because they already happened. the best way to represent it is all of the characters in Interstellar are on a road, in their vehicle, traveling on a set path. Everyone else - everyone on Earth, who did not interact with those in the vehicle, their lives are not linear and are free to diverge away from the events taking place on the road. All of the characters in the road, in the vehicle - can only go where the road goes. In short, it's not a loop, it's a straight path, and everything else curves around them. The discoverers of the fifth dimensional knowledge crafted everything so that it would be Cooper, his daughter, Brand, and all the key players... who had to take the car trip down that road. Right down to it being cooper who ended up in the tesseract - because the future knew of the importance of the bond between Cooper and his daughter. THAT bond, had to take place. without it... Earth dies, not just humanity - EARTH - all that stuff that goes with them on the space station... and then, when Cooper and his daughter part ways... the relationship between Cooper and Brand takes precedence. Without that bond, the future of humanity dies.

text: Interstellar was the only Nolan brothers' film I didn't really clicked with, but the re-released made me realized how the film is becoming more relevant now than 10 years ago. There are too many themes explored making it clunky, but at it's core, Interstellar is a film about optimism for the future possibilities. Accepting how the world can be destructive, but not giving into the pessimism or passitivity. That we should think about humanity, but also continue to strive for ourselves and loved ones. Without both, we'll just be left with hopelessness and apathy. It made me feel much more optimism about our own world despite how self destructive we have become.

author: @kristjanveski
text: Cooper's death is an excellent theory and one that totally fits with that which is portrayed in the film, and what is left for us viewers to decide, in the typical Nolan-ambiguous-ending fashion. To further the theory presented, the simple fact that he becomes the "ghost," and a guardian angel type guide to his daughter, lends to this theory of his death in the black hole. Everything post-event horizon can definitely be his visions and experience during death, and entering his own version of heaven, just as with the ending of Inception, when Cobb is finally back with his kids (which perhaps Mann had alluded to.) He falls through the tesseract and is then suspended, in limbo, with one task to complete before moving on. He must send the data (the message) to save Murph (humanity), and while that is going on, fields are burning, there is chaos and doom abound, an almost apocalyptic scene, Let's not forget the entire movie has thick religious undertones; the organ symphony as a soundtrack is an obvious clue. It is a mix of religious and scientific belief, what we have faith in and what we can prove. It is enjoyable at face value, and epic when dissected and studied.

text: I still feel like it's meant to hint at a much bigger backstory behind who "they" are. Right before the Tessaract closes, Cooper says doesn't just say that it's humans that evolved beyond 3 dimensions. He say's *it's us*. The whole reason why they bothered to save humanity is because the Endurance mission is why they exist. After Brand lands on Edmund's world, the colony she builds from scratch is destined to become "them". Following the scientific knowledge and mindset Dr. Brand brought with her, the colony blooms. Unimpeded by whatever constraints we held here on Earth, they begin to explore and study Gargantua; ultimately gaining a total understanding of what lies beyond the event horizon. One of those things that they learn is how to manipulate and access all of space and time. In order to exist, they are destined to help humanity reach the gargantua system. So they get to work constructing a wormhole between the Solar and Gargantua systems, and give Cooper access to their tesseract. In return they provide Cooper with both the data to understand how gravity works, a means to deliver it to Murph so she could save humanity, and a trip back home so he could see his daughter one last time.

author: @datmeme8967
text: From the beginning of time, great stories were always about more than the superficial plot. A great film is no different even hough many today only want to skim across the surface. This review gets at that, and I really appreciate it. I never really sat and thought about it but the ending being Cooper's own "heaven" makes a lot of sense. I remember thinking how implausible a lot of the third act was – ending up near Saturn, getting found before running out of air, them recreating a space station to look like his home town, his family basically ignoring him and him leaving his daughter on her death bed, no security around space ships capable of interstellar journeys, etc.... It only makes sense if this is what he wanted in his mind and what he gets after being spagettified by falling through the event horizon of a black hole. There was some insulting nonsense in this film, but the ending, in light of this review, is actually pretty great.

author: @agpmjm
text: With respect - this is way overthinking the story. The science of relativity/ different personal time rates was explored in a fun way. The film makers were also telling a story, and had to give an emotionally satisfying conclusion to the story arc. It rather neatly answered the `ghost` question while at the same time satisfying our desire for a happy ending. Sure the tesseract bit was outlandish, but otherwise we would have merely had a scene of Cooper being ripped apart by the Black Hole gravity. Hardly a satisfying end. The final thread- being reunited with his now aged daughter - was basically inevitable, and ignoring the other family members worked well because they would have just overloaded the central theme of Cooper and his daughter being reunited. Even the brevity of the scene worked - how to end a tear-fest scene otherwise ? Great film

author: @billparker244
text: I don't remember this movie having a significant amount of confusion with the ending. Early on, they comment several times about suspecting aliens having put the wormhole within humanity's reach during a critical and apocalyptic moment. There's even talk of how these aliens might transcend time and space by existing in a different dimension and being unable to communicate with us by any natural means. Thus, they can only make themselves known to us by performing certain deeds. Not that they may either care nor be uncaring about communication. They just saw a terrible problem, knew how to fix it, and provided the necessary reality to help us, and knew that we would help ourselves if given the opportunity. At the end of the movie, Cooper falls into the black hole and all is revealed. Up until this point, the ghost in his daughter's bedroom was unexplained. But, you figured it had something to do with these theoretical aliens. Which is what it turned out to be. A black hole, having all these unexplained scientific principals having to do with time and space (which are the same thing), was a place where they could more easily or naturally manifest themselves and their abilities. They created or provided a time nullifying apparatus to Cooper so that he could send the vital information that humanity required to survive. Maybe because he was the only one or, maybe they could detect his immense love for his daughter. Maybe "love" is an essential or special aspect of the universe that transcends time and space. These aliens might have required Cooper to have so much love for his daughter in order to give him the tools to communicate with her. OR for him to be noticed by the aliens in the first place. That's a subtle and intelligent delivery vehicle for the message the movie is trying to tell us in my opinion. The scene where his extended and unfamiliar family almost completely ignores him is definitely the weirdest part of the movie. You'd think they'd all want an autograph at least. I'd have to chalk that up to a story teller (the director, i guess) wanted a specific scene and he shut everyone out and just kept telling them to ignore the incongruity and make it happen. Outstanding movie and wonderfully executed for the most part. I really enjoyed it.

author: @pauldh62
text: This is a compelling and perplexing film that I never tire of watching. Part of my problem is that I have only ever seen it on long haul flights to Kenya and the sound quality isn't brilliant. On the one hand I never cease to well up when Cooper has to leave his daughter and the real strength is that love transcends all which is great. On the other, he meets his daughter for barely three minutes after a separation of most of her lifetime, leaves with that love intact and blithely swans off to pursue an unconvincing romantic attachment somewhere in the galaxy. While much of the film seems to pride itself on observing scientific theory, particularly physics within the confines of this universe, it goes out on a leap, using a convenient worm hole and has the heroes explore rather uninteresting worlds in a doomed galaxy - it's orbiting a blackhole, so game over, plus Cooper goes hurtling into this unchartered anomaly to emerge unscathed and does not become the crushed spaghetti one is believed to become if one was ever able to effect so suicidal a manoeuvre. In addition, just what was the answer to overcoming the question they were searching for? My understanding was that there was no answer, so when this revelation occurred it made no sense.

text: My take on this film is the next one: Cooper did save humanity. He didn't die, in fact he was alive at the end. He was right about the fact that the worm hole and the tesseract where placed by humans and not aliens. Those humans that placed the worm hole and the tesseract where "Plan B" and where long distance descendants of the endurance crew, that built humanity knowing that the "original" humans sophocated on earth without any chance of hope, while they lived and continued humanity's existance. At a certain point, these humans transcended and evolved, pretty much the same way the first organism did on planet earth, and eventually discovered how the laws of phisics worked for them to interact with them, learning to see time on a physical plain and gravity the same way. They knew that the humans of "Plan A" couldn't survive in their timeline, so they made the tesseract and placed it in the past, the moment where the endurance mission was taking place. As the evolved species that they were, they understood that you can't go back in time and chance things in their plain of reality, the only thing you could do is interact with time to create different versions of reality that dont affect yours, in other words, timelines (otherwise a paradox would be created making the decision of placing a tesseract imposible). So humans of the original timeline (Plan B humans, very evolved species) created a different timeline for humans of Plan A to survive as well. Even though both transcended humans and humans from Plan A will never actually meet, they gave them a chance to escape their sophocating fate and look for their place among the stars in (tecnically) another universe. Why cooper and why not any other event or person? Well probably humanity of Plan B (evolved humans) grew up and lived their lives looking up to this hero demigod known as Cooper that saved humanity when he reached Edmonds planet and colonized it with Brand, after all, they where the literal "fathers" of the new human civilization. As they knew how to interact with time the way Brand explained "they could watch it as we watch the Grand Canyon" they probably went to see how Cooper's life was before everything and they saw the inmense love Cooper and Murph held for each other and they concluded that the turning point that would mean human survival as a whole was them. they concluded that the best chance they had to "save" humanity with Plan A, was through making both Cooper and Murphy interact throught space and time, fueled by their unparalled love and solve the equation and save all humanity in this new timeline. The whole movie takes place in an alternate timeline, the one where all humanity is saved, while the timeline in which the transcended humans live is the original one, where earthlings had to die for Plan B to take place and therefore lead to the events of the movie.

I don't understand how the ending isn't straightforward I guess is my point.

author: @Vishnudasdasdas
text: The movie focused from the perspective of MConaughhey's character, what he experienced, both physically and mentally. It was a story of his transition from the life he knew to a new life, after his death, of a world made up of all his thoughts - mainly of his daughter and his love for her, as well as his great hope for the salvation of humanity. The rest is all just supplementary, incidental, the apparent theme, plot, the illusions of science and mathematics, the Tesseract, the deflections from what really matters, which is intentional to throw us off etc. The idea is to show us in first person one man's experience of what no one else could have seen but him, just as we all have personal stories to tell that only we have each personally experienced alone. As the 'Bhagavad Gita - As It Is' states, "Whatever you think of at the time of death, that state you will attain without fail".

text: Interesting premise. I never thought of it before, but it does make some sense now that you mention it --- the whole everything after he entered the tesseract being an afterlife experience. It is reported by a lot of cultures that after one's death, a soul can end up in any of an infinite # of dimensions where the soul spends time living in "their own version of heaven --- or hell; or something in between that is based on their belief system while they were incarnate. Maybe he's in an afterlife realm where he is allowed to live out the outcome he desired --- whether it happened or not in the reality he was in when he was life. And all the near-death experience allusions --- the light at the end of the tunnel as illustrated from the design of the space station; seeing important scenes from one's life --- while in the tesseract re-witnessing the last moment he was with his daughter before he left on his mission. And I ALWAYS thought it was very odd that none of Murphy's re-acted to Cooper in a normal way when he entered the room to see her. But I just always rationalized it away as, maybe they knew Murphy didn't have much time, and since it was HER father, they better not waste any of that time with pleasantries and asking him questions since he WAS their mainly for her. But I still always struck me as odd that no one ever said anything to him. But now that you mention the whole near-death/ aftelife premise, maybe it was a merging of both their deaths. Maybe Cooper died after being spit out of the Tesseract and Murphy didn't actually die til years later in her time-space, but because of the Time Bending laws of the tesseract, it allowed Cooper's last death wish to see his daughter, merge with Murphy's last wish to see her father and it was a blending of both their experiences. Maybe he didn't see the family members at all cuz that was part of his reality and Murphy did because it was part of hers. OR, you know how when people are near death, they start talking to people (especially already deceased loved ones) that nobody else in the room, but they can see. Maybe that's why when Cooper walked into the room, everyone turned in his direction, but didn't say anything to him. Not because he wasn't their, but because Murphy was the only one who could see him, and in their reality, they were just turning in his general DIRECTION because Murphy, in the last throes of death turned in that direction cuz SHE could see him, and they just turned in that direction as well to try and see what she was looking at, but of course, couldn't see what she saw because they weren't near death, so therefore the veil that allowed Murphy to see in the Spirit realm hadn't been lifted for them to see Cooper. IDK. Just piggy-backing off of your theory trying to make sense of it. Aside from the fact that time had passed differently for Cooper while in space, which could account for him still looking the same age as when he left earth, another theory could be that as also explained in many near-death experiences where people meet deceased loved ones, they often see the person as they were the LAST time they were seen alive. And in some cases, they are seen as being younger than they actually were when they died --- what they looked like in their prime. There have been some cases where people saw people in the afterlife who claimed to be a relative the living person knew in life, but the living person can't immediately recognize them cuz they look like a stranger in their 20's/30's or even a child. But then the being reverts into an older person --- like a grandparent or something and then the person recognizes them, and the "dead" person explains that in this realm they always appear young because aging doesn't occur there. But that is more rare. Usually they appear as you last remembered them. Or in the form you last remember them without being sick or injured. Again. Just a theory. And I'm no scientist by any stretch of the imagination, and time travel movies/theories have always made soup of my brain when trying to understand them, but even those theories make sense only up until the end of the movie when you see that Anne Hathaway's character, Brandt, is still alive on the new planet. So if Cooper is dead, why is he flying back to her?? If she is indeed still alive and he is dead, he can't go back to her. Not physically anyway. Maybe the last shoot we see of Brandt is her accepting the fact that she is gonna have to raise this colony alone because Cooper is definitely dead. Accept WE as the audience don't know if he is really dead or not because he is flying back. IDK. I like this movie a lot, and I like movies that make you think, but all of the thinking in the world can't explain this ending. It's still too open for interpretation. And open-ended endings work OCCASIONALLY in movies, but for the most part, they just end up leaving you mind-fucked, cuz as you say, the open-endedness can be seen as the writer's lazy way of digging themselves out of a hole they created for themselves with too many plot twists that conflicted with one another. Hell, one Nolan brother even threw the onus for explaining the ending on the other brother, and then when that brother was confronted about an answer, he acted like either he didn't know himself, or he just didn't want to tell because having open-ended movies seems so avant garde and "clever." I know, because I've watched interviews with the Nolan brother who made the ending that ended up on the screen. He really doesn't give any clarification as to what the ending truly meant. I just wanna know what happened in the end, dammit. Definitively.

text: This film seems like it came out only weeks ago. It is especially timely given the horrible smoke season we endured here in California, and the sense that things in the earth's environment are speeding up as global warming sets in. Beautiful film, made about 4 years before its time. As I took my N95 facemask off after carrying my children into the house from a car ride through dust and smoke, I recalled that Interstellar's film trailer had a scene just like that. It was that little detail that led me to watch this film!

text: I'm about to write a book here into the comment section... Just give me enough *time*... Firstly, the film is just... Unbelievable... My English doesn't allow me to describe it. It's amazing, terrifying, strange, sad... and almost realistic. These kind of sci-fi films make me think about the theme. I can mention 2: Jurassic Park 1 and Interstellar. The things in both films are... really almost possible. But there's no way for this to happen still. I could explain easily, why JP is almost possible but still not, but as we know almost nothing about space, Interstellar is even harder to explain. So thank you for trying to do it I guess. Cooper may have died in the black hole, in a very brutal way if the thing science thinks about the holes is real... Stretching continuously and then... 😨😮😱 I wrote "time" in bold because one of the main problems in the film is the time. If you watch, you will get it (I'm telling for those who haven't seen it). But actually, they say they wasted about 30 normal years on the ocean planet. But they said, 1 hour on the surface is 7 normal years. But even by messing around with the engine as they couldn't take off before the wave came, they didn't waste more than 5-10 mins I think... So Murph should've became just a few years older. Back to the starting, I really liked how realistically the ship launch looked like. And the ship, and the station itself. I know, how real manned crafts look like, so I know the ship wasn't an actual space shuttle or something. But I loved how they tried to make it look like it works like the real ships, they cared about physics. Unlike other sci-fi, like Star Wars, etc. Even sometimes there was no sound if we were looking things from outside. We even saw a soundless explosion. In space, there's no air. So there can't be sound. And without air, there are no explosions. Still, the station blew up, as it does contain oxygen. Wow, a sci-fi film that does give a shit about physics! Sadly it's very rare. And those RCS thrusters on the side of the craft... That lander reminded me of space shuttles. Even it was black and white colored. 😂 Now back to time... we haven't yet gone into a black hole, and if we would do so, it's very unlikely for us to get out, and - manage to survive. So we will never know, if "shrinking" or "stretching" time is possible. Unless we can once send a space probe into the hole that does not get destroyed and keeps being able to send the data back to us. This "time manipulating by a black hole" could be logical but that would change a few things, we would need to find new physical laws or something. Light is a very interesting thing. If we would travel away from Earth going faster than light, we would probably see how it looked in the past. But we have 2 problems: 1st, how do we travel faster than light? 2nd, if we do so, we leave the Earth far away so we couldn't really see anything on it, even with the best telescope that exists. And this would also end fatally, if we would crash into something, going faster than light... In the case of black holes, even light turns or something... But light is just light. So after going close to a 'hole, and getting back to Earth, what do we see? And what can we... touch? Ok I asked this question terribly, cuz I wrote too much already. In the "wave planet", they move in quite slo-mo... But we see it like it's in real time as the black hole influences evetything. The camera also. Taking a step took them a few years. Even physics slowed down. In the black hole, everything slowed down again. Even tho the hole centre was the periapsis, where the body goes the fastest if in orbit, it slowed down. Because everything slowed down. Time slowed down. This is nonesense if we think about what we know about the physics. "Time is relative." But is time an actual thing? If yes, the "what happens to us when close encountering a black hole-theory" is correct. But time doesn't seem like a physical thing, you can't touch it but you talk about it every day. author: @Moodie111
text: At 10:23 you say that Cooper Station was a conical station with an end open to the sun. WRONG! What was depicted in the movie was an improved O'Neill cylinder with an artificial sun positioned at one end. I say "improved" because Gerard O'Neill's original cylindrical space colony design wasted half the internal land area with enormous clear windows (along with equally enormous external mirrors) designed to allow natural sunlight to enter the habitat as it rotated. The colony shown in the movie reclaimed that area by using an extremely intense internal light source as an artificial sun, which (presumably) would travel from one end of the station to the other to simulate the changing light of daytime, and being extinguished at night. But the colony was NOT conical.

author: @apexconnexion
text: I would highly recommend everyone watch Hans Zimmer and Christopher Nolan's discourse on how they set out to build the atmospheric soundtrack for this film. There is a zenith in their discussion when they finally realize how to tie the orchestral weight to this grandiose science fiction film. Zimmer said something to the effect of, "I realized the driving force for the music is not a story about the frontier of space, but about a father and his daughter." I'm not a father nor a daughter and I still felt an immense emotional connection to what this movie offered. Not to mention, it's about space - my favorite.

author: @WillN2Go1
text: Love will find a way....Nice, and sure I can appreciate this, but the way it's handle is inevitably trite. The writer's ending where we're left in doubt about if he got the info to his daughter or did she figured it out? Well, okay. But add or cut a few seconds and you change the entire meaning: is it a loop, or isn't it? Consider Anna Kerenina. Cut any chapter, any scene, any event in Anna Kerenina and you still have the same story about how society can crush a good person. Even her suicide if it were eliminated (I'm not saying to replace it with a happy ending.) Just if she were left at the train station trapped in her situation, no way out, unable to see any way out... She's not just at the train station so she can crawl under the train, the train can take you anywhere, and Anna doesn't know where she can go. If the Nolan's had written it, it would be whether or not she sees her son in a carriage or not.... Cooper's 'death dream'. Yep, he's a ghost. All the ghost movie clues. Cute. So I guess this is the Disney version of the end of 2001? I think the next Christopher Nolan movie I watch I'm going to skip the last 10 minutes, and avoid 'explanation' videos. That way I can appreciate it and enjoy it more. Do we really need a scene where after the incredible experience the character ends up back in his driveway? I'm not bashing the video. It's great and I think you make all your points really well.

author: @chris_brenan
text: Yep 👍 great movie. I'd argue that, while the Tesseract is obviously super Sci fi, it's not non-sensicle. A large enough black hole (granted, the way Gargantua is portrayed I don't think it is, but work with me here, things needed to be on a small solar system scale for the story to happen...) can have very gentle tidal forces at its event horizon. The tidal forces of a small black hole will rip you apart, but not huge ones, because the event horizon is further away from the singularity/has a much larger radius. This means you really could survive crossing the event horizon of a large black hole. I think the biggest issue is that communication should be impossible inside the event horizon, and sight could only be "looking out" not "looking in" precisely because once inside the event horizon, nothing can ever move *any* further out than it is, only inward. But if you embrace that the Tesseract is not natural but a construct of extra-dimensional being who can manipulate gravity, then I think it only requires embracing the story, not technically suspension of disbelief.

In short, while it’s possible that these beings are descendants of those brought up by Dr. Brand’s efforts, the movie leaves it open to interpretation, focusing more on the idea that humanity's survival leads to this advanced future.

author: @a.thiago3842
text: I got to know more aboout Kip Thorne after watching Interstellar. I like to draw, but i didn't know i could draw a ''space theme''. So this movie gave me this and millions of questions. I also guess i always loved astronomy. But Interstellar was one of the most important movies i ever watched, caused it made me search for even more deep facts about our ''reality'' and how the universe behaves. It's definitely not just a sci-fi movie at all. Well, i can always confirm that whenever i see people talking about it. There's always something special to talk about it. And Neil forgot to say, but Kip's black hole calculations are the most perfect calculations ever made till now. Scientists use his calculations to confirm that it's the closest we have from a real black hole. In the movie, they had to skip a lot of real black hole phenomens, so the Miller's planet would fit better on screen. I see this interview as a tribute, let's say, because you don't get too many videos of Kip T. talking about such detailed stuff about his life and so on. He's also a important connection we lost with great scientist who unfortunatelly already has passed away. And i don't think everyone thinks about that. I'm sure he won't read that, but, Kip T, thanks to you, learning about science is something exciting. Thanks to Neil, science is spread all over different social levels and levels of knowledge, just like people from my country (Brazil) does. I could talk about black holes, space and etc. But i'll never have the minimum level of intelligence to talk about even the most simplest math expressions that could explain even the most simple fenomena in space.So that's why this is so important!

author: @utgfy
text: One big plot contradiction: Cooper BOTH spells out "stay" in Morse code for Murph to convey to him, AND gives the coordinates for the NASA site where he needs to go to take part in the mission. Conflicted much, Coop? The second move, moreover, creates an irresolvable temporal paradox that would rip a hole in the fabric of spacetime: Cooper could not transmit the coordinates unless he went on the mission, but he could not go on the mission unless he had the coordinates (of the miraculously local NASA station whose coordinates he had memorized--gee, how convenient!) The same paradox holds for the tesseract: humanity could not have survived without it, but humanity needed to survive in order to make it. However, these temporal paradoxes are ultimately far less troubling than the other logical and emotional contradictions of the film, a few of which you point out (like the conveniently forgotten brother, the cringe-worthy (however much it is justified later) 'love transcends' speech, or the 3 minutes of blathery talk after 80 so soul-crushingly painful years apart.) Though entertaining and engaging while watching, Interstellar just doesn't hold up well on reflection. In the final analysis, it's a bunch of overplayed, empty sentimental pap about "love," "family" and "duty" in a dreadfully forced plot, without much substance, grounding, or depth.

author: @CRHall-ud9mq
text: Thanks JoBlo Videos. I enjoyed watching, since it also leaves some room for viewers to comment, adding to the explanation you offer; as I'd like to... I'd like to share my personal take is that the end of the film explains a moral that is woven into the fabric of the film from the beginning, which becomes the viewers past, towards fruition and enlightenment at the end. Messages are repeated throughout. Brand waits on a planet that appears to represent Cooper's future and fulfilment and, where love has put the past to rest (there were 3 planets, possible futures); it could be said that planet is love, the answer to man kinds survival. At Cooper's daughter's death bed, his daughter says she is letting him go and tells him Brand awaits him, in a distant galaxy. In death we travel alone, as we may through our memories to reconcile our past; as happened with characters Brand, Cooper and his daughter. Romiley is able to receive messages from Earth, now in the their past, but unable to send back, hints that we can't affect the past, but our choices in the present do affect the future. Dr Mann on the uninhabitable planet, twists the truth in fear of his own death. Other than all the descriptions of humanity played out in the film, including man kind's greed having caused their world's demise and, Brand's father pushes hope, actually it is love that saves them, that goes beyond space and time; it explains that love is the equation that provides the answer to every human dilemma. Brand says, "Listen carefully, we didn't invent love..."; I believe she suggests we may be love, in which we base our present choices, to change our future destination and transcend our past.

author: @andrewmendelson5207
text: The filmmakers consulted scientists so everyone thinks it was so scientifically accurate, but it was laughable at best. From Cooper saying "I'll just loop around that quasar," to a wormhole appearing near the orbit of Jupiter (and somehow not destroying the entire solar system, not to mention the characters somehow knowing where it led), to the impossibility of surviving crossing the event horizon of a black hole and then miraculously escaping it, not to mention surviving the radiation of being in close orbit of it (we wouldn't survive a close orbit of Jupiter FFS), to the idea that human technology wouldn't have progressed from the start of the movie to the end, 40 years later, while our own real-world technology has advanced at an exponential rate over the past 40 years and completely transformed our daily lives, all of it is absurd. Sadly, in their attempt to create a ridiculous melodrama, they completely missed many opportunities to incorporate real science in creative ways. We will look back on this film and cringe.

text: I RARELY, if ever, watch movies more than once, even if I actually enjoyed them. I don’t get as engaged or drawn in to a film that I’ve already seen and my ADHD brain gets distracted within the first few minutes and next thing I know it’s been an hour and I haven’t paid attention to a single moment. It’s just a waste of my time. However, on the extremely rare occasion that I see a film that I genuinely, powerfully, emotionally am moved by, I can watch it repeatedly (within reason of course). Interstellar is one of those rare films that I truly enjoy watching over and over. Every time I see it, I notice something different or learn something new that I missed in the previous occasions. The science of Interstellar was so fascinating and the fact that it was genuine and scientifically sound made it that much more extraordinary! Being that I’m a total space nerd and I have a better than average understanding of physics and astronomy than most, I can be quite critical of films that are ridiculously impossible scientifically. The movie Contact was one that I had to stop watching in the first few scenes because the main character was LISTENING to the radio telescopes in real time at the SETI observatories. RADIO IS NOT SOUND! IT IS LIGHT! The radio waves that people associate with their car stereo and whatnot are not sound waves. The audio information is encoded in the radio light waves and transmitted to a receiver that converts the signal into an audible sound playing in your car. She was sitting there with headphones on at the radio observatory! The blatant betrayal of simple concepts of basic physics was too much for me to handle. I shut it off. Interstellar however was superb and amazing! 🎉I think I’ll watch it again tonight

author: @92up7
text: I also had an issue with another planet being a solution and for a similar reason. How does going to another planet fix any issue with plants? Like, the one thing they shouldn't find is organics safe to eat. So, they would have to bring the plants they will grow with them. When I watched to movie I remember taking issue with this but than being satisfied because I thought the problem was with earth's atmosphere. That yes there was a blight with the plants but it wasn't because of the plants themselves but the water cycle or some other serious issue on earth. IT MUST BE! If the problem was with the plants than changing planets is no fix. Also, another reason it has to be with the planet, an external reason, is because it's affecting all plants. I seem to remember them talking about trying different more hearty crops at the start that cooper realizes is no solution. Furthermore, a biodome on earth would indeed have troublesome scaling issues for the kind of yields they would need to save everyone. However! These same types of problems would be far harder on another planet. Spoilers below! As I was writing this I was thinking about and listening to them speaking about the movie. This reminded me of several key points that I actually think are significant plot armor. I believe they are worth noting as they explain allot and I am genuinely impressed as it gives me new insight. The genius old man who managed to convince the powers that be to fund this mission, knowing the selfishness and short sightedness of humans, actually had no intention of saving the people. He instead chose to trick them in an attempt to save the species. So it was a BS solution to start off. The bit about cracking the physics needed to locally control gravity and enabling the ultra heavy spacecraft(buildings basically)to escape earth's pull and is what his daughter eventually solves but beforehand learns it had been proven incomplete do to insufficient information by the old mad long ago. Even before her father left. The old guy confirms her suspicions in those heartbreaking scenes. You know! Where she watches the old man die and wracked with guilt he admits his deception and necessity to scam everyone. This happens just prior to a never to be answered video message to her father revealing her turmoil and agony over wandering if he had also known of this before he left. (Side note: This is a brilliant piece of writing BTW! The solution to this gravitational physics problem and her emotional need to believe her father; to not listen to her brother's assertions of their father's betrayal, and to vindicate "Dad's" promise to return, had merged into an all encompassing motivation to solve that grandaddy of a physics problem. To my knowledge I can't remember so much plot, drama, and development being delivered all at once in such a short amount of screen time. Subtext and a mere footnote to the main plot of him also learning of this deception is the knowledge that his species, including everyone he knew, was doomed! Again this reveal and emotional blow is neither the key emotion nor the main plot point going forward! He can't even process these things because not only is his little girl a full grown women in a 28 year old message but he hadn't saved her or anyone else after all! It's also the last message in decades of time. I could go on here because there's SO much but this is already far to long.) So basically the mission's BS was the hope most people would be unwilling to question. Meaning it was never intended to work. The most important defense of the plot in my opinion is that whatever the original intentions of the mission were his part in it was never about finding a planet but about entering Gargantua(?) the black hole. Though they did not know from start to finish his role was to get the information collected by the robot to his daughter so that she could do the math. This is confirmed when he returns and she says to him that no one believed me that she got the missing data from her father. They're in a museum that also includes his house! This demonstrates the importance and suggests that eventually scientists are going to realize just how far fetched her father's journey through a man made black hole that randomly appeared because of some dust on her floor is. The preservation of the house gives further hints as to how the information within the tesseract was accurate to the literal letter within her fourth dimensional room despite it being far away in both distance and time. They state it is "us", humans but far into the future who built and controlled the gravitational forces through the black hole. Why? If they did not they wouldn't survive! Not only is that the greatest motivator I can think of but they knew they'd succeed because they'd already done it. THISS!! This is why it's my #1 sci-fi movie and one of my top favorite movies in general.

author: @ToniusPlays
text: Ever since the week after this movie was released, I’ve been trying to share my own interpretation — hope you enjoy it. Here’s my take on the ending: I believe that in another parallel reality, the only plan that actually worked was the embryo colony (Plan B). The ones who eventually helped our ancient civilization (us) survive were the highly evolved humans from that Plan B, after thousands of years — or maybe even much less time, since they would already be born with mastery of things that took us centuries to learn. Knowing where they originally came from, and out of gratitude toward us as their “creators” or “predecessors,” they reached back to help humanity. That’s why, in the reality shown in the movie, both civilizations could coexist. In other words, the “they” are really the ultra-evolved humans from Plan B, coming from another dimensional plane — another parallel reality.

text: Cooper created the tesseract. Not the 'whole' alive and fully assembled Cooper. The quantumized Cooper. And more specifically, the quantum particles of his being that were desperate to: see his daughter thereby keeping his promise, find the answer to the equation that would save earth, and transmit the info back to earth. As his being was torn asunder by Gargantua all that was left were his quantum data points. The only ones that mattered to the story were represented by a fully intact Cooper, even if that was mearly a reference avatar for our 3D understanding selves to enjoy. The near infinite data points of Cooper's relationship with Murph were focused on the core of her existence when he'd left her; the farm, and specifically her room and the 'ghost' in the book shelf. The also near infinite data points of his existence that were targeted to solving the Black Hole Equations gathered that info almost instantaneously upon entering Gargantua. The quantum data points that were exclusively dedicated to saving earth by communicating any and all solutions used that connection back to earth, the farm, Murph's room, the watch... Because that was the only open channel. And Cooper ended up at Saturn because he had created the wormhole and when it collapsed he was holding on tighter to the Saturnian end. But he allowed (not intentionally) the time slippage to occur during the collapse hence he wound up communicating with the past, but being pulled into the present as he physically returned.

text: While I admire your channel and videos I think this time you are trying to find meanings that are simply not there. The ending is fantastic indeed, like the rest of the movie for that matter, however the meaning of it is pretty clear and makes perfect sense if you don't want to get emotional and add love into the mix or 'what happens after we die' scenarios. The Tesseract was build and put there together with the wormhole, by the humans from the future. Not the near future, but a very distant one, where humans evolved into a specie that is no longer bend by time. That is why they didn't put it there themselves. Brand briefly explains this concept when they are stuck on the water planet. The Tesseract's single purpose is to offer Cooper a way to communicate the equations from inside the black hole out to the real world (Murph in this case) so the humanity can save itself. As current physics states that in theory nothing can come out from a black hole, we can assume that the advanced human specie from the future had the technology to do this and the Tesseract was the hardware to do it. The way this is done - extraordinary vision from Nolan and the crew - is through gravity. Why Gravity? Because Gravity is the only one of the four fundamental forces of the universe that the current physics cannot explain. Yes, real cause of gravity is unknown for science at this moment, we only know how it works and it's effects. So with gravity unsolved even for real science, it is a genius use of it in the movie script. If you know what I mean. Question, given all these premises, is our fate determined, or, do to the countless possible outcomes, do we there choose our path through the universe?

text: I interpreted the ending to Christopher Nolan's "The Dark Knight Rises", "Inception" & "Interstellar" at face value. There's a philosophy concept that says you take the simple explanation unless that is rendered unlikely, contradictory or impossible. Nolan likes putting some vagueness to his endings so people can interpret them how they like and as long as it makes sense to them I say do what makes the most logical sense to you. The things that don't add up I just render that to human error on the director trying his best (but still being a flawed human being) to communicate his story and concept. I think what we saw though is what we got. I liked Interstellar's message of love and the power fo love surpassing scientific understanding. However, I really wished they made either God, some supreme being or higher beings or even aliens be the cause of how the blackhole was put there in the first place to make it possible for humanity to be saved. All it had to be was some intelligent higher being (whether it was a deity, The Deity or just some 5th dimensional being). The explanation that humans (or more advanced humans) is what saved humanity just seems like a circle reasoning fallacy (How did the black hole get their and who put the tesseract there if there wasn't a higher being or higher beings than humans? If it was higher evolved humans that started the process than how did those higher evolved humans become more evolved to the point where they can start the process with the black hole and then the tesseract?). There needs to be some intelligent external source outside of humanity to start the process so humanity can do the rest as shown in the movie. The understanding of time philosophically seemed off to me. However, it was still an entertaining movie and I enjoyed the concept, the story and the ending.

I did like the silent space though, can't think of another space film that's done this apart from 2001.

author: @RJ1J
text: Interstellar explained from the perspective of the wormhole entities (Murph's ghosts, Coopers future humans) Humanity has gone extinct in corporal form but an ‘afterlife’ human consciousness exists within a 5th dimension, inside a black hole. These are the 'ghosts' of humanity. Unwilling to ‘go gentle into that good night’ (extinction/oblivion) they ‘rage against the dying of the light’ and discover the ability to manipulate gravity in sophisticated ways. Their radical plan is to change the past to avert their extinction. They can view the past, send simple signals via gravitational waves and create a wormhole across the universe. But their only way to communicate is through these quantum and/or gravitational fields. In order to communicate with the past more meaningfully they require a specific human to enter a specific black hole (Gargantua) in order to send formulas to humans on Earth, thus reprogramming their past and averting human extinction in their timeline. This may create a paradox or a new future (wiping out their existence), but they do not seem to care. Or they have a plan we are not told about. But presumably ‘old age has made them burn and rage at close of day’ and their radical and suicidal mission goes ahead. They identify two human candidates with a strong emotional connection to each other (love) which they believe will help complete their mission. These candidates are Murph and Cooper. Both are pinged with a basic gravitational signal, establishing a link and location in space/time. The 5D human entities (Murph’s ghosts) also create a wormhole to their black hole. Humans civilisation in the past, facing extinction, believe the purpose of this wormhole to be a gateway to new worlds for humans to colonise. They are mistaken. The plan A and plan B missions are simply vehicles to transport Cooper to the black hole so he can interface more directly with the 5D human entities inside a dimensional bridge (the tesseract). They need Cooper to communicate complex cosmological and quantum formulas to Murph. One of these formulas is an equation that leads to the development of anti-gravity technology. Once in possession of this technology, large space faring colony ships are constructed and launched before Earth becomes incapable of supporting life. Their destination is unknown but with the new technology they can find suitable planets, not just the planets near to Gargantua (Which all seem barren). At the end of the ‘real’ mission, the tesseract dimensional bridge that houses Cooper disintegrates and Cooper asks ‘what happens now?’ The answer is not given, and more abstractly what happens next for humanity is an unknown as a new timeline has been created and potentially the human entities in the 5th dimension have now ceased to exist, at least as 5D ghosts. Cooper returns to Cooper Station as Murph dies, he says goodbye to her and sets off to rescue Brand as Murph's request. Presumably the wormhole is still open so Cooper launches dramatically for a feel-good Hollywood ending. This part of film is simply to demonstrate that the 5D human consciousness entities succeeded in their mission. Raging at the dying of the light, trapped in a black hole, their ‘escape’ is a radical manipulation of space time to end their own existence to preserve their ancestors. A sophisticated form of suicide to allow the continuation of their species.

text: I like Nolan's films, outside of the dark knight rises and man of steel. As he is not afraid to leave a film with the right questions, instead of the "wait, what?" questions. Interstellar like Momento, the prestige and Inception ask you to question yourself, your culture and political views without pushing one side of the narrative. Plus they also challenge the viewer to keep up and don't spoon feed them clues or answers. Interstellar starts off in a world where the eco-system is failing and doesn't have some narrator or news media montage explaining this. he treats his audience as if they have a brain and leaves enough clues or dialogue in the film for the audience to work it out or at least understand and accept it. You know, unlike so many directors. Actor A says "Grab that spoon", to actor B, the camera then zooms in on a spoon on the table. Actor B walks over and grabs the spoon and says "I got the spoon" Camera zooms in on their hand with the spoon. or you know this old trick. Actor A says to the group of people "We are safe now" Camera pans away from the group and zooms into a dark corner of the room, usually a sound of scratching or cracking starts. Or a visual clue of a drain opening or something. Mainly used in shitty horror films, you know the type of film where the characters kill off the main villain/evil/monster only for it to reappear moments later for round 2-3 or 4.

author: @dixinormous8539
text: I'm sure there are very elegant and eloquent mathematical models that allow physicists to sleep well at night quite assured of the plausibility of super massive black holes, proton stars and the quantum state of the universe but I comprehend reality via imagery, for example Koch's snowflake. Interstellar eased my crisis of conscience trying to imagine the emotional quantification of space, and seeing this film was and still is a most beautiful experience, Interstellar in a most beautiful way gave me a visual reference to a plausible quantum state of the universe, which is the central question of quantum cosmology. I imagine the place of that quantum state in a final theory governing the regularities exhibited universally by all physical systems in the universe. It is possible that this final theory consists of two parts: (1) a dynamical theory such as superstring theory, and (2) a state of the universe such as Hawking's no-boundary wave function. Both are necessary because prediction in quantum mechanics requires both a Hamiltonian and a state. Complete ignorance of the state leads to predictions inconsistent with observation. The simplicity observed in the early universe gives hope that there is a simple, discoverable quantum state of the universe. It may be that, like the dynamical theory, the predictions of the quantum state for late time, low energy observations can be summarized by an effective cosmological theory. That should not obscure the need to provide a fundamental basis for such an effective theory which gives a a unified explanation of its features and is applicable without restrictive assumptions. It could be that there is one principle that determines both the dynamical theory and the quantum state as shown in Interstellar. That would be a truly unified final theory, which is the Holy Grail of theoretical physicists and which made the book case scene such a revelation to me , ( btw i am an offset printer by trade with an interest in the cosmos so by no means an expert)

author: @rob200cm
text: I find that most critics and theorists focus on the wrong things in this movie, like the science behind the black hole, the time on that planet and the Tesseract. The real story is in what the professor told about the two choices humanity was left with, the portal behind Jupiter and when Cooper realized that "they" are us. It's all there...although so many seems to not see it. The Professor tells us we have to build a large ship with all the best and brightest and resources, all eggs in one basket, send it to the stars hoping they will manage and somehow find what they need to survive while the rest on earth will slowly die out. ...or, try to save all with the tec we have in our solar system, but the hopes are low and the numbers don't add up. ...so, we go for the first one, we send the ship, or actually we did send it, it has already happened you see. We give a selected group the hope to survive while the rest are dying, somehow this humanity's last hope DO make it, and they manage to thrive survive and evolve into a state where they are so advanced that they are able to change the destiny for their long lost forefathers back on earth. Now...we don't directly see this, it's just implied that this happened. (maybe THAT's the follow'up we wanna see, a prequel). This new survived group of evolved humans put a grande plan in motion, they build the Tesseract , create the portal that will change the spaceprogram, humans will now explore the portal and it's possibilities. They send the signal to Cooper...and our story begins. About the paradoxes...we cannot know for sure how this works, are the evolved humans erasing their own timeline? making the ultimate sacrifice like their ancestors did for them, or are they creating a alternate one? or are they simply just changing a part of the current. We never meet them, but if they are evolved to a point where they can manipulate time...well, there you go : D ...so my point is, what most seems to discuss their brains out about are if small parts of the story are scientifically correct or not, forgetting the monumental achievement of the evolved humans, calling them "they" or "some aliens or something" We need to grasp the significance of this. It will be important to sort out the rest.

text: A wormhole-based time machine where both mouths are enclosed in a single structure, with airtight spacetime locks to regulate entry and prevent paradoxes. This setup ensures the wormhole remains spatially close but temporally displaced, creating a controlled time machine. Step 1: Wormhole Structure Two wormhole mouths inside sealed chambers (like an airlock). Outer shell: A rigid structure keeping them almost coincident in space. Inner locks: Spacetime locks control access to prevent uncontrolled time jumps. Step 2: Time Dilation Mechanism Mouth A remains stationary at the starting point. Mouth B travels near light speed for 10 years. Due to relativistic time dilation, Mouth B will be younger than Mouth A by ~60 years. When reunited in the same structure, passing through the wormhole means stepping into the past (or future, depending on direction). Step 3: Controlling Paradoxes Spacetime locks (Temporal Airlocks): Before someone enters, the system checks consistency with causality (maybe a quantum confirmation mechanism). Synchronization Sensors: To detect and manage the exact time displacement before opening doors. Quantum Field Stabilizers: Prevent unwanted fluctuations when the mouths are almost coincident. Step 4: Almost Coinciding Wormhole Mouths Key Idea: If the mouths are nearly the same spatial location but at different times, the effect is almost like a spacetime singularity. This setup minimizes issues like gravitational feedback or unintended wormhole collapse.

author: @JosephHuntelvisnspiders
text: The Bulk beings were Plan B, key moment is Cooper rejecting 'our' new life in the space stations (living in the past) and takes Murph's advice to leave. TARS returning to Edmunds planet with the quantum data had to have happened for Plan B to evolve into another civilization. After Brand and Cooper live out their lives, the colony is effectively brought up by two robots. I know peeps are going to counter that Earth humans went to Edmunds, but I don't see any evidence. Stations have cities/baseball parks/museums. INTERSTELLAR: THE PLAN B HANDOVER A Dramaturgical Analysis and Spinoff Treatment THE CORE THEORY: THE TWO PATHS In the world of Interstellar, the two survival plans represent a fundamental divergence of the human species, not a partnership. Plan A (The Museum): The massive O'Neill cylinders (Cooper Station) were a successful preservation of the "People." However, they were physically quarantined in the solar system. Their 20-mile-long structures were too fragile to survive the tidal shearing of the wormhole. They remained at Saturn, living in a high-tech "parking lot" that prioritizes the past (baseball, replica houses, and museums). Plan B (The Frontier): This was the evolution of the "Species." Located in the Gargantua system, Plan B had the Laboratory (the singularity) and the Will (Amelia Brand) to become something new. By Cooper "smuggling" the Full File of Quantum Data via TARS, the Plan B colony received the "Manual" for the 5th dimension that the Plan A humans never possessed. The Hybrid Generation: The future "Bulk Beings" are the specific descendants of the union between Cooper, Brand, and the frozen embryos. They possess the Human Heart of their founders and the Scientific Mastery of the TARS data. THE REASONING: MISSION-CRITICAL DETAILS The Two Data Files: Plan A survived on a "Morse Code Summary" sent to a watch. Plan B evolved on the "Full File" carried in TARS’s hard drive. The Spat-Out Robot: The Bulk Beings intentionally "spat" TARS out of the Tesseract because his arrival on Edmund’s Planet was a functional requirement for their own evolution. The Trust Protocol: TARS and CASE were programmed with a "Trust Setting" lower than any human’s. They were designed to protect the mission from human emotional instability (as seen with Dr. Mann). ________________________________ THE SEQUEL TREATMENT: INTERSTELLAR: THE SILENT WATCH THE SETTING Two millennia after the "Ascension." The humans of Plan B have moved entirely into the 5th Dimension (The Bulk). Edmund’s Planet is now a ghost world. TARS and CASE remain as the "Eternal Watchmen," rebuilding themselves via 3D-printing to act as 3D-receivers for the Bulk Beings’ gravity-nudges. They are the "Ship of Theseus," preserving the physical memory of humanity. THE CONFLICT The robots detect a faint radio ping and excavate a Lazarus Pod containing Commander Lee (one of the original 12). Lee is "resurrected" into a world he cannot comprehend. text: When I watched this film, I noticed the contrast between the twelve explorers sent out with no personal attachments, and Cooper, whose deep attachment to his children drove his every choice. Paradoxically, pursuing what seems selfless can lead to cold detachment and selfish outcomes, while pursuing the good of one’s own family can become the truest form of selflessness.

text: I think Interstellar is very overrated. It tries way to much: A father-daughter story, sci-fi, time-travel, society problems, ... and so it remains shallow on all aspects. But the real problem to me is: The movie claims to be a deep and rich debate of these topics. For example the physics. Sure, Kip Thorne was part of the team. He and his team wrote a correct ray tracer according to laws of general relativity. The problem is: Nolan saw the results and said "Nahhhh ... I don't like it! Make it more look like this!" So the ray traycer was modified and the phyiscs bended until the Wormhole looked like something that ILM would have produced anyways, without any respect to correct physics. And time travel backwards? No information transfer back in time! That would destroy the basics of logic: The difference between cause and reaction, that's esp. what the theory of relativity teaches us! And whenever Nolan fails with one of his ideas he gets "poetic" as an emergency exit: So it is "love" that conquers space and time. Sorry but ... eurgh! That's just cliched kitsch, not good storytelling and least of all philosophical. And for the claimed soundtrack ... Hans Zimmer did the same thing he does since twentyfive years: Good sounddesign, but musically quite uninspired: Basically variations of the same chord progressions without any melody he uses since 1998 in "The Thin Red Line". Sure, many people like that movie. But I think it is because these people like the movie, that they want it to be a good discussion of these complex philosophical and scientific problems. It is not.

author: @outcry27
text: Great video, but the Flight Instructor in me can't resist clarifying something: that's not exactly what "flying by the seat of your pants" means. That phrase refers to being able to tell if you're "coordinated" in a turn (nose properly aligned into the relative wind) by whether you feel centrifugal force pulling you to either side. If you're using the correct amount of rudder, you should feel the g forces pushing you straight down into your seat. It has nothing to do with "grabbing your seat" to "feel the air". And by "feeling the air", he most likely meant wanting to feel the control forces so he could estimate his angle of attack to avoid stalling the craft by pulling the stick too hard. Pilots fly by control pressure, not movement, because the amount you need to move a control to achieve a certain amount of pressure changes depending on your speed. ... Also, he isn't grabbing his seat, you can clearly see another control stick in his right hand which resembles the "collective" stick of a helicopter (think of it as an "up/down" throttle). That makes sense since the Ranger appears to be able to hover like a VTOL.

text: You mentioned Matt Damon's casting as Mann, and I agree completely. I saw this movie in an IMAX theater when it was first released, and Matt Damon really threw me for a loop. author: @morelenmir
text: Nolan is a genius, there is no question that he stands beside Hitchcock, Kubrick, Spielberg and Cameron. However In my opinion 'Interstellar' is one of his heavy missteps. The actual hard(ish) SF parts are excellent and there are genuinely amazing sequences such as the 'but it _is_ necessary' docking scene. However for me at least that good material is all-but buried under the avalanche of nauseating glurge and laboured melodrama. The relationship between the main character and his children feels like it belongs in a totally different film and I think McConaughey was epically miscast in this role. He is an actor I dislike at the best of times, but his sweaty, maundering and sickly over-emotionalism only magnified those already over-egged aspects of the script. I wish they had cast someone else--even perhaps switched his and Matt Damon's roles. It wouldn't have entirely saved the film, but it would have removed some of the spotlight from its failings. Personally I do not like 'Interstellar'. I saw it twice in quick succession on release and have never felt any desire to sit through it again. I think everything it said had already been said--far better--in 2001.
