text: I'd always found Nolan films brilliant, but somewhat chilly, before Interstellar. You never really cry with his Batman, or his monstrous, obsessive magicians. Even Dom Cobb, though he goes through an emotional catharsis, the film Inception never quite connects his experience directly to the audience. Maybe it's Leo DiCaprio's performance, which never quite feels authentically grief stricken, leaning more into the paranoia and caginess of the character. But Interstellar is shift in Nolan's storytelling. It begins with science, then trots out the cockamamie notion that love is a powerful universal force like gravity. This notion matches the weird science of The Prestige, the deceptive real-ish-ness of his Dark Knight, and the mad rules of his dream-invasion world in Inception. But then, Interstellar clobbers you over the head with the truth of that notion, and the whole film becomes a profound exploration of the extraordinary experience of love. For me, and I think for many, the shot of Cooper enduring the agony of watching his children's lives pass always brings tears. It doesn't matter anymore whether it's in the context of watching the whole film, or just the clip in a video like this one. The story is embedded into the shot, and the universal human experience of love, loss, and grief are embedded into the story. I feel that empathic experience is the universal force Brand is talking about. It connects Cooper to his children across time, and across the galaxy, just as it connects Brand to her lover, Wolf Evans. It connects us with the artist, Chris Nolan, who uses the story to tell us of his own emotional experience with his children. That kind of vulnerability seems like something Nolan had always been resistant to in previous work, carefully putting a veil of story complexity between the emotions and the audience. But in Interstellar, through Mathew McConaughey's raw performance, he lays his own emotions bare. So when Eric tears up a bit telling his own story, he shows how Nolan's personal vulnerability effected him, through time and space, through the medium of art. Which is what I think art is for. And by telling us his story with such tender vulnerability, he shares that feeling with is, again through time and space, connecting us to him in a very personal way. Thank you so much for sharing this, Erik. If humanity is gonna make it, this is how it's gonna happen.

text: Interesting. Kip thorns approach to research is similar to mine but for different reasons. We both avoid research crowds. If there's a problem with a lot of people working on it. I don't find it interesting. I don't care about competition. I want to go work on problems where the community is avoiding. If there's too many people it usually signals that the problem is too easy. It might be that information is preserved... but I'm in the camp still that it could be "destroyed". But I disagree with calling it destroyed. If our big bang happened the way we think... quantum information should balance out to equal effectively zero. So why couldn't the ledger get balanced in a compact ultra dense region? Thats not deletion. Its recombination. There is no conflict. Otherwise if information is eternal. Than during heat death, provided thats our fate, in principal, a magic machine should be able to read all the particles and patches of empty space and recreate what it once was. But You cannot. Information being fundamental to this isn't broken. But anyways... whatever the real answer is will be interesting. I just don't think the information paradox is as big of a problem as it initially sounded.

author: @TearDownGenesis
text: The self fulfilling Time travel is the more narrative concise option, but it still has flaws, even ignoring free will. Simply, first cause. While in the loop it fits, but what cause one action, was a later action, yet, if you look at it further out, the action caused itself. This violates causality. Its a closed loop. So, the question is, what caused the very first instance. If the cords weren't given by the future, which only reached that point by getting the coordinates, then how could he have ever gotten to that point to give the cords. Basically, if you are given a book by your future self about how to time travel, you then use that book, travel back in time, and give that same book to yourself. That book would continue to age, as its timeline continues through the closed loops, infinitely, eventually the book would fall apart, leaving no book to be given back, meaning the book was never receives, causing the entire loop to collapse. Ironically, I don't believe in free will but this time travel, which is argued fits with determinism (lack of free will) doesn't sit well with me. Since it is more reliant on fate, which is different than determinism. Fate often has a significance to something, which, in an objective universe, i.e. one where causality isn't guided by things being assigned value, wouldn't matter. Movies like The Time Machine, where he tried to go back and save the woman he loved from dying, only for her to always die, just in some other way, assign weight to her death, yet nothing else like, the damaged fence, or light post, etc. that wasn't impacted every time. That carries over to the book example. The book and its components, down to core atoms, and further, is allowed to exist with no consistency between each run through the loop, yet people would argue "well the book could be written again" etc. which is a statement based on the value of the material rather than the actual objective nature of reality. Another problem is all time travel would have to occur, every time. While we watch the scene play out and see 1 single loop. What would need to happen is every loop would occur, all at once. This can't really be envisioned, but in the book example, the first time the book is handed off and the last time where it would just be dust would all but occurring at once. There is not "one time through" the loop. Rather the entire casual action would need to continue. Simply put, Time Travel (backwards) isn't possible as it violates causality, a governing principal of reality. And while someone can say, well maybe at a location causality wouldn't be a law. The issue there lies, that as soon as that space would interact with causal space...well, they aren't compatible, so they can't interact, thus anything within that space can't cross from one to the other.

Events in the past that are caused by time travel have to always happen or the time travel even never takes place, to begin with... attempts to time travel just don't work. Think of it like Contact when the people believed that Ellie never went anywhere, the time travel event would be the scenario all the stuff would get started and as the person who attempted to travel did so, the ability to time travel would just stop as they were about to go. This would be a paradox collapse and it would go all the way back to the moment the time travel would have been initiated. I'm going to have to rewatch Interstellar.

text: 3:30 - One amazing thing about the visualizations - while scientists had known, theoretically, how a black hole _should_ actually look, and there were even a few low-resolution renders and sketches (see the black hole hand-drawn sketch by Jean-Pierre Luminet in 1978, already predating the "sci-fi black holes" that are just funnel-shaped.) Oh, there were wireframes, or "false color" renders made to visualize specific aspects; but Interstellar was the first *GOOD* visible-light representation of one.

text: I am going to apologize right away if this comes off as overly aggressive if you read the comment fully you'll understand why. I just finished watching a YouTube video on why modern movies are all similar in their style and why people feel nostalgic for older movies more so then excited for new ones. This video in first 2 minutes wraps up exactly what I was thinking after watching it: modern movies are out of touch with reality, directors focus more on their own individuality then on the uniting views of the audience. What you get is an overly complicated story that fails at really accomplishing anything. Interstellar is a fine example, you can sit here and break down the effort that went into each scene but when you try and wrap it into a full story it's just about a guy who abandons his dying daughter to seek out a next generation of love and procreation. It's selfish and completely lacking the human connection. I didn't like the movie and this is why, it wasn't made more me, it was made for the director and anyone that relates to his views and how I am supposed to enjoy it is to not think and instead enjoy the collidascopic scenes. Just like this comment it wasn't made for this video specifically, it was made for myself and its probably just as out of place as interstellar is to the majority of people.

text: Few things I found to be interesting after i watched it a second time: Dr. Mann's robot is destroyed, by what he claims was an incorrectly identifying something or other and then the robot's power source was apparently used to continue the mission. I think that given Dr. Mann's false story about the planet itself, it's possible that Mann disabled/destroyed the robot in order to keep from having the robot stop him from relaying a false message about the planet's habitability (Mann could have sent the message saying that the planet can sustain human life, but the robot may then know that Mann is not completing the mission and is just trying to be rescued and thus try to stop him). This would be an interesting little subtle similarity/homage to 2001 as well. Another thing about the flaw in the time loop in regards to question of who "they" are. "They" could likely be humans from the future, but simply descendants of Plan A embryo-bred people, and they are simply creating this 5th dimensional rift to save Earth's humans that died the first time around. Actually that still has a typical time-loop plot hole in every time travel movie. Either way, enjoyed the movie a lot, both visually and intellectually. Can't really go wrong with Nolan and sci-fi.

author: @ninok199
text: Just saw the movie and liked it, here is my take on the possibility of the whole future affecting the past, chicken vs the egg thing. It is known that time travel is possible but not in the sense of affecting one's own past, but rather by the relativity of the passage of time. Time goes slow for me, fast for you, you age you die, i'm the same age, etc. They reiterate this in the film by saying "you an squash it, you can stretch it but you cant travel through it" or something to that extent. However, that is not to say that you can not affect time for a timeline separate of your own. I could theoretically figure out a way to convey a message to have myself murdered in the past via existence in a 5th dimension as described in the film, yet it would have no effect on me personally (i already exist as I am), but only on the 'me' that i murdered. That me would perish, and that timeline would be altered. The second I influenced it, 2 copies would exist, the one in which i was murdered and the one in which i ordered the hit. I believe this is what happened in the movie. At some point in earths history the blight was swallowing up the planet and perhaps a mission was formed along the lines of the plan B to relocate whats left of mankind. That plan would have to succeed, humans would have to evolve and perhaps being aware of their history (that at some point their original home was destroyed and billions of humans suffocated), decided that they should influence a particular timeline of their own history in hopes of allowing a different timeline an opportunity to succeed in saving more of humankind. So they create a wormhole from our galaxy to another and they also build the tesseract, which is actually a communication device that looks like a black hole. The tesseract is placed on the other side of the wormhole as to not damage our original solar system, but close enough to the wormhole on the other side as not to be missed by our astronauts. Once Cooper is trapped in it (perhaps by design), it allows him to convey the message and affect the events of his own timeline, and also preserves him via the relativity of time until he is rescued within hours of his oxygen tank depleting on our side / our solar system of the wormhole, which makes it seem like it was calculated and deliberate. Also note that only he and the robot were 'sent back' not all the other probes that were shot into the black hole again making it seem like it was all deliberate. Anyway, that's just my take on it :)

text: People keep confusing the Black Hole with the Worm Hole... they're two different things, not the same. The Worm hole is the pretty, glass-Christmas ornament-looking "tunnel" (which stays in a predictable orbit next to Saturn for whatever reason) through which the astronauts and radio communications from earth pass into the other galaxy. The Black Hole "Gargantua", a trillion times bigger than -- and six months away from -- the Worm Hole, is a collapsed star (singularity) that has reached an equalibrium where pretty much everything it's going to pull into itself is orbiting it at incredible velocity, except for a couple of planets that defy physics and rotate at speeds where a small shuttle can catch up to them. Yeah, but cool robots, mate!

author: @davidlean1060
text: What ever your thoughts about the questions the film brings up, do go and see it for some of the visual sequences. I thought that 'binary room', so to speak, where Cooper sends the messages across time, was stunning. Nolan likes to do a lot of effects in camera and it is hard to spot where he is using CGI and where he is filming in camera effects. That sequence was a triumph in terms of film making. Nolan does get muddled sometimes with his themes and plots (I guess to either keep us guessing, to cut a corner or a little bit of both of those) but he certainly knows how to put original and exciting images on to a screen. I wouldn't of had as much time for Inception if it hadn't been for the Paris folding over itself scene and the Zero Gravity Hotel sequence for example. Perhaps then, he's still got a way to go to make a metaphorical and thematic master piece, but visually, the guy can be outstanding.

text: Nice breakdown, but black holes are naturally occurring, so the super advanced humans didn't have anything to do with that. text: "Bootstrap Paradox via Cooper" is still a bootstrap paradox. You don't get to claim the future 4th or 5th dimensional humans are not influencing the past directly (even though they're viewing it) and thus not causing any temporal paradoxes (like the aforementioned bootstrap or causality loop paradox) because they're achieving their aims through using Cooper. It's still a bootstrap paradox. Without Cooper's actions, the human race doesn't make it into the future where they become 4th or 5th dimensional-capable and essentially become an extinct species. But Cooper doesn't do what he does without the direct intervention of these future humans (them placing the wormhole that enables human beings to leave the Solar System and eventually discover Gargantua and the secrets to what lies behind a black hole's event horizon - another......MASSIVE.....scientific goof-up by the movie). That's a Causality Loop right there. A.k.a. a Bootstrap paradox, or a "God created Himself" paradox. Essentially the movie is one big gigantic Bootstrap Paradox trying to pretend it's not, and this is the reason it annoys many scientists (aside from its loopy pseudoscience)

text: I both LOVED and HATED this movie. I loved it because of the science, the action, the sci-fi futurism, the music, etc... it is obviously a high budget movie with top notch effects and I did find it entertaining. But I hated it because the ending felt contrived and phoned in. I think the IDEA of the ending, that is, the concept they conceived, was cool. But I feel the IDEA vs. what can be feasibly achieved with current camera and AI tech were still just a bit off from one another, and I bet it pissed off the director to no end to have such a cool concept written, but then such a bizarre "Bill and Ted" visual actually produced. The idea of transiting a black hole event horizon only to get stuck inside a 4D bookshelf STILL makes no sense to me, even with a bunch of explanation/exposition videos. Why on Earth would a black hole not crush him to subatomic particles and destroy his information for eternity? We already know that is what happens to EVERYTHING that enters a black hole. It's annihilated for eternity so far as we know right now. Oh, but this one is a "special" black hole made by 5D people? What? We cannot figure out how to grow anything but corn, yet some special "interdimensional" people are throwing black holes and tesserects around? It just left me feeling kind of empty. I think they could have shown Coop enter some "hyperdimensional" space a different way than stuck in a bookshelf and it may have been more compelling. Maybe show him enter some God-like state of "thought turned to action" or do a scene where he is in multiple planes of reality at once. I dunno... it just gave me this "Oh really? THAT'S our climax? Damn..." feeling.

text: Interesting video. The best part was the return of the classic closing credits. The 5th dimension is purely speculative. I would categorize it with dark matter and dark energy. They are something we made to explain something we do not yet understand. Have you ever heard of the “Arrow of Time”? The Universe as we know is comprised of Space-Time, which is three dimensions of Space and one dimension of Time. The Arrow of Time moves us relentlessly forward. More about that in a moment. Mathematicians have been able to better understand what occurs inside the event horizon of a black hole. Time and Space swap places inside of an event horizon. Instead of Space-Time, you now have Time-Space. The math supports the concept of three dimensions of Time and one dimension of Space. Instead of an Arrow of Time, there exists and Arrow of Space, which relentlessly moves you toward a singularity. This is what being “spaghettified” means! If the Arrow of Space inside an event horizon moves you toward a singularity, then what does that say about the Arrow of Time outside an event horizon? Are we moving toward a singularity? No, the reality is the exact opposite. The Arrow of Time is moving us away from a singularity. The singularity has a familiar name, The Big Bang.

text: Am always ending up curious to this unique movie. Barring all the esoteric philosophy and the audience debates on how good it is or how it doesn't live up to expectations, I'd like to see how Interstellar will go for audience perspectives, later moviewatching generations, and sci-fi relevancy in the ever changing interims. Meantime, the robots are deservedly among the best characters of the film, and they should be how our "A.I.s" should be, not as chatbots who make ugly painting hands. Another meantime, I don't get the views on it being "too sappy" or "too heavy-handed". To me, this movie didn't get overboard on those, unlike the Ender's Game movie adaptation and Gattaca. And as a personal aside, my gut says Interstellar is a better film than The Dark Knight Rises. That film was just... very awkward as a finale to Batman Begins, The Dark Knight, and being generally a Batman work.

author: @detromaniac
text: As much as I loved Interstellar: people really need to stop depicting time as a dimension. It isn't, we just conceptualize it as one even though it behaves nothing of the sort. Time is more like a Force. It can be slowed to the point of essentially stopping, and sped up/amplified, but as like a force, the application of it can not be undone. The best you could do is pause it and wait for the past to catch up. Bi-lateral translation is not possible with Time. It can not be a dimension. In fact: I would go so far as to say that Time, the way in which we abstract it, does not exist at all. The difference between moment to moment comes down to change in state or configuration, and the flow can be described as rate of change. All of which is governed by Forces, not dimensionality. This is what is meant when Time is spoken of as an illusion: because we convey what's happening in a totally incorrect manner because it is practical and convenient for us to. The truth is: we hardly understand it at all.

author: @CyPony
text: The action scenes were actually kind of cool, but at times, I could tell that they used a computer to make the special effects, especially on the wormhole. It looked like someone blew a bubble and let it float off into space, and it looked like they used some cheap video manipulating effects to make the stars in the background distort. Other than that, the other effects were excellent. Characters were likable, and the movie made me feel how I should have felt. Also, the paradox seems to be self-resolving, since they basically save themselves, so that part of the movie works out ok. Overall it was pretty entertaining, too. But the love aspect completely ruined the movie for me, as well as the scene where he went into the black hole. The audience in my theater was laughing quite a bit when he appeared to be behind the bookshelf. There's a difference between setting up the rules in the universe your movie takes place in in a way that's believable, and just blatantly breaking one (or many) of our beliefs completely just to allow the story to progress. If we didn't have the widespread belief that a black hole would turn you into a spaghetti strand, and if we didn't already know that love is just a bunch of chemicals, both those aspects of the movie would have been fine. Case and point: this movie (and Gravity) are both pretty overrated, and this movie definitely doesn't deserve to be in its current spot in the top 250 of IMDB, as well as almost every movie since 2000 that has made it on there. I'll watch it again on video at home. Who knows? Maybe those things won't bother me as much and I'll love it. Or maybe I'll dislike the movie even more. At the moment, it seems like yet another over-hyped movie that people will forget about in less than a year.

author: @Lowraith
text: There's no paradox if everything is predetermined. 1 timeline, 1 species (humans, both present and super-future in 5th dimension). No paradox. Passing through higher dimensions means we're not "changing the past", because it ALWAYS happened exactly as it was shown in the movie. All moments of the timeline exist simultaneously in 5-dim space, so the entire timeline, even the parts that loop back, are static. The future messages would happen, because they ALREADY happened. A static timeline which loops back on itself at some point has ALWAYS looped back on itself. The future humans didn't change the past, because their messages had already existed on the timeline in their past long before they ever existed. They simply fulfilled their past as it had already occurred.

Future humans figured out how to manipulate gravity so well that they created a wormhole from one point in their ancient past to another so that their ancient ancestors possibly million or even hundreds of millions of years in the past (us, modern times) could learn to manipulate gravity and escape their dying planet to then live on and eventually breed, evolve, breed, evolve into the future humans who setup the wormhole to save them. The PROBLEM IS! its ridiculous and stupid. This is a time paradox that could never have begun. The same thing happens in interstellar. Humanity died on earth unable to get a sufficient population and the needed supplies into space. Therefore they had no future generations who eventually evolved into super advanced (from our perspective) beings who could drop a wormhole in the past giving us the ability to save ourselves. Again no way to start the time loop. Hollywood is lazy and relies on the ignorance of the general population to never ask the question.... How did the time loop start? Imagine that since lucy died in the original time line humanity never evolved leaving space for perhaps another primate species to evolve since we weren't around to hunt them to extinction or simply compete with them for food and land. This could create a time loop where earth at the very least is stuck in those few hundred million years over and over. All live would be gone in very short order so if humans didn't survive there certainly wouldn't be time for any other species to evolve technologically far beyond us in just a few decades. So if humans died on earth that was it, game over. There is no possibility based on anything in the movie for the time loop to begin let alone be resolved in a way that would allow the time line to progress beyond the loop. text: Regarding the importance of love. Murphy's Law.

author: @joseywales7930
text: That is one trippy movie. 4 humans travel forward in time to save earth's civilization. They basically create a new civilization. The new civilization then travels back in time to the old civilization 'future time' to show them how to save the old civilization. Let's say the old civilization lives in year 2000. 4 people from year 2000 travel to the year 2500 and start a new civilization. That new civilization is now living in the year 3000. The civilization in year 3000 then travels back in time to the year 2500 to show those 4 how to save the year 2000 civilization. What makes it confusing is there isn't a year given at any moment, other than 'past 'present, future'. That's kinda the point of the movie though. Once mankind learned how to manipulate time and space, time is no longer relevant. To me, this movie is kinda a snapshot of how I imagine Heaven in a roundabout way. I heard the most profound statement many years ago that will stick with me for life. We were discussing the paradox of time/space. A pretty wise old man said 'Time is God's way to keep everything from happening at once.' You have to think about that one. That's exactly how we can live in Heaven forever. God will stop time because time is no longer needed. Nothing 'new' will be created in Heaven. Everything you need for eternity is already there. It was created in the beginning (past) it's there now (present) and will always be there (future). Thats the time paradox in a nutshell. That's the way I see it anyway.

author: @manb4war
text: What a fantastic ride, best sci-fi movie of the last decade in my opinion. As with any good sci-fi, it can't be considered great unless you can devote endless hours to dissecting it and complaining about how the writers and directors "got it wrong". Loved the premise, I just saw Ken Burns "The Dust Bowl" documentary on Netflix, so I recognized the interviews at the beginning of the movie immediately. The premise and complexity of the film were spot on, I was good with it until the very end when they decided to get preachy. The greatest contradiction in the film is the idea of the persistent ever evolving human mind that transcends space, time and overcomes every obstacle with love. The biggest problem with that actually begins in the first minutes of the movie with the Dust Bowl interviews. The Dust Bowl was actually a man made disaster due to improper farming techniques in the Oklahoma flat lands. Farmers there plowed millions of acres of land that created enormous dust clouds and disrupted the ecosystem. They were subject to literal plague like conditions that included hordes of rabbits or hares and swarms of grasshoppers that swept the countryside. The driving force behind these conditions was greed, farmers wanted to get rich. The film mentions how NASA has been driven underground in order to conceal government spending on a space program due to strong public opinion regarding wasteful government spending. Without going into detail about what's wrong with how the actual mission comes to fruition, including the imperialistic undertones that suggest America (aka NASA) saves the world and all humanity all by themselves, the film never really explains how we get there; to that 5th dimensional existence. If love is the determining factor that ensures the survival of humankind, the PRESENT humans must possess this trait not the FUTURE humans. If the present humans possess these saving traits however, there is never need for future humans to reach back, create wormholes or correct the mistakes of the past. Learning from mistakes restores the natural order and it is what ultimately preserves human life and the world. What this means is man has no need to alter the past, leave the planet or evolve to 5th dimensional realities. Instead of treating the destructive endeavors of humanity as a caveat, the film treats them as admirable human virtues. In the end, the film has this to say, WE ENDANGERED OUR OWN LIVES AND SAVED OURSELVES. For that you get a C+, it would have been better with a "happily ever after ending".

text: I've never really liked the explanation that "They" are humans from the Future. You don't get advanced science like the Library Cooper was allowed to use without a solid society/civilization behind it. This needlessly complicates the story. And can filmmakers stop with that corny "Love transcends all" stuff? Only Maths can do that. Still, superb movie and soundtrack. Is there even a single Nolan movie that isn't gourmet food for thought? Except the "Dark Knight" trilogy, of course. There wasn't much he was allowed to do lest he be accused of disrespecting the source. And yet those are still the best Batman movies ever.

text: NO, NO, NO. There were no "future humans." Humanity indeed dies off. (You need to listen even more closely.) Robots, like TARS, equipped with artificial intelligence are given the directive to "find a way" to rejuvinate humanity. And this is how: (Remember, the robots have all the time they need to do this)...After humanity dies off, it is the robots who learn how to create a worm hole. It is the robots that learn how to build a teseract within a black hole. It is the robots who can run an infinite number of iterations to revive the human race, through Cooper being grounded, surviving a crash, his daughter "reading" the codes given through the "holes" in the library, her father understanding that this code is binary. And on and on, with seemingly random actions pieced together to form... A TIMELINE. Yaayyy! But with errors happening each time (look no further than the loss of Doyle--that was an iteration "slip up" that had to be overcome. Going to Mann's planet, first and not Edmund's And certainly, all the other potential slip ups that caused the entire iteration to be scrapped and started all over again. Probably MILLIONS OF TIMES, before getting it right.) Each iteration, with its genesis like a COBOL run program was initiated in the 5th dimension. There is just no way some equation solving would produce a teseract in a black hole and then overcome the energy requirements to keep open a wormhole for 48 years. That would take much longer than Dr. Brand's assessment of the remaining time left to live on earth. That time "budget" should clue you in to my assertion that it were the benign and benevolent actions of compassionate computers, which are your "future humans." After all, what such future human would want to be stuck in a monster nano-tube, orbiting the sun for warmth, when all you'd need to do is "scale mountains and jump canyons" of time?

text: My main issue with the film was that I couldn't understand why humanity had to abandon earth or die. Perhaps it was explained and I just missed it, in which case I would be happy if someone would clarify it for me. Alien worlds are very unlikely to be as habitable as earth was shown to be in the movie after all. There are sandstorms and a lame virus that consumes nitrogen and oxygen? Still not even remotely as bad as Mars is, and planet-hunters today would be extatic to find anything as promising as Mars as an extra-solar planet. Also, I'd say stopping a desert spreading (or what ever is causing the sandstorms) as well as curing a single virus (or even mechanically preventing it from infecting crops) hardly constitutes a reason to assume humanity will go extinct, and the only hope would be to abandon the planet entirely. If a rogue neutron-star was hurtling towards earth, or the sun was expanding, or any other literally earth-shattering event was afoot, then sure; I'd be on board with the "abandon ship" plan, but as things appear in the movie, it all just seems incredibly silly.

author: @rodorvh
text: I absolutely loved this movie, but it had consistency flaws that elicited disbelief, thus breaking immersion, a core value to me when I watch movies or play games. The argument is big on complex narrative/science stuff -which is why I love it- but all of the sudden, it throws love at your face coming from one of the less sentimental characters... it makes sense, but it just changes the mood so much, it feels out of place. And then, later on, you have a very complex moment inside the worm whole. The mere situation in itself stretches most people's comprehension, and on top of that you have Cooper talking about "tesseract" and "pentadimensional". I understood were Nolan was going with it, and it was amazing, but since the slang was so... over the top, it just took some people out, it reminded them that this was a sci-fi crazy movie, which in some cases even lead to laughter ―people behind me where laughing because they just couldn't catch up with the terminology. I commend Nolan's ambition here, I just think he could've chosen more seamless ways to blend in concepts like "love" or "pentadimensional beings" in order to avoid those disruptive issues. That's where it could've been better. As a whole, though, it was an amazing, enjoyable movie. It made you think, for a change.

author: @Epyon2007
text: It aims to be 2001 Space Odyssey and it becomes everything but stellar. I was with the movie until the last act and then it became a simple dump fist fight flick. What made 2001 Space Odyssey an epic is that people strive to be the best of mankind and not drowned in pointless recriminations and none sensible drama. I am so tired of movies that keep propagating the belief that man is the problem to mankind. Another movie that did this same stupid plot twist was Sunshine. In addition: thinking about Anne Hathaway's roll. She fails to deliver a female role model admirable of her convictions, she crumbles when confronted with the consequences of her decisions. All the while Chastain though thorough and convincing not enough exposition was done about her to really appreciate her roll better. I felt like that dim-whit of Sandra bullock’s role in Gravity made its way into this flick along with her emotional basket case “oh I need to be rescued by my charming prince” BLAH!. I also would like to point out Wes Bentley died because he was a dump jack ass who got mesmerized by the gigantic wave. His death was pointless and unnecessary. I enjoy Matt Damon as an actor and I'm not saying he’s doing a bad job at acting - it’s just that his character is terrible. The whole time I just kept counting the minutes before ambiguous evil dude was going to reveal himself. Finally, we get to watch an intergalactic space-wrestling match between Cooper and Mann that involves head butts and flying booster rockets. It’s a scene from a completely different movie, and one that would have made more sense in ‘Armageddon.’ Actually, Dr. Mann is a lot like Steve Buscemi’s character from ‘Armageddon’ – the formerly sane genius who starts blowing everything up for no reason. He wants to go home! – But for the life of me, I can’t figure out what Mann’s plan was supposed to be. I don’t consider this a “plot hole.” Instead, I just hate this character. Everything about this sequence felt like it belonged in another movie, seemed to last forever, and made me actively hate a movie that I had been enjoying up until that point (and then enjoyed again once Mann was gone). Damon took Mann from “reasonable human being” to “nut job who wants to kill everyone” in what seemed like seconds. It reminded me of the last act of ‘Sunshine’ - a poor narrative with a cliché twist that gives the uncomprehending viewer no choice but to watch the vomitrocious disaster that it becomes. Nolan read this plot below! this makes sense. Imagine this scenario: Prof. Brand and the NASA team are trying to figure out Plan A but they can't solve the equation. Originally there is no wormhole, and they are stuck on Earth as the blight is happening. Brand sends a team of astronauts and robots on a ship and travel to Gargantua without a wormhole (it just takes hundreds of millions of years). During this time they are in hibernation. They finally arrive on the planet, colonize, and send a probe into the black hole that relays the data to solve Plan A. After a long enough time of living on Gargantua, they evolve into 5D beings, and using the data from the probe in the black hole, they create the wormhole. Since its 5D, they can go back and change events (time is not linear anymore). They make the wormhole, place it near Saturn, and then the events in the movie play out as we see them. This way there is no longer a temporal paradox, because the wormhole was not constructed out of thin air. This fits well with the movie's tagline: "Mankind was born on Earth, it was never meant to die here". Originally, mankind did die on planet Earth except for the select few that made it to Gargantua and colonized the remaining humans. It was only after evolving into 5D beings that they could go back and prevent mankind from perishing on Earth. The tagline is alluding to this theory because mankind did originally die on Earth, but eventually they went back after evolving to prevent mankind from dying on Earth in the first place.

Basically branches of universes are made for each possible decision. The question is, where does it start and how? Also, who are they placing the wormhole for? Obviously for the humans, but when? As for the whole Brand's colonised humans on Edmunds planet become the 5D beings is impossible. Someone needed to have placed the wormhole there in the first place, otherwise the colony couldn't exist. I hope these theories (please remember they are theories!) have helped anyone who needed to know an answer. :)

author: @ShootBigBird2
text: Some comments: 1. The universe doesn’t need to “fold in on itself” as every point in spacetime can be connected to every other place in spacetime via a wormhole. Theodor Kaluza suggested this back in 1921. The ‘folding’ of spacetime is merely a visualisation method typically done with a flat piece of paper. In reality, a 5th dimension would exist everywhere, so spacetime doesn’t need to do anything (for all we know our subatomic particles may surge through higher dimensions constantly). 2. In Kips Thorne’s mind, the Waves on the planet would have been attributed to A) extreme Tidal Forces or B) Tsunamis caused by the planets crust being deformed (pulled up and down) by the extreme Tidal Forces…perhaps a combination of both. 3. The Time Dilation on the wave planet was due to its proximity of the Black Hole, more accurately, its’ deep position within the Black Holes Gravitational Field. Gravity is a field of acceleration, therefore, even though the planet holds orbit around the Black Hole (freefall around it) the effects of the accelerated field show up as Time Dilation…they would also look thinner from certain angles if viewed from an observer further out from the Black Hole (Lorentz Contraction). 4. As Cooper descends into the Black Hole he accelerates toward the Event Horizon where, spacetime reaches near lightspeed. Even though from Cooper's perspective he would actually pass through the Event Horizon (as radiation), an external observer would see his ship slow and eventually freeze in time, slowing down and never really reaching the Event Horizon. Cooper would seem to remain frozen in time from an external perspective, including clocks running back on Earth. Coopers’ radiation would finally be released once the Black Hole dies, about a trillion, trillion, trillion, trillion….years later, when all stars have long since died and the Universe is full of dying Black Holes and radiation. So no visitations with a 90yo daughter on her death bed. The movie conveniently used future human medalling here. 5. The Tesseract Dimension located within the Black Holes’ Singularity was actually very good. Cooper pointed out that it was, what he thought to be, our future selves (humans) giving their own survival a helping hand. It allowed the plot to stitch together a few of the Paradoxes relating to both Special Relativity and Time Travel. 6. Time Paradoxes. A) If Cooper didn’t send the coordinates, then they would never have visited NASA. Additionally, the MUST have found NASA first, before he even left for space, otherwise, how could he have even sent the coordinates? This is of course a typical Time Travel paradox just to mess with you (Neo’s Vase in the Matrix). Also, B) would the future humans even exist if they didn’t give Cooper a hand and link Murph’s bedroom to the Singularity? These are both ‘The Chicken Or The Egg’ type paradoxes.

text: There is, of course, one tremendous flaw in the whole premise of this movie---> that future humanity created all this to save the past humanity from extinction (can you see the flaw?). In any supposition of time travel, you must understand that there must always be an original time line where time travel did not exist. Once that time line progressed to where technology allowed time travel, any time travel to the past would 'alter' the original timeline from the point of interference. BUT there would have always been an original timeline. Therefore, if humanity had gone extinct in the original timeline, there is is NO WAY a future humanity could have existed to then have effected the past. Good movie...very flawed premise.

author: @shannonmcstormy5021
text: Mankind faces, right now, three primordial problems that we must solve to continue. The first is management of our instinctual, genetic predisposition/drive for hierarchy. While I don't think it is possible, arguably even desired to get rid of it entirely, humans are capable of managing this far better than we currently are. I am speaking of xenophobia, racism, sexism, nationalism, homophobia, etc. Our salvation is a genuine meritocracy balanced with compassion to keep the socioeconomic disparity between all humans to a minimum. Scandinavian countries are the most advanced in this area and a model for the direction we need to go. The second is to live in sustainable harmony with the planet. I believe that the key for us is to move 90% of our civilization underground, just, leaving communal spaces open to the sunshine and fresh air through towers, parks and perhaps biodome-greenhouse kinds of places, etc. Most of the land surface and most of the oceans should be dedicated to the natural world. Third and finally, Humans also need to start limiting our growth as a species, as the planet cannot sustain this many humans and certainly not more. If we can do this, as a species, we can survive. However, it is otherwise a tremendous barrier to our longevity as a species. We are on the verge of reaching a point of no return on all three of these issues. Sadly, I don't know how we accomplish the above. In Star Trek, we do so through First Contact. While obviously, we can't know for sure, but our current information about the universe doesn't include any evidence, any credible evidence, that aliens exist. Even if there is a First Contact situation, the above will remain a barrier that we would still need to resolve. Anyone reading this should keep in mind that our understanding of nature is poor at best, one where we perceive/understand the damage we are doing to the planet's biosphere as gradual. However, like in the movie, "Interstellar," it is possible that the damage we are doing to the planet may reach a sort of critical mass and then suddenly, starts to fail at a rapid rate, a catastrophic, unstoppable cascade. We clearly have the ability to do the above, and we must if we want to survive as a species. .

author: @brendan1871
text: tl;dr I thoroughly enjoyed this movie until about 4/5 through where this 'science-based' movie fails to stay consistent with its own established rules. Honestly, I liked the first ~4/5 or so of the movie. I loved the characters and how they made sure to pay attention to physics. Except for the Deus ex Machina dust that leads them to NASA, I was liking it. The movie explains relativity and the workings of a wormhole relatively well. I also liked how there were these mysterious 5th dimensional forces/beings that played into it. When they actually paid attention to how tides would work on a planet orbiting a black hole, caused me to think, "nice job on the director's part" (albeit planets orbiting a black hole in the first place doesn't really make sense seeing as a red giant supernova is required for its creation). They nailed relativity for the audience and I appreciate that. I even became teary-eyed at Cooper watching his children grow up as well as when Michael Caine's character died. I also became emotionally involved further by Spoiler: Mann's betrayal to the team. Despite all of praise however, ~4/5 the way through this movie, something happened. It was as if all the scientific understanding the plot was built on was thrown out the air lock. When Cooper sacrificed himself, I empathized a lot with the sadness. I was just about ready to cry again, when I saw that his part of the ship was surviving the accretion disk on the outside of the black hole. Mind you that a black hole's accretion disk is one the hottest places in the universe. Not only that, he enters the black hole as if it were something to enter, completely unscathed. Mr. Nolan, they are not actual holes, they are dense balls of matter. I mean a human and/or a ship would be torn apart and annihilated before they got near the event horizon. Even then, why is this mystical, 5th-dimensional space found in a dense ball of matter? And this not only affects my logical brain. Literarily, all of my sadness for the protagonist's sacrifice is swept away because hurr durr he survived the black hole. The movie then tries to tell the audience this 5th-dimensional space happens to be visible to our rudimentary visual senses and tangible to our physical bodies. It also argues that we have evolved to be 5th-dimensional beings. Christopher Nolan (or whoever made these decisions) apparently needs to go back to highschool Biology for an explanation of natural selection. They then include time paradoxes where it seems like we, humans, seem to have no free will after all (what would have happened if Cooper didn't go into the black hole, who would have been the Deus of the Machina). He then miraculously goes from the magical inside of a black hole in another galaxy back to near Saturn and none of my emotional investment is used except for the black astronaut (forgot his name) because everyone ends up living anyway and they could have just colonized around Saturn in the first place. This movie had potential, but it wasted it on some sappy, love-is-inherent-to-the-universe ending where there could have been actual emotion. On anotger note, for being all about using scientific explanations for things, the movie fails to stay consistant with them. In conclusion, if it had a better ending then I would have loved this movie, seeing as I loved the beginning.

author: @TheReaMrBurntSausage
text: I think what ruined the ending of the movie was the whole "Ghost" and "Evolved humans controlling other dimensions". I wish they just left it as a tragedy, and allowed Cooper to experience the Majesty of space, and how unforgiving time is. It could have sent a very powerful message, but I couldn't help but scoff at the arrogance of humanity, able to eventually bend time. How love transcends. Also, is it ethical to move humanity to another planet/universe in Plan B? I understand wanting to move those who are already alive to another planet in Plan A, but why bring embryos or whatever to another planet? Wouldn't that just be an invasive species? It was not meant to live there, I'm sure aged humans will face health complications, and its just not natural. I really appreciate how they tried to send a message to us about the loneliness of space, that scene with them floating by Saturn, which was much much larger than they were was amazing. The planet that was covered in water was breathtaking and also terrifying. I wish they drove home the impact of time, how that one guy waited 27 years for them to come, they probably should have time lapsed his life or something. He wouldn't possibly have stayed sane, let alone just jump back into completing the mission with them. What happened to Cooper's son at the end of the movie? Did he stay on Earth? Why did Cooper communicate with Murphy? He caused himself to leave by doing so. Anyway I really liked the movie, it's been a while since I've seen Inception, but I think this may have topped it in thought provoking-ness. I might watch this movie again, not 8 times like I did Inception, because Interstellar was soooooooooooooooo long. EDIT: Cooper had all the time in the universe to correct his mistake. They made it seem frantic when he could have done the watch thing at whatever point of time he wanted, I mean he could fly around to an earlier time. He could have written out more binary code earlier than when they went to Nasa

text: Gabriele Sessa nailed it and no one answered his question. PLEASE respond with an intelligent answer. Since Cooper communicated to Murphy, the equation was finished and they could launch the ship to saturn. Simultaneously, Anne Hathaway's character is starting a colony on the other side of the wormhole. Isn't this an oversight for the film? Since the equation was finished and the ship launched, what does it matter that there is a colony starting? Also, if the spaceship people were more advanced/older than Anne's colony (assuming you fast forward in time), wouldn't it be the spaceship humans to grow quicker and develop that extra dimension- wouldn't the future generations know of the wormhole people and the ship people? text: A couple things to note is that Dr.Brand sent the crew with only the intent to find a new hospitable planet and colonize the eggs. He had lost hope for the humans on earth. Once the purpose of the tesseract was accomplished, it closed and sent Cooper back to the solar system, eventually found by Cooper Station. The Dr.Brand death scene was the main plot twist in my opinion.

author: @somanytakennames
text: For me it was pretty average overall with some great moments sprinkled throughout. I buy all the science within the plot and was willing to suspend my disbelief to overlook and problems there might have been with the science, after all, it is science fiction. The problem I had was a major problem I've had with Nolan's films in general, it wasn't engaging on an emotional level. Considering how important the emotion is in Interstellar, that is a huge flaw. The only two moments that had any impact on me were the 'Goodbye' sequence and the part when Cooper watches the videos of his kids messages. Every other moment that was obviously meant to have an impact just fell flat for me. It was too long and it's hard to engage on an emotional level when most of the dialogue is exposition. So, no, don't think it was anything close to a masterpiece (Prestige and Batman Begins I still think are his best films). That being said, the docking scene was perhaps one of my favourite moments in the cinema this year.

author: @annonymousmaniaciii
text: There are a lot of things I want to say about Interstellar. And most of them would be about all the issues I had with the movie, like the continual exposition, or the uneven structure, or the fact that it tries to be so many different things at the same time and that not all of it is executed as well as it could have been. I could talk about the bloated running time, or the way the story funnels in on itself at a point and gives way to a partition of countless potential plotholes. I could think my way into Mandelbrotian spirals just contemplating the scientific accuracy. And I feel that the sheer volume of misgivings I have to say about it would deter from the fact that I highly recommend it, that it is a really good movie. It is intelligent, beautiful, consistently astonishing, and it really didn’t have to be three hours long, but it was still three hours of a captivating experience. I walked out of it silent, brow furled, thinking. That’s how I stayed all the way home. And I still had the rest of the day. 9/10

author: @megalomanninen
text: Here's my review i wrote on Facebook, please excuse some grammar flaws: As a huge sci-fi fan, who loves ‘2001: A Space Odyssey’, ‘Contact’, ‘Gravity’ and many other films that deal with the topics also covered in INTERSTELLAR, I have to say, I have major difficulties to dress my thoughts into words because this movie just took me for one hell of a ride and made my head spin! Also, the themes are so deep and mind-bending that my English vocabulary might not be sufficient enough for writing this review, but I’ll give it a shot. Try to understand. There are filmmakers who make excellent movies but still don’t bring anything new for the genre. Christopher Nolan doesn’t belong into this category. When Nolan makes a film, he doesn’t follow anyone’s footsteps and creates something that nobody else couldn’t even imagine. This is a part of that magic, how Nolan has made himself a strong fan-base and why he is so respected as a filmmaker in Hollywood. Interstellar is one of this year’s most anticipated and ambitious films, that, yet again, pushes the envelope. ‘Interstellar’ tells a story about a group of explorers, who surpass the limits of space travel by using a worm hole that they’ve just recently discovered. This worm hole allowes them to travel interstellar distances that otherwise have been impossible for the humanity. This is the plot in a nutshell and the less you know, the better. Without giving away any spoilers, I must say, that this story of saving the mankind from hunger and suffocating is one of the most fascinating and spectacular I’ve ever seen. Cooper (Matthew McConaughey, did i spell that right?) is a widowed farmer and a father, who lives with his children at a secluded farm. He’s also a former test pilot / engineer and throught particular coincidences ends up on NASA’s mission to secure mankinds survival. Cooper is the guy who you root for – he’s the “average joe” of the film, but still very intelligent. He focuses his love into his children and especially to his daughter Murphy. All the actors did an excellent job. To mention a few most memorable, David Gyasi who was one of the explorers and of course Nolan’s most frequent collaborator, Michael Caine. There are also a few fun surprises in the casting, which I also wont reveal. ‘Interstellar’ deals with many complex scientific theories, such as the theory of relativity and worm holes, but they’re explained in a very popularized way, so nobody would fell of the tracks. Space traveling in this film is visually the most beautiful ever put to screen. Every single shot feels carefully made and keeps the viewer gasping. The worm hole -trip is almost equally good with “2001’s” outstanding lightshow. Where Kubrick made abstract art of his worm hole-trip, Nolan pursued a more “realistic” take on his own. The way how Nolan has succeeded to keep a movie this magnitude from falling apart is a art form of its own. It is almost 3 hours long, but Nolan’s steady way of storytelling takes care of that there’s never a boring moment and nothing repeats itself. The score provided by Hans Zimmer was an extraordinary piece of work. It fits the movie so well that it was like the movie was made to fit the soundtrack and not the other way around. There is an interview with Christopher Nolan, in which he states that he wouldn't allow Hans Zimmer to know exactly what the movie's plot device is, he only told to him that he has to focus on the connection between father and daughter. If this is the truth - WOW! It worked flawlessly. Interstellar is definitely this year’s biggest film and seems to be Nolan’s personal “ode” to science fiction-movies. By time to time there are many references to the big classics, such as ‘2001: A Space Odyssey’ as I mentioned before. Where ‘2001’ speculated on the ultimate questions with an analytical and “slowly but surely”–type storytelling, Interstellar combines the analytical with the sentimental. Love is the whole foundation of this film, the core. No matter where the movie takes place, even in another galaxy searching for a inhabitable planet in dangerous circumstances, the love-theme is always present. The sentimental side is maybe emphasized even a little too much, but it doesn’t ruin the movie. The script is solid gold from beginning to the end. The small plot holes and technical things might bother a bit, but considering the movie’s magnitude and ambitiousness, there’s no question that there will be some minor flaws. But nevertheless, that doesn’t change the fact, that ‘Interstellar’ is a fucking great film and movie-event of the year!

text: My Personal Interpretation of Interstellar's Ending (With Spoilers and Evidence): During the infamous docking scene, Brand warns Cooper that the Endurance has no heat shield. Now, this is all fine and dandy, as they manage to pull the Endurance away from the planet's atmosphere before it burns up, but a plot whole seems to appear when you sit down and think about the black hole scene. author: @patrickometry
text: I found the film very frustrating and very disappointing. Here we have huge sums of money and energy and imagination spent placing a film realistically in space. It looks amazing. Unfortunately, the story itself devoted too much time to ordinary human relationships that we've seen a million times in countless other movies set in countless settings. Yes, we get it. They love each other. Yes, we get it. They'll miss each other. So instead of using the limited time available to explore more fascinating dramatic aspects of space travel, time, wonders, dangers, alien worlds, etc., we get large chunks of movie time devoted to convincing us that these human characters are emotional and have the "feelzies". So. Much. Time. Wasted. I also found big chunks of the philosophical dialogue stilted/awkward/eye roll worthy. One note, some of the space travel distances and travel time was conveniently fantastical/unrealistic. Sure there is the black hole/worm hole/time dilation explanation for some of it but outside of that, travel seemed to be almost instantaneous for those on board the ship traveling. And I hated the big revelation. No spoilers. I'll just say I found it incredibly dumb. Nothing can compare to the unfathomable immensity and awesomeness of the cosmos itself. No need to add silly craptacular hocus pocus mysterious plot device to bring home more of the "feelzies". In the end, a movie that immaculately set the stage for a story of grandeur and profound beauty and awe instead wasted the opportunity to satisfy the director's wish to show us how people can love and feel tormented by their love. My eyes cannot go back far enough in my head to emphasize how I feel about this. LOL. I could've just listened to the musical Rent or watched Meryl Streep in Sophie's Choice. My final thought to sum up: Why?

text: I enjoyed this movie immensely, but it was FULL of impossibilities and plot holes. For starters, the void near Jupiter? It was unnatural, and the future harvested 5th Dimension humans created it, yet in order for them to exist, we'd have to harvest the planet at the end of the movie, and for us to do that we'd need the void, but for the void to exist the 5th Dimensional humans would've had to make it and for them to exist...you get the idea: it's an infinite loop and it would have made sense if non-humans made the void. No, I'm not going to accept "alternate universes" either because A) the movie doesn't even come close to discussing this, and B) I will not accept fan fiction or nonsense to fill in the plot. Another point: since Cooper "solved" the puzzle he get's to escape a black hole and meet his daughter instead of being crushed by the greatest gravity conceivable? How did the daughter know he'd escape or when he'd escape? She makes this massive replica of the farm for him to stay for one night, then casts him off after seeing him for less than a minute? We saw their glass windows shatter from the super Tidal Wave: wouldn't that pose a problem getting back to their station through space? Those waves should have done much more damage considering they were 1000+ feet tall, right? Also, these waves came every minute or so, and if they managed to escape during the second wave, how did their trip of less than 5 minutes come out to be 23 years considering the rate was only 7 years per hour? Ice Clouds? The 5th Dimension is limited to a bedroom? Not really a plot point, but more of an error with Cooper: 5th Dimensional Cooper wants himself to STAY so he sends coordinates to NASA? If he had stayed, the whole movie never would have happened and 5th Dimensional Humans never would have existed.

author: @Silverwing_99
text: I disagree, I found this movie to be one of my all time favourite Nolan films after memento and inception. I also disagree with your assertion regarding the ending, the last 10 minutes were truly mesmerising. I found the scene where Cooper met his dying, senile daughter to be an epic, emotional milestone, and was well engineered, masterfully acted, and left the viewer feeling rather emotional, tearful, and able to connect with the daughter's naive, and chid like disposition - that she held onto the belief her father would return after almost 90 yrs of being away. The closing scene with Brand setting up a new colony, not knowing if she her attempts to establish a new human colony on Edmond's planet, plan A would be fruitful, and whether the sacrifice of all those people that had died for her to get to that point was in vain? Furthermore, would anybody come rescue her, would she simply enter the long nap to simply be forgetten and eventually decompose from neglect? For me, the ending was certainly profoundly emotional, more so than inception. My interpretation was that Nolan epitomised and conceptualised... dare I say an epistemological interpretation of two rather fascinating constructs: Murphy's law, and the boot-strap paradox. Furthermore, as an academic, a scientist, i was mesmerised by the way he depicted an abstract / conceptual paradigm of depicting a 5D world in 3d, and using gravity as an inter-dimensional vector was genius, and certainly plausible. Furthermore, the movie narrative for me was a journey, on so many level,s and had a profound emotional core, wrapped-up with a complex and intellectually captivating matrix of ideas and constructs, which for the most part remained faithful towards the current understanding of astrophysics and quantum mechanics. The fact the film used actual mathematical modelling grounded on astrophysical paradigms to render a realistic as possible visualisation of black holes were commendable. I can not emphasise the beauty and unprecedented accuracy of the way Nolan and Thorne depicted the black hole - truly astounding. This was thanks to having an actual scientist as an executive producer - Professor Kip Thorne, a monumental authority on his subject (Theoretical/ astro physics) in particular gravity, specifically the astrophysical implications of Einsteins theory of relativity, conceivably kept the script grounded in scientific rigour and accuracy. Moreover, Thorne also quite literally wrote the book on worm holes, even advising the illustrious Carl Sagan on the theory og worm hoes for his book. Finally, i only came to know of this film, as Kip authored two peer-reviewed academic papers on the computer simulated modelling on how light would be dragged into the black hole Gargantua.

author: @combustible287
text: -------------SPOILERS--------------- I really liked the first half, maybe 3 quarters of the film? But there was a point in the movie (You might know what point I am talking about) where the whole suspension of disbelief was thrown out the window. It became ridiculous really fast, and I personally do not think it was needed. If you haven't seen the movie, spoilers ahead. The part I am talking about is, of course, when the main character goes into a black hole and finds the singularity, can warp gravity, whatever. Seriously, what is up with this? The whole point of this was so that he can make the coordinates in the beginning with the dust and... a ghost thing. I just don't think that is enough to justify the black hole part. He could've found the coordinates somehow else, or even more logically, been reached by NASA for being a great pilot and all. I doubt they would spend so much money on a rocket just to find that no one could fly it. You may say that I "Just don't understand the complexity" but to be honest, it just doesn't work. I love when movies can get complicated. Source Code did a great job, because the surprise ending made sense in the world Source Code built. In Interstellar, we get the wormholes, yes, but those are hypothetical. So suspension of disbelief works as far as the wormholes go. But nothing about a singularity opening dimensions make sense. And the explanation that "A future civilization did it" it kinda bad writing. I loved the movie up until that point. I was at the edge of my seat, it was fun, it was great. But as soon as he entered that black hole, damn, I was pissed off. I'm not going to lie.

People immediately turned to each other and started discussing "optimistically" what they just watched, plot meaning, plot holes, plot success, over and over again. And I do mean everyone was talking about this film. Typically people just get up and leave, but people were trying to figure things out. Now I'm a space nerd, and I did understand a bit what some people didn't. So If you haven't seen this movie and want to, please stop reading now. This is the first real time I'm going to spoil your movie... but for those who saw this movie and didn't quite get the overall plot, here it goes. In the beginning of the movie, Michael Caine is telling McConaughey that there are two plans. Plan A and Plan B. Plan B is if plan A fails, Plan B is for the surviving Astronauts to fertilize the human eggs and grow people on a new world. And Plan B really sucks, because it means all of the people on Earth were left to die off. Now here's where some people were lost. When McConaughey is leaving on his voyage, he believes that Michael Caine is trying to solve the "Gravity equation." In science today, we observe Gravities effect, but we don't understand how it really works. We don't know how to "change" gravity. We spin a spaceship to simulate the effect, but NASA's biggest challenge is lifting mass into space. That is why it is expensive to go to space, and the space stations are flimsy. We can build gigantic aircraft carriers, and submarines. Those things are engineering marvels, but we can't get something that large into space, not even much smaller parts can be sent up and assembled in space. Working on the Hubble is daunting. At the "near" end of the movie, McConaughey learns that Michael Caine gave up on solving the gravity equation before McConaughey ever left the Earth. Caine was supposed to be solving the equation. (Realistically that isn't going to happen in one mans lifetime, Einstein worked on it, and those working on it today are exploring theoretical dimensions of space because it's completely baffling them) I think the explanation on Caine's death bed was that he knew he couldn't solve the gravity equation, or his answer was always going to be bad. So at the end of the movie, McConaughey and a Robot go into the black hole. And that's when he finds out that the black hole was artificial and there's something inside the black hole. Some far superior alien or human civilization from the future, that can send information back in time, is trying to give McConaughey the needed Gravity Equation. McConaughey uses the robot to translate the advanced message into binary code. Mind you, McConaughey is floating inside this giant space corridor, that is supposed to be a doorway to transmit information to someone on the Earth. It happens this door is locked, but on the other side of the locked door is his daughters bookshelf at his home on Earth. The aliens or humans from the future selected this one small space on the Earth and all of time for the rooms existance... So if he moves to his left, he sees his daughter as a child, he moves more to his left, he sees his daughter a little older... and so on and so on.. He can see all of the time play out like a reel of tape. If he tugs on these gravity strings, he can influence the gravity on the bookshelf, or anything in that room. So he uses gravity to send information to a watch on the bookshelf. He uses Morse Code on the watch minute hand to send the binary code information. He's moving the minute hand of his mechanical watch, and at a young age, early in the movie, McConaughey and his daughter realize something is weird with the gravity and the watch in that room, but never undertsttod what was going on. It's a plot device that led McConaughey to a secret NASA site. Later in the movie, we find out iMcConaughey is actually sending the information from the future back in time to Earth via the gravity string waves. And finally his adult daughter understands the Morse Code on the watch is binary cod information, and she brings the data back to NASA. McConaughey is then released from the black hole, and picked up in space by this giant human spaceship that is transporting cities, and baseball fields, and Museums, and probably millions of human beings. Not everyone in the movie theatre seemed to understand that Plan A was to save as many human beings as possible, not just the frozen embryos. So what happened..... they provided NASA the gravity equation that allowed humans to build and launch things into space with no weight limits. Imagine if you could just turn off gravity or reverse its flow, you could jump into space. And at the beginning of the movie, an Astronaut was afraid of how flimsy his spaceship wall was, at the end of the film, humans were having a good time on massively well built Goliath Generation Space Ships. They were either heading for a new planet, or just enjoying being in space on a new artificial planet. The movie ended with McConaughey going after the girl, Anne Hathaway. We figure humans didn't want to live on her planet, so McConaughey is going to rescue her or something.

author: @maxrakuscek9135
text: MAJOR SPOILERS I was disappointed by the movie. It wasn't bad and we could argue that it was all the Nolan-fanboyism (because I seriously loved everything else he's done) and all the hype to create a feeling of letdown, but if you think about it, the whole movie feels as if all of the fiery passion behind the project didn't translate to the screen completely, it has this feeling of unfinishedness, if you get what I mean. The whole twist of humanity being doomed from the start isn't half as twisty and gut-punching as you would expect from Nolan, there's a whole lot of science stuff I didn't quite understand and left me very confused at the supposably intense spaceship scenes, the emotional scenes didn't work as much as they would have to for their amount (It really tried to play on the audience crying and similar, while a lot of people were actually laughing in my theatre during Michael Caine's poem reciting and the "we lost 20 years" scene. Sure, they were dickheads, but when half the audience chuckles when they're supposed to cry, something's wrong.) and most importantly, the movie overweights itself. Inception is a great, smart film, because it knows exactly how smart it is and doesn't aspire to be anything bigger, while still being an exceptionally intelligent movie. Interstellar, though, tries to be this gigantic 2001-ish meditation on the existence of humanity and just isn't as smart as it thinks it is. Just because you touch amazingly deep themes doesn't neccesarily mean you explore them and some of the acting and dialogue (KHM MATT DAMON KHM THAT FIGHT SCENE) were just too silly to fit in the serious tone they were going for. Props for the ambition, but Nolan simply tried too much, which sounds odd after already accomplishing so much with his previous work, which I feel like half of it is better than Interstellar, for which he quite obviously intended to be The Mindblowing Movie of the Century. For me, it will always be Inception. 7.5 / 10. The score and visuals are PERFECT, though

author: @LukeCampbellBrennan
text: Wow I don't really have a dog in the fight of film glitterati. I can say the Prestige is probably in my top 20 tho, and I also should mention I LOVE sci-fi, am a total sucker for it. Give me Zach Quinto, some technobabble and a mystery from beyond the stars, and I'm in heaven. You did talk about the good parts of this movie; the set-up of his family life, the launch into space, and the special effects. Unfortunately, 2 out of 3 of those are gone by act 2, (and then the fact that we learn his daughter has worked for NASA and knows full well that her father left on a mission TO SAVE THE HUMAN RACE - makes her 'my daddy left me here to die' grudge she's carrying into her 20s well, unbelievable.) And that's where interstellar breaks down for me - the characters stop having coherent motivations basically as soon as they pass thru the wormhole. The fact that the characterization and internal logic of the film shatter to pieces in the second act, and the ending that you said felt like everything tied up with a little bow, well, what about humanity? The planet? Why is there a space station around saturn but Brand is all alone on the colony world? This is a movie that does not reward thinking, and I wish it weren't the case, but the movie passes itself off a smart space action film, but at the end of the day, is not only not clever, but in fact pretty stupid. It hits important emotional points all the way thru, so I guess it could be said this is a movie that rewards feeling. But can't I have my cake and eat it too? Can't sci-fi have a logical plot AND emotional depth? 3/10 in my eyes for this one, sorry to say, and your review has me questioning your judgment (this is my first time on your channel). I hit the subscribe button because I'm all about second chances but wow are you wrong about this flick.

author: @waxwingvain
text: The people that didn't understand this movie either had the wrong expectations or they just don't have the sufficient physics background to truly admire this movie. I agree with Chris regarding the flaws in the narrative structure but it's not something that could ruin the whole experience. The plot was fairly consistent in my opinion and everything fell in its right place, which is not something wrong. The emotional bonds are very strong and the main characters are well developed, even the robots! The CGI was more than amazing and the score by Zimmer doesn't disappoint. The last 10 minutes of the film Chris describes it as a bit unnecessary but I disagree with that. The last 10 minutes were consistent and showed perfectly how abstract/imaginative Nolan can be with this movie. But would it have been better without these last 10 minutes? The problem is that we can't know for sure because we experience the movie as it is and saying it could have been better without x or y is nothing but speculation. If you're going to see this movie and expect an emotional punchline at the ending just as in Inception or something similar to it, might leave you disappointed. Expectation is a bias that can ruin your experience. You should rate a movie for what it is not for what it could have been. At the very least an A does it more justice in my opinion.

author: @djstud1987
text: Just saw it. I would not boo it for the lack of ambiguity or a thought provoking story line usually associated with Nolan's work. The ambiguity is there. You just need to understand enough science (not saying this in a rude way), to get to a point where you can distinguish between what made sense and what was ambiguous. In my opinion, you should not be a physicist to understand a commercial movie. The dependence of the movie on such complex concepts is what weakens the movie's story line, if at all, and is probably the reason why a lot of people are not liking it. On a different note though, I don't want to play spoilers here, but a few black hole related concepts depicted in the movie are really interested and thought provoking, especially for science fans. If you care even a little about space time, relativity, time dilation etc. this movie should be an epic for you. I bet you will love it. I would not say that the science the movie showcases is wrong, but a few of the concepts the film decides to ride with, will leave you ambiguous. In other words, if you care about the scientific concepts I mentioned above, you will certainly want to discuss it with your colleagues and friends to clarify a few things. The story chooses to stick with certain theories out of all the possible options available in case a particular event were to happen. This certainly leaves a room for discussion and hence the ambiguity. But for the people who care little about the science behind the movie, there will be no ambiguity because they basically wouldn't want to spend several hours to understand the basics of those concepts, in the first place.

author: @achilleshoplite
text: Christopher Nolan attempts to make his own version of "2001: A Space Odyssey" and overreaches himself. He does this by attempting in a convoluted and near desperately contrived manner, to explain the mystery that "2001: A Space Odyssey" left intentionally unsolved. A transcendent presence in the Cosmos that is above space and time is best to remain unexplained, ambiguous, and enigmatic as "Contact" also managed to do. But Nolan really tried to give it an explanation and it can only leave you baffled, confused, and bewildered. Not because it's necessarily esoteric, but because it's near nonsensical.

text: I agree with some of the critiques of this film, but I thought the narrative structure was fine -- definitely better than some of Nolan's other works. But B+, really? I definitely feel this is an A-quality film. Hell, Nolan actually allowed more humor in this than usual, and he very much is against the presence of too much humor.
