author: @Epyon2007
text: So imagine this scenario: Prof. Brand and the NASA team are trying to figure out Plan A but they can't solve the equation. Originally there is no wormhole, and they are stuck on Earth as the blight is happening. Brand sends a team of astronauts and robots on a ship and travel to Gargantua without a wormhole (it just takes hundreds of millions of years). During this time they are in hibernation. They finally arrive on the planet, colonize, and send a probe into the black hole that relays the data to solve Plan A. After a long enough time of living on Gargantua, they evolve into 5D beings, and using the data from the probe in the black hole, they create the wormhole. Since its 5D, they can go back and change events (time is not linear anymore). They make the wormhole, place it near Saturn, and then the events in the movie play out as we see them. This way there is no longer a temporal paradox, because the wormhole was not constructed out of thin air. This fits well with the movie's tagline: "Mankind was born on Earth, it was never meant to die here". Originally, mankind did die on planet Earth except for the select few that made it to Gargantua and colonized the remaining humans. It was only after evolving into 5D beings that they could go back and prevent mankind from perishing on Earth. The tagline is alluding to this theory because mankind did originally die on Earth, but eventually they went back after evolving to prevent mankind from dying on Earth in the first place.

I wouldn't see this in theatres again. Maybe I'll watch it on Netflix one day, maybe not.

text: This movie hit my brain like something dumb that thought it was really smart and then tried to distract me from its dumbness with SPACE. The main character could have been played better by Dennis Quaid. The setup undermined credibility at several points. If they had just started in space without all the backstory this could have been better. But then it would have been a more direct ripoff of a Disney movie no one remembers called The Black Hole. Real astronauts would have been more concerned about not introducing Earth's blight onto new planets. Wouldn't it be easier to fight a plant blight (fungal pest?) than go to a new planet and reinvent all of agriculture? Why do the textbooks say that the moon landing was faked? How would that inspire people to work together instead of competing in society?!!! Why can't society have cooperation AND competition? Why does it seem like Paul Ryan wrote this script and shoehorned in his pet ideas? If the economy collapsed and everyone starves, how is there a space mission hidden in a convenient secret mountain? Is this whole movie actually a figment of the main dude's imagination? Actually that would make slightly more sense than trying to take it all seriously.

text: I agree with Chris, the ending was a bit of a let down. Its hard not to compare it to 2001, and one of the things that I loved about 2001 was that the ending, and in fact the entire film wasn't spelled out, you had to go and research what it meant and so that sense of wonder and awe about outer space carried on after the film ended. text: When I first watched this film, I could understand not liking the ending. the whole string theory thing was just weird and seemed so outlandish compared to the other events that happened up until that point, which had all been in space or on a planet- fairly normal in comparison. But after rewatching the film years later with a better understanding of dimensions and space time, the ending is utterly amazing. They found a way to depict a 5 dimensional world that a 3 (4 with time) dimensional being like us can perceive and interact with. the access to the extra dimension allows Coop to travel through time just as we travel through the three dimensions of space in our world. The incomprehensibility of the ending is perfect, as we aren’t able to comprehend dimensions beyond our realm anyways. We aren’t supposed to understand it, yet it really makes perfect sense. This movie is a masterpiece. It sparked an interest in made me understand things about time and relativity i hadn’t known before. Revisiting the film with these understandings just hits even harder.

text: Just to clarify, "Moby Dick" is actually seen in the opening shot of the bookcase at 4:13 and not only at 20:03. The sequence of the books in that set order are actually Easter eggs for the story that have significant meaning. For instance, if we look at the books "The Stand," "Armistead Maupin," "Moby Dick," and "House of the World" in this order, we can see that each book reflects a key theme in the movie: "The Stand" is about the aftermath of a catastrophic pandemic and the rebuilding of society. This serves as the first hint of the story, emphasizing humanity's struggle and resilience in the face of disaster. The two books to the right, which are not clearly identifiable, likely hold their own significance. "Armistead Maupin" chronicles the lives of a group of people in San Francisco over several decades, depicting the changes and developments in their lives and society. This parallels Murph and Tom aging and explaining their stories without their father over decades. "Moby Dick" delves into existential themes and the relentless passage of time during Captain Ahab’s obsessive quest for the white whale. This reflects Murph's obsession with finding the answers to the gravitational equation and understanding the message left by her father, as well as Coop's obsession with finding a new home for humanity. "The House of the World" spans multiple generations, exploring the history and legacy of a family over time. This is seen through Tom getting older and having kids, and Coop missing out. Similarly, Amelia Brand and her father John Brand's relationship highlights generational sacrifice and legacy. By placing these books together, "Interstellar" subtly emphasizes the importance of time in human narratives, reflecting the film's exploration of time dilation, generational legacies, and the enduring impact of human actions across time. The juxtaposition of these books serves as a metaphor for the complex relationship between time, memory, and storytelling, all of which are crucial themes in the movie.

text: I loved Interstellar. The only quibble I have with the film is the casting of Matt Damon. I don't have a problem with Matt Damon in general, but he seemed a little too young to fill the role of Dr. Mann. Mann was presented as someone who was an almost larger-than-life inspiration for the Lazarus program... I think one actor who could have played the role a little more convincingly would have been Gary Sinise. SInise is older, and could have added a bit more depth and maturity to the character. I associate Sinise with roles like those in Apollo 13, but in Forrest Gump he showed that he could play a character with a little more edge, but not to the point where that quality overwhelms the character. Just my opinion...

author: @Noone-of-your-Business
text: Weeeell,... meh. I was quite disappointed by the way that the movie builds great expectations and then completely fails at delivering. Take the super serious science approach, for example: the film invalidates all that setup with silly turns like the scientist who explained time dilation to the audience later being surprised at how dilated time was. This insults my intelligence as a viewer. Very much the same way, Hathaway's ultra-rational scientist character later proclaims love to be the most powerful force in the universe (*and* the only one capable of exceeding the speed of light!); that's right, no points for gravity! I can't wait for the Big Bang Theory episode in which Sheldon ridicules this nonsensical script writing. And that is pretty much what ruined the film for me: the story breaking its own premise - moving from super scientifically correct to wishful thinking, Disney style. "Sunshine" had the same problem (only that it veered from ultra-science to flat-out moronic zombie apocalypse from hell, Doom style...). So, sorry: I quite disagree on this one, but I do appreciate your approach.

text: I’d give it a B. Exposition can work sometimes, but the exposition in this film was excessive. Plus, all the exposition the film had was confusing and hard to follow. You can get the gist of it, but it’s just not good enough for me. In Inception, Following, and Memento, the plots were complex, but still made perfect sense to me. I couldn’t understand much of anything going on in this film. On the bright side, however, the character development between Cooper and Murph, Hans Zimmer’s score, the brilliant cinematography made up for some of the convoluted plot. I really liked the realism in Cooper and Murph’s relationship, the score was both riveting and heartbreaking, and there were some shots that I just stared at, wide-mouthed. A specific shot of Saturn actually brought a little tear to my eye.

text: Hi Chris. I'm afraid I'm going to have to respectfully disagree with you. I think this movie is criminally OVER-rated. Hanz Zimmer's score is SUB-standard. It consists of ONE...count 'em ONE 4 chord theme that is played over...and over...and over...with someone turning the volume up and down for emotional effect. The last act where Matthew McCanaughey's character fell through the event horizon of a black hole...survived(completely impossible) and ended up in a tesseract(also completely impossible) destroyed my ability to suspend my disbelief and enjoy it...And I was enjoying it up to that point(music, notwithstanding). Those who think this film is on the level of "2001: A Space Odyssey" are seeing something in this film that has completely eluded me, as I consider "2001: A Space Odyssey" to be one of 5 of the best science fiction films ever made and had so many layers of profound exploration into the human condition and levels of existence, that very few films will ever reach for. "Interstellar" has none of that. It's just another soap opera with a science fiction setting film that had exceptional special effects. Of course, your mileage may vary, but that's my opinion for what it's worth, my friend. Peace.

author: @NightWanderer31415
text: Interstellar really is a movie that improves with multiple viewings. The first time I saw it I felt something was lacking... yet I was intrigued enough to go see it again. And then everything clicked. One of the most ambitious movies I have ever seen, and at least a solid A for me. Also daunting (although not necessarily relevant for a review) is the enormous amount of solid science behind the movie. 'Interstellar' is the only movie that I know of that actually produced scientific papers (concerning the advanced black hole visualizations produced for the movie). In fact, renowned physicist Kip Thorne (recently awarded the Nobel Prize for the detection of gravitational waves) was deeply involved and did a ton of calculations that were then used by the special effects team. Advanced topics of General Relativity and Quantum Mechanics make an appearance (you can actually see some String Theory equations on the blackboards). In this regard, I think the movie is truly inspirational (enough at least to inspire me to learn GR).

author: @rickbishop-i4j
text: Time dilation can be better understood by considering space not as a vacuum, but as a dynamic ocean of energy and matter. Our solar system is a low-density, highly charged environment due to our sun, allowing energy to move freely. Outside of it, space becomes denser, with more resistance to energy flow. Einstein's model of relativity is brilliant but based on observations limited to our solar system. Time dilation, in my view, isn’t about spacetime bending but energy moving slower through denser, more charged regions of space. Light itself slows as it interacts with these mediums, creating the effect we perceive as time dilation. Space isn't empty—it's full of energy, pressure and density,, evidenced by phenomena like massive water clouds retaining their density in space. This suggests that time dilation is a result of energy navigating through these complex dynamics.

text: Since black hole time dilation depends on the distance someone is away from the black hole, if the people who landed on "Miller's planet" were at the same distance from the black hole as the ship orbiting above them, then the people on Miller's planet would age at the same rate as the person left behind on the ship in orbit. As long as the ship orbited around Miller's planet in a plane orthogonal to the black hole, and the people on the planet were in that same plane, then they would all age at the same rate. "Miller's planet" would be tidally locked to the black hole much like Mercury is tidally locked to the sun. So the guy in the orbiting ship wouldn't have aged any more than the people on the planet.

text: If time dilation is associated with both mass and speed playing a part together, it is the movement or no movemement of mass that creates time dilation. The speed at which mass moves through the aether determines how much time dilation there will be. Mass plus its speed determine how much the time is slowed down. A massive body moving "slowely" can have or create as much time dilation as a small mass moving at extreme speeds. It comes down to how much aether is displaced over a set period of time. A small object traveling at extreme speeds can displace as much aether as s larger mass does that moves slower. In both cases, it is the aether displacement pressing against the mass that causes time dilation and gravity. This pressure, I call gravity. The pressure causes the matter, its true mass, the quarks, to expend energy fighting the pressure and thereby the vibrations of the atomic forces slows down. The atoms experience a slowing down of time, how they "experience" the passing of "time". Time, itself, does not slow down. What does slow down is the matter and how matter reacts to other matter. Computers' functions slow down. The half life of radioactive elements increases. Our brains, our bodies move slower because the matter that makes us, runs slower. We move slower because our cells cannot move any faster. Think of that SiFi movie where the actor moves fast past people who seem to be frozen in place. Each person, all matter, is moving as fast as the matter it or he is made of allows. A big mass moving slow and a smaller mass traveling fast can experience the same amout of time dilation. It is the reaction of mass to the aether and visa versa that controls. A black hole, because of its intense mass and “gravity”, stops all matter from moving; the strong forces are neutralized. The protons, neutrons, electrons, quarks.. become one big mass with NO space between them. Their linearity contracts to nothing. Their mass expands to “infinity”, as measured per volume compared to what it was before being a black hole. Matter traveling at or near the speed of light experiences similar results. There is extreme length contraction; the matter is compressed so there is no room at all between the protons, neutrons, electrons. The mass of the matter is compressed to a small point so that mass per cubic nanometer reaches infinity. Mass per volume increases.

text: To understand better about gravity and time dilation, it is best to look at gravity differently. The "majority" of the Einstein physicists look upon gravity as an "attraction" between two masses; the greater the mass, the greater the gravity. They do not think of gravity as a force. This view does not help with understanding why "time" slows down for mass traveling at great speeds; or explain the time dilation near large clusters of matter. They use math unnecessarily to create an explanation. My view: matter and the aether do not mix or react well with each other. Matter is made up of baryonic "matter"; not much smaller than the protons and neutrons in an atom. The aether has "energy packets", strings if you will, that are hundreds of times smaller than the protons and neutrons. These "unknown" items make up the aether, the fabric of space. When mass intrudes into the aether, the aether is pushed aside and the aether pushes back with what we call gravity. Much like when you pack snow together to make a snow ball. The strands of force, or gravity, are close together near the earth and become further apart as distance increases away from the center of mass. This does not mean that there is "no" aether inside the earth, between the atoms or inside the atoms; it means that there is LESS space for the aether. This gravity presses on the matter and distorts it, causing its internal parts to move slower. This is why atomic clocks, computers, our brains, the half life of radioactive elements are running at the speeds they do. Away from the earth, say, at the lLegrange point of the moon, directly opposite to the moon on the other side of the earth, all those bits of matter will run a bit faster. Gravity is not pressing them as much. As matter speeds up, leaving the earth and sun behind, it, the matter, is first running faster than the twin matter on earth. At some higher speed the tome of the matter slows down to the same time as experienced on earth. Going much faster, the time of such matter starts to run slower than the twin matter back on earth.... WHY IS THE DIFFERENCE that the Einstein physicists do not see. That fast moving matter ALSO pushes against the aether and the aether ALSO pushes back with gravity. This gravity again distorts the matter, causing EVERYTHING TO SLOW DOWN. --- much slower than the same matter left behind on earth. It is because of this "gravity" effect that ten years on that space ship equates to perhaps a thousand years passing back on earth. When you watch the move "Interstellar" think on the above to make sense out of it. No math needed. cbodor@roadrunner.com

text: I still want a sequel. Also, when I was a kid, before the term Wormhole had entered the pubilc's lexicon, someone explained to me why it was necessary for mankind to actually explore using space technology in the absence of a "Wormhole". Kinda goes like this... In the beginning, the Earth was perceived to be so big, that because man could only walk and ride animals, he probably thought of the planet the same way man does today about the universe. But his human spirit-for-adventure told him he had to try and find out what lay beyond the horizon. Man 2.0 was Christopher Columbus and those we today refer to as Explorers. Man 3.0 came to be when he defied gravity and flew. Imagine though, the small amount of years between the first crossing of the ocean by boat, and the first time it was done by a plane... Only because the planet is now so small can it argued that: If that ocean had been sufficiently large, Columbus would have been wasting his time. Could you imagine being two-hundred yards off the shores of a new land only to see this new-fangled flying machine go over your head and land while you're still bob on the water? author: @tomkam9783
text: I know this is already in the comments somewhere, but...Millers planet orbits Gargantua. In order for it to maintain an orbit, it must be going fast enough - or far enough away, or both - to maintain that orbit. Mercury orbits our sun at at maximum of ~59 km/sec. Almost twice the speed that Earth does. Mercury is much closer to the sun than Earth, yet the gravity on Mercury is still less than that of Earth. It doesn't matter how big or how powerful Gargantua is, something can still orbit it safely. A ship could land on it, and you could walk around on it without issue, because that is the gravity of Millers planet. They never said (I don't think) how far Millers was orbiting from Gargantua, but it's possible it's as far away as the Kuiper Belt for us, and the orbital velocity of Millers is in the THOUSANDS of Km/sec. (not going to do the math, thanks). Regardless, Millers is STILL under the influence of Gargantuas gravity well, just as our suns gravity well extends light years into interstellar space, and it's under THAT influence that cause the time dilation effect. Everything SEEMS normal because EVERYTHING is being affected equally by Gargantua, and we're all moving at the same relative velocity, together, in the same orbit. And really, it's not the gravity that will kill you, if you get close enough, it will be the radiation and the tides: Gravity so strong that the difference between your feet and your head REALLY makes a difference. This is what Neil DeGrasse Tyson means when he says you will be "spagettified."

text: Seriously this whole time dilation thing is just an illusion. I'm sure that if we could actually send someone through space at the speed of light and come back both him and us on Earth would have aged at exactly the same rate. Then scientists would look like fools and have to revise their precious theory. Too bad we can't test this on living beings to see if the actual aging process of cells is affected by moving at higher speeds. Satellite's running at slightly different speeds is no proof of actual time itself slowing down for three simple reasons: -The radius of a satellite's orbit is greater than the radius of Earth which has to be taken into account to calculate the exact time for a specific position on Earth. -It takes time for signals to be sent back and forth (lag). -Mechanical devices (such as clocks) and the electrons which power them function differently without the interaction of gravitational forces. The only way to really prove time dilation is to study the aging rate of cells from a living organism moving at near lightspeed. Which is basically impossible. And until we find a way to do this, time dilation remains a fantastic science fiction theory.

text: Time doesn't exist. It's great for metering human consciousness, but the cosmos doesn't operate in time. Time isn't constant. Your body would surely last much longer far away from gravitational bodies pulling you down and weather/atmosphere/bodily functions/entropy aging you. Going FTL to a different galaxy/solar system would create a dilation between the aging of those on earth, and the aging of those on the ship. You may find another solar system has more density and faster aging may occur. You may find a system that extends your life. Either way, going FTL away from the Earth could put you in a position where time moves slower. We could also find that going FTL will kill everyone on board. No one's done it yet.

The gravity of the black hole would be AMPLIFIED by the time dilation factor as well by the same factor of 60 thousand, meaning just by traveling at that speed, the tidal force felt by the planet would be 60 thousand times greater than it would be if it was in freefall directly into the black hole, which would already be an awful lot. And even if the planet was strong enough to hold together under those forces, there are no stable orbits within much further out from it than that, meaning all orbits either slowly spiral out from the black hole or they spiral in. If they tried to "land" on this planet, they would careen into it with such speed that the resulting explosion would make the asteroid that hit the Earth 66 million years ago look like a firecracker. Now if the black hole was rotating, as it would be, as any black hole is, you could have stable orbits much closer to it, but only within certain feasible limits, and those limits don't even come close to allowing a ratio anywhere near the ballpark of 60 thousand. MAYBE, just MAYBE, you could have a situation where it's 6 days on the planet, one week back on Earth. text: Why did the ticking sound start at only 48 BPM, to end up at 60 after a step of 50 BPM? EDIT: I realized there must have been a gravitational wave to make this delta-time possible. But there is no grav-wave needed to make a water-wave! The water-wave is constant, relative to the mass attracting it. Because only recently I have learned that a water-wave is not moving to "us", but a location of the planet rotates towards the wave! And if a planet-location rotates towards the wave, then that location will experience a difference in gravity, and therefore time! And now it makes sense and explains why the tick-speed increases. But now there's a problem: why did it start with 45 ticks/second? This only means the ticks we hear is from the perspective of earth relative to the astronauts. But in that case, as the astronauts are rotated towards the grav-wave, their time - according to earth - must go even slower! So the tick-speed should go even slower! Not faster! It appears I've identified a well hidden flaw here.

author: @SashaPshenychniy
text: Astronauts orbiting Earth feel 0% gravity because of orbiting our planet. However that doesn't mean they are not subject to time dilation. You better check some interviews with physicist who have been Nolan's consultant and was doing tough job to find compromise between plot and physics as to how far can time dilation be on a stable orbit around a rotating black hole (7 years per hour is theoretically impossible for regular non-rotating black holes). It's also fascinating how a team of software developers worked on simulation of how black hole should look like (because no graphics engine supports curved space-time) and how it appeared to be 'visually not appealing' for such an extreemely rotating one, so they had to compromise. However, when few years later a real photo of a black hole was made - it proved simulation from the movie was very accurate.

text: This is actually not how time dilation works. It's an observational phenomenon. In extreme fields of gravity you do not age slower than people that are on earth. The rate at which the light you emit is received by the observer is slower than the rate of light the observer would receive if you were standing both in the same gravitational field.

text: Something never dealt with in space movies is the mechanics of landing on planets, or going into orbit around planets, then trying to leave. Just take a look at the size and power of the rockets needed to lift the tiny Apollo spacecraft and accelerate it to over 25,000 miles per hour in order to "escape" Earth's gravity well and head for the Moon! That's why going to Mars is "easy" when it comes time to return home, but landing or, or even orbiting another planet the mass of Earth is virtually impossible with current technology. Whereas you can "drop into" orbit quite easily using the Sun's gravity to accelerate you to the needed insertion velocity which is of course dictated by how CLOSE you want to be to the freaking SUN! Orbit at distances similar to Earth-bound satellites would require about 900,000 miles per hour velocity which is a bit faster than the 17,500 mph needed for a low-Earth orbit. To break out and leave you'd have to accelerate up to over 2,000 feet per second which is a lot faster than escaping Earth at a piddling 37 feet per second! To go to a massive object, planet, star, or black hole and "orbit" anywhere even remotely near would demand you be carrying a GIGANTIC spaceship filled with all the resources to manufacture fuel from the materials found in space! Even then, going down to the surface and tryhing to loft back up again would require massive engines, burning huge amounts of fuel - lifting both the lander and all that fuel back into orbit, where the giant fuel-factory space ship would have to do the REAL WORK of accelerating out of orbit.

And then I see them liking comments saying it's the best explanation ever, when it's literally incorrect.

text: So I'm going to hold you up for a second. I think the reason behind millers planet's time dilation is not it's own gravitational warping but due to the planet's orbit within the extreme gravitational field of gargantua. Given how close it was to the event horizon without actually having crossed it, that would make sense. One thing that would've been much more iffy is the transiting of the black hole not stopping time completely for the spacecraft as he was able to go back to earth and his daughter was still living (if only briefly). If he has gone past the event horizon, and if he hadn't gotten spaghettified or just ceased experiencing time, the dilation would still be tremendous. And given how long he spent inside the singularity, he could've literally watched the whole universe crunch and bang several times over. I get it though, there is indeed lots of amazing science in the movie and I am endlessly appreciative of that but there's also the fantasy aspects like entering the singularity and traversing all those dimensions and seeing earth and shit. I'd it was all scientific to a fault I will (begrudgingly) admit that the poetry and emotional weight of the movie would be diminished. Interstellar really does strike a nearly perfect balance between science reality and science fiction. And the musical score just is absolutely maddeningly intense and beautiful.

author: @liteney
text: Am I the only one who feels this movie lacked all emotion and that the characters failed to behave like people at all? The first hour and a half was so boring, they refused to go into depth on any of the characters other then, 'Murph is smartest and greatest person in Human History, all puny humans bow to Murph!! Oh... and side note, he has a son as well. Now Bow to Murph puny humans, bow to Murph!!!' We didn't get any background or history on the 'blite' that was killing all the crops. They failed to explain why they couldn't just move underground and re-grow them in green houses. Why they couldn't move to another planet like Mars or even the Moon, move underground there and again re-grow the crops in green houses and populate until they found a another Earth through the worm hole. They failed to mention what was going on in the rest of the world, ie: food riots, wars, civil and national, etc: other then that stupid little town that just happened to be sitting on top of NASA, what luck... derp... This super science-y movie failed to mention where the water for the mountain sized water waves came from, 'There was only about 2 - 3 feet of water on that planets surface right, and if you stand on the beach when waves come in or know what a tidal wave or Tsunami is, you would know that all the water gets sucked out to form the tidal wave or Tsunami. But the water they were standing in did absolutely nothing not moving at all while giant water mountain waves just kept running along the surface on about three feet of water, for reasons... That is until they needed to kill off a useless character and the water suddenly moved to kill him on command, again for reasons... The videos sent to the astronauts by their families was the worst part of this movie in my opinion, because it was a chance to add character development showing the kids grow up, but yet again it had no emotion at all. In 23 years of messages all you see is his son send one video message in saying he met a girl, one where he said they had a kid, then a third where he says, 'Grandpa's dead and we buried him with grandma and our baby in the back yard, oh wait, I didn't I tell you your grandson died? Yeah well he died...' 'Anyway... back to Murph the Awesome and all powerful, isn't she great!!' Murph grows up to be a Super Smart, Awesome, Godlike human, better then all puny humans, but we don't see any of it in the video messages. Because even though she knows what her dad did risking his life to jet off into space trying to save humanity from extinction, because she's super smart and awesome, and she joined NASA, left her home and her family, to try and save humanity herself. Yet she's still mad at him and won't talk to her dad who risked him life by going off into space to save humanity or send him any messages because... reasons??? There's so much more I could go into about the total lack of plot, story line and character development but... 'Look at the Special Effects!!!' 'Listen to that awesome soundtrack!!!' ''Wow... they said science-y explain-y stuff in this movie, they said wormhole, isn't that awesome, what a great movie!!' 'If Murph don't solve some bullshite science-y explain-y gravity stuff then they can't build space stations or spaceships, put people on them and send them into space!!' 'But we've had space stations and space ships since the 1950's, they have space stations and space ships in this movie without all that gravity bullshit, they're already underground, why can't they just place thousands of humans underground, built more ships and keep going through the worm hole?' 'Because Murph Awesome... My daddy love me, I'm his little girl, he always send me money and buy me what I want... I'm Murph, Murph Awesome... this movie greatest movie ever!! So Shut Up and bow before Murph!!!' 'All Hail Murph!!!'

text: I get how Brand colonizes the new world, regardless of Cooper's success or doom, so They can exist in a distant future. Humans from thousands or even millions of years ahead placed the worm hole, built the tesseract, making it possible for the black hole observed data to be relayed back to Earth for us to have saved ourselves. So all that "works." But I'm still left wondering why. If the new colony, starting from zero has populated and evolved technologically and in their own humanity to the point that they supposedly did, Why? Why pick that point in history to intervene? They themselves were in no reported danger. There have been many examples throughout history that a handful of survivors have had to carry on while so many others perished. If They were so advanced and obviously knowledgeable, they would have had to have an inkling of the notion of to great of a step in technology can have serious perils attached to it. And why not, if to save anything with their tech and knowledge, go back further to prevent war or the damaging effects on the earth of the way we have conducted ourselves for millenia? Give us clean power. Teach us recycling before it got out of hand. Leave a note who God is or isn't! Hell! Send a space bus a couple years earlier and just help us move. Good movie for a movie, but try not to think about it too much after it's over.

author: @gustavobravetti
text: The movie is WRONG, and also my favorite space sci-fi movie period. I watched it at least a dozen times. Just by pleasure, I got it for the first time. Anyway, it presents a paradox: Future humans help present humans to find a new homeworld and avoid extermination. Remember, there are no habitable planets that can be reached alive with the current technology, and life on the Earth will be over soon. That's why future humans constructed a wormhole to facilitate present humans to travel to Gargantua, where there is one habitable planet. So without the help of the future humans, the present humans will perish soon; but the problem is that if they die, they'll never be future humans to help present humans. You need something from a particular future for that future to happen, and that is a classic bootstrap paradox. Anyway, I'm deeply in love with this movie, and I'll keep watching it without overthinking it too much, also Hans Zimmer's music and those giant waves worth enduring a paradox, even two.

You need something from a particular future for that future to happen, and that is a classic bootstrap paradox. text: So in summary, humans on earth are aided by future humans, and the black hole is the key to everything. It leads to a habitable planet, and provides crucial information for a gravitational equation. Cooper gathers crucial information that he relays to his daughter back on dying earth in real time, while inside the black hole. Afterward he arrives in a near future with his daughter now elderly, where humans have escaped earth, but have yet to settle upon a new planet. Afterward he travels through the black hole to the habitable planet in order to aid in colonizing. The future where humans have settled on a new planet is distant and we do not see it, how ever, it is assumed that the colonies in space will later follow suit and travel through the black hole to the planet. The very distant future is one in which humans exist in a 5 dimensional reality, and through necessity, they aid their species with survival in the past, in order to ensure their current existence. Only thing I’m confused about is how the future advanced humans got to where they were. Did they just happen to survive and advance, and now are able to look in the past and help when they see it is needed? Or are they just repeating the help they received to survive and passing it on to their past selves, similar to how Connor experienced help with his daughter and gravity in the library, and simply repeated his experience. In that case its like a closed loop and survival is inevitable. Food for thought, what if the future 5 dimensional humans go extinct, because they focus so much on helping the past to ensure their current existence, that they don’t focus on their future? After a certain point, the last interference with the past they had would be the last “help” that humans would receive from “them.” This would mean that if the current humans had not yet reached the 5 dimensional stage, they would not receive any more help, and they wouldn’t not be able to send any help to their past selves either, ultimately resulting in the end of humanity way back to beginning of the movie, before the artificial black hole appeared, back on dying earth.

Perhaps this is closer to the movie the Scientologists should have made.

text: No, I understood it quite well. It's just that a couple of parts of the movie still blow my mind, even after watching this video which didn't quite explain them. In fact, the knee-high water planet with waves the size of the Himalayan Mountain range and an incredibly slowed down field of time was the most mind blowing concept to me. That and fifth dimensional physics. A fourth dimension is a relatively easy concept to grasp. Take 9th grade algebra, with a simple two dimensional (x,y) plane. On it you can draw two dimensional objects such as a parabola, cube, and circle. Now add another dimension, z, this allows for more complex shapes, like a cube or a sphere. This dimension is the one we live on and it allows for 360 degree motion in any direction. Now, a fourth dimension. Well, if I can already move in any direction, then what would the next range of motion and perception be? Time. Moving forwards, backwards, or diagonally in time. But what could a fifth dimension be? But that water world. I understand that it is quite near a black hole, so the gravity exerted on the planet is immense by comparison to earth. But I am unsure as to how gravity would have such a bizarre impact on time. Why would the astronauts not age like it had been 7 years in one hour? How did the same time distortion not affect the hero astronaut (don't remember his name and have no idea how to spell the actor's) when he launched himself into the event horizon of the black hole? How did it not affect him more when gravity increased closer to the event horizon? Lastly, when the fourth dimension within the black hole collapsed, why did it place the hero where it did in space and time? Could it not have dumped him anywhere in space-time within the conceivable universe? Such as a million years in the future in the Andromeda Galaxy, or 81 billion years in the past in some forming nebula?

author: @lieutenantgruber8706
text: This probably would have been better served as a series. Too much 'in between the lines' that an audience are intended to guess at, i.e. too may gaps, and holes. Perhaps they're thinking of releasing a sequel that will bring sense to the movie. Frankly, I just never gave a shit about this because any movie dealing with manipulation of time (time travel, or I should say 'space-time' travel) based on the instance of the our future selves helping our present selves means the movie is a non-starter for me. By that I mean, we already know we'll be fine in the end since it's our future selves helping us, right? That would mean I know we made it okay through whatever was plaguing us ever before the 5 min. mark of this movie. The only way this movie is worth the time, is if the so-called "them" (our progenitors) are a distant version of us, i.e. the one's that put us on Earth to begin with and left us here, 'as opposed to us ourselves') -- in essence if "them" meaning "God" in real world sense. Secondly, this movie is too gratuitously circuitous, i.e. start false plan A in order to do a plan B which we would've done anyway even if plan A never was thought of or proposed. I could go one with other nonsense in the story plot, but wtf for, right? The best time-manipulation story I've seen to date is "Looper," where there is the conventional cycle or 'loop' and it's the main character's decision at the end that determines if the loop continues or not. This is what we yearn for in film -- the decisions our characters make, right? Kinda like the same reason the old "choose your own adventure" books used to rock.
translated_text: This probably would have been better served as a series. Too much 'in between the lines' that an audience are intended to guess at, i.e. too may gaps, and holes. Perhaps they are thinking of releasing a sequel that will bring sense to the movie. Frankly, I just never gave a shit about this because any movie dealing with manipulation of time (time travel, or I should say 'space-time' travel) based on the instance of the our future selves helping our present selves means the movie is a non-starter for me. By that I mean, we already know we will be fine in the end since it is our future selves helping us, right? That would mean I know we made it okay through whatever was plaguing us ever before the 5 minute. mark of this movie. The only way this movie is worth the time, is if the so-called "ththem" (our progenitors) are a distant version of us, i.e. the one's that put us on Earth to begin with and left us here, 'as opposed to us ourselves') -- in essence if "ththem" meaning "God" in real world sense. Secondly, this movie is too gratuitously circuitous, i.e. start false plan A in order to do a plan B which we would have done anyway even if plan A never was thought of or proposed. I could go one with other nonsense in the story plot, but what the fuck for, right? The best time-manipulation story I have seen to date is "Looper," where there is the conventional cycle or 'loop' and it is the main character's decision at the end that determines if the loop continues or not. This is what we yearn for in film -- the decisions our characters make, right? kind of like the same reason the old "choose your own adventure" books used to rock.

author: @gustavoturm
text: *THE END EXPLAINED:* They got lost in a common mistake that happens often in anime, the necessity to show and explain an "increasing sequence of awesome things": They went to space to save mankind, right? And things involved in this are easily explainable. Now they need something more interesting than that, yes! Landing in another planet! Awesome! This is a little bit harder to explain but it's still doable - we land on earth all the time, Isn't it? Now... What would be cooler than that? Spotting a black hole, from far away a black hole is just another random space object, there is not so much trouble in explaining that. But now we need something much more cooler! Yeah! GOING INTO THE DAMN BLACK HOLE! Wow... Now we're stumped, if even the best scientists have no clue on what happens in there, then movie writers obviously don't know either. How do we solve this problem in the plot?!? We resort to two stupid but very common devices in movie writing - (1) Get emotionalism from the viewers: The black hole was built by "friends from the future" and these guys just made all this because they wanted to see him love his daughter! And... guess what?! (2) To pretend there is something deep about it and let the viewers astray thinking they weren't intelligent enough to understand, the viewer gets entirely for free A JIBBER-JABBER ABOUT DIMENSIONS WRITTEN BY PEOPLE WHO CLEARLY HAVE NO IDEA WHAT THE MEANING OF "DIMENSION" IS! The dialogue basically becomes: "Here is 3 dimensions, there is 5 dimensions and 3+5=8 dimensions and 8=16/2 dimensions... This clearly means we are in √19 dimensions and all this means I love my daughter and should try to chat with her on the new social network: DimensionGram! Which is basically moving IKEA furniture around the house so that we can save humanity from extinction!" and in the end, they actually meet so that the viewers go "a ;'( ". It's really sad to see that people think that "there is an explanation for that" instead of downright observing that the movie is downright stupid.

author: @Trans909
text: This is the most lucid explanation of "Interstellar" I have yet seen. Well done, Looper! The plot, I think, is deliberately complex, perhaps contradictory--but that's only because we're used to thinking in three dimensions. Actually, it's only been very recently that we think that way. Until we invented air flight and spaceflight. most of our perspectives were limited to a two dimensional planar format. This movie forces the viewer to discard Time as a linear phenomenon, action before reaction in a way we refer to as Causality. But that's an illusion imparted by something else called "entropy," the tendency of a complex system to break down into less ordered conditions and eventually fall into a chaotic state. Think of entropy as water running downhill. (Remember, this is only a metaphor. We also think in terms of metaphors and comparisons--which is inexact because all metaphors fail at some point.) Water begins at a high point, such as a mountain lake, and runs downhill, eventually to the sea. This is why we often compare Time to a river--but again, that's only an illusion. Time does not pass by, it's actually one of many locations in a vast, complex matrix of conditions. ("Arrival" examined this condition, too. In fact, the two movies complement each other very well.) Gravity, on the other hand, may not be a "dimension,"--not as we're used to thinking about it, at least. It's definitely Universal and permeates the whole of the Cosmos--it might even slop over into other universes too--but we've recently discovered that it may not be a constant as we once thought. In fact, it MAY be a variable--which might be why it's impossible to reconcile General Field Theory with Quantum Theory. At the quantum level, gravity does not exist as it does up here in the macro-universe. It's just another point in the matrix. But we DON'T KNOW for sure. That's why, in the movie, it was so important to have data from inside the singularity of a black hole. We don't know, exactly, what happens inside the event horizon of a black hole. Lots of theories but NO hard data. We DO know that all our math breaks down and is useless in describing the conditions that MAY exist, just as General Field Theory is useless in describing things at the quantum level and vice versa. I can tell you that physics is in an uproar about this. The data from the Large Hadron Collider confirmed SOME predictions (Yes, the Higg's Boson does exist and yes, it seems to have much to do with generating gravity--but there seem to be several manifestations of that particle and we don't know why. The data are incomplete and confusing as hell.), but the LHC also produced some really contradictory results. More test runs are required because what data we acquired implies that there are larger, more massive particles possible--and we have NO idea why they exist or what function or purpose they serve. A lot of physicists have suggested just dumping EVERY hypothesis, EVERY theory, and starting all over again. I think that's counter-productive. We know that the math agrees with some of it and can predict at least most of what we see in the observable universe. But those damned black holes are hiding something REALLY important! Until we get some hard data about what's going on in there, we're dead in the water. Oh, don't worry about creating a black hole here on Earth that will swallow us up. Hawking's equations showed us that the really small ones "evaporate," produce "Hawking radiation" (named for him, of course) and disappear like a popped soap bubble. We're safe, so don't fret. Until then, contemplate Time and Causality and don't confuse them. Consider that there may be as many as eleven or twelve dimensions. Imagine that there may be infinite universes like a vast sea of bubbles that recede into Infinity times Infinity. Then pray that we survive the coming disasters on this Pale Blue Dot long enough for our descendants to figure all this out and take our rightful place among the many Cosmoses. Our children's children's children will grow up to be good beings someday and do Good Things. Let's give them that chance, just as the Builders gave Cooper and Murph the chance to save the world. It's a thing worth doing, isn't it? If you must have faith in something greater, have Faith in that.

author: @INTP-PatternWeaver
text: I don't get the concept of "time goes faster here than there". I know that time is relative, and I know it's a made-up concept. But it's still physically a thing. Most clocks in the world will countdown exactly in the same way, because everything on Earth is relatively the exact same, in regards to environment. But then, a wild physics zealot appears! People can time travel! So he's on the planet. And apparently their body seems to function fine. Which means that, on an atomic level, there is no hyperactivity. Which means that if he got a wristwatch - it would physically do the same thing, relatively speaking. The atoms would move at the same speed, making the clock tick at the same speed. And not only that, even if he by some magical means gets 7 years older, relatively speaking, and just 1 year "has passed on Earth" - that doesn't mean the same amount of time didn't pass, relatively to an "objective" source! He still spent 1 year on that planet, relative to Earth, and likewise 7 years went by on Earth, relative to him. It doesn't make sense to me to separate these facts like some magic. Can someone explain to me if this "relative time theory" is the "magical" theory so many use; that they could come back and just have aged 1 year and their family died 1000 years ago? The aging process in a human being is unstoppable, if you can exist, you must be in an environment that allows you to exist, and as such can't be supernatural, because it's natural that you live (and every physical process that allow you to function normally), and as such won't "age faster" or slower than you would on earth. It is that thought I just can't accept. I also get the concept of potentially travelling faster than light, but that just means for an observer, what you'd observe is something that has already happened for the subject travelling faster than light. So I don't quite get the concept of time travelling using wormholes (in theory) either. Is there any way physics, in observeable dimensions, could interact with a human body at all to hasten or slow the aging process and concious interpretation of time, without the subject noticing any difference? Hence "oh what, 100 years passed?!" We all know the "oh was I asleep for just 15 minutes?! I thought I've slept for an hour", but come on. I'm really open to mostly everything, but I've yet to see or hear an explanation about time being a farce and completely subjective to gravity's whim and it not being relative to our consciousness at all, that doesn't seem to be some "I just disovered Pluto is not a planet" rambling... Thanks if you read all this, and I don't really expect to get any particular attention, but I needed to write it, it's been annoying me for a good while (and nobody seems to be able to explain, or they can't be arsed - I like to think I'm trying to view stuff from different angles but THAT is truly relative)

Interstellar was still overall a great movie but that was just a nit-pick with the plot.

text: Everyone missed two huge clues that Nolan put in to make you question if it’s all real just like inception. Cooper actually died. Christopher Nolan shows us this when Cooper is traveling back after the library he sees Dr Brand , reaching out trying to touch her on the ship while they were going into the black hole. This is the first clue that Cooper is actually a spirit. Then the second clue is when Copper visits Murph you would think everyone in her room would greet him being that he saved them all and they are family but we see some look but no interaction with him or when he leaves. Murph then explains that he was her ghost and she has her kids here for her now. Then she says go, Cooper ask “where?” Which Murph answers “Brant...” then he leaves. So in reality they do not interact with him because he’s not really there in person he’s a spirit. Of course it leaves into question wether Brand did survive? I always viewed the ending as though Dr. Brand actually reached Dr Edmund while he was alive. It’s at the end when she’s burying him we hear Murph saying she’s settling in with her new (sun/son up for debate because she’s looking at the sunset/Mann), and new home. We can elude to Cooper that home meant getting back to his family. Edmund and Brand were in love so it’s safe to say she was either pregnant at the time or they had a child that we don’t see which is why Murph addressed it as home. Seeing that Dr Mann was still alive means Edmund must of not died so that is a good guess of what happened there. Of course Edmund and Mann were still alive because earth received transmissions so we know what happened is real. But the fact that Cooper was still alive and he gets on a short range space ship to go search for Brant is highly unlikely that’s real. But Nolan definitely makes you question reality, God, and life just like in Inception. When we don’t know wether Cobb actually made it back to reality or wether Limbo became his new reality. Of course you could debate that Cobb made it back to reality because he can see his children’s faces but Mal did die in his mind so it’s up for debate wether his mind chose then to accept them as his kids since Mal was no longer there. But of course the spinning top did start to wobble towards the end and in the dream it was a consistent strong spin. So chances are Cobb did make it out. But here in Interstellar Cooper reaching out his hand to Brant as they go into the black hole being that his hand has no form to Brant it’s safe to say that was his spirit and he did die. When he sees Murph she is on her death bed as well. It’s also possible Cooper and Brand did die and they are both spirits visiting what they loved most and letting go in which there spirits will now go to be with each other now that they have finally let go of what they loved most. Most definitely up for debate and this would make sense because now there is no point to go to Edmunds planet because humans have now learned to survive without planets. Also why doesn’t Murph say they are going after Brand which you would think that’s where they would go because it was habitable but guess not. Hope this gives more healthy conversation on how amazing Christopher Nolan and his Brother are at creating master pieces of art in film!

text: One thing to note is that it isn't just "love" that guided Cooper to Murphy, that's plain hokey. It was their emotional connection to a specific point in time where he would be able to connect with Murph in the past. The beings in the black hole can see all events throughout time but can't pinpoint where to send the information without a frame of reference. For them it would be like trying to identify a specific drop of water in an infinite ocean. Put another way, think about a very emotionally significant event in your life such as a wedding, birth of a child or death of a loved one. You know the exact date and can tell specific details about the whole thing. Now, describe the details of what you did two weeks before that and you'll probably come up short. The ability to recall events in our past is directly tied to their emotional significance.

text: They (future humans) had already found a way to survive, they had had to leave the planet, the planet must have become uninhabitable at some point of time in the past. "They" had already survived. Perhaps this was something that movie tried to allude to but wasn't taken any significant note of by the audience.

text: There is a time loop related to multi-dimensional space showing that in some circumstances physically related to intertwining of gravity and dimensions of space-time you can show your attitude to some decisions made back in time and this will have caused some kind of anomalies in the key moment of decision-making. The guy sees falling books and the information is "stay", however, he decided to leave his kids and go into space nonetheless. Why? This is just about that. This guy will not have reconciled with the fact that he had gone into space and thus we have the anomaly (in the context of "now" related to decision-making), anomaly in a sense bound to closing the other way - the parallel universe in which the consequences of staying would have occurred should he do it. Why don't we see such anomalies in any moment we make any decision? Probably this is due to our inability now (or in the future) to steer gravity in such a way to change our past. And we cannot change our past because this would create some kind of inconsistency. The chosen world, in which due to our non-reconciliation with the previous decision we try to change our mind, would have to collapse right away as other, parallel universes do. And so as for the world to not collapse, in the currently being changed world there must appear an anomaly, which of course will not cause the change the decision, since (as I muse) this anomaly induces the collapse of parallel universes and thus the decision is irrevocable. This would mean that there cannot exist parallel universes with parallel different decisions. I think that even in the quantum sense (however, you never know how's with quantum mechanics) such a statement would be true as it is with the Schroedinger's cat - making a decision - opening the bag with cat - causes the alternative to collapse. After opening the bag the cat cannot be both alive and dead. By the way, there is another movie which says about the irrevocability of a decision - "The Matrix": "The Oracle: Do you see her die? text: Nooo guys you’re not understanding Christopher Nolan’s maneuvers. That’s why he’s the GOAT in mind bending movies such as inception. Cooper’s death started when he was floating in the space. Okay let’s make things clear..Remember when Matt Damon said before trying to kill him? “Last thing you will see before dying is your family you’re beloved one” pay attention here.. that was a hint for us! When he decided to go through the black hole, the gravitational pressure of a black hole is so strong that a human being couldn't survive in it without suffocating. He made a choice, there was nothing to lose. Cooper was already dead when he entered Gargantua, or close to dying. In that case, either the 5D sequence was only hallucinations, or maybe he acted unconsciously. Cooper is in his ship, heading straight for the black hole. He sees light projections coming from ahead and begins to scream, suddenly we shift back to his son Tom on Earth, in front of the burning farm. The scene cuts, and we're back in the cockpit, where Cooper regains consciousness after (we guess) he was out for a couple of minutes. this when the film goes into NDE ( near-death-experience) a phenomenon that humans experience while dying (google it) The fact that the bright lights disappeared as he woke up, and the fact he lost consciousness before entering the black hole, a geometric shape, makes it all very possible. Now it's up to you to decide. The second clue is in the music playing during the space drifting scene. Just before it cuts, Hanz Zimmer (who delivers a masterful partition) concludes his song 'What Happens Now' with a high organ note, that remains constant and lingers in time. Just like an hospital's electrocardiogram and its continuous sound when a heart stops beating. Nolan is known for writing lines that always have a deeper meaning that makes sense further in the story. The lines are never just said for the sake of it. As a matter of fact, Dr. Mann who played by Matt Damon, tells Cooper an intriguing fact, about 30 minutes earlier in the film. "The last thing you see before you die is your children." Five minutes later Mann betrays Cooper, leaving him agonising on the glacier, and asks him "Can you see your children now? They're with you right now." While he escapes and Brand attempts to save Cooper, he tries to remain conscious, and pictures his last memory of Murph, from years before. Why is this line so important. Because if it comes up twice in the story, even though it doesn't bring anything to the story, there must be a reason behind it. In the final act, just before Cooper really dies in space, Dr. Mann's theory comes into place. Cooper imagines the life he would've had if he had been saved in time: Healed on a space station and finally reunited with an older Murph. On top of that, who hasn't noticed that when he enters Murph's hospital room, the family members around the bed make space for Cooper, but he doesn't care for them. We don't even really see their faces in the shot. After two minutes with Murph, he retires the same way, walking back, and Murph's grand-children (and his) surround the bed again, without paying attention to their great grand-father and hero. You'll also notice Nolan's craft in this shot. Cooper doesn't recognise his grand-children and great-grand-childen. He imagines their physical presence, but has no idea what they look like nor who they are. And just like a DREAM, he leave the room walking backwards as they come closer to Murph. since Dr. Mann mentioned his "children",where his Cooper's son in the hospital scene? Well to begin with, if he imagines his daughter 100 years older, it's very likely Cooper already imagines his son to be dead, since he was older than Murph. Secondly, I think everyone who saw Interstellar knows it by now, Cooper doesn't seem to care much for his son. And when Cooper was agonising on Dr. Mann's planet. waiting for Brand's help, he only pictures his daughter since their bond reflects Cooper's personality, even if it's a shame for poor Tom. Tunnel, TV and TARS... Hmmm? And please remind me what people who go through NDE experience? That's right, they see a tunnel with a light at the end of it. Moreover, the representations of this tunnel coincides with the images of Interstellar. Scientists claims that people who go through NDE they experience mystical things, raised from body, pleasant, family. The men that saved Cooper on the station put the dysfunctional TARS in Cooper's farm. And it just seems very unlikely that, from the point of view of the rescuers, they would leave the robot to rust. TARS might be the only witness to all of what happened during the interstellar trip. The station's engineers would've tried to work on the robot to collect valuable information. Especially since Cooper manages to fix him using only a screwdriver. If we follow our theory to the end, and we consider Nolan's greatness, once again TARS waiting for Cooper in his living room is only his visions, that he imagines before dying. Finally one last odd thing in the film's end, and I think everyone noticed it: the TVs in the station that plays in loop testimonies of life on Earth, from when Coop lived there. Some of the extracts are used at the very beginning of the film too, as shots within the story. So yes, you can suggest the TVs are here as a kind of memorial, or that Cooper's recreated farm is like a museum (which would explain the red ropes guiding Cooper in the house when he enters), but they also look like something out of a dream. In fact, at the very beginning of the film, we hear the first testimony of an old lady saying "my father was a farmer", Cooper is asleep, as if he was just reliving his last moments on Earth in his final visions. But I understand this last point is a toughie to demonstrate, even though I prefer to believe in this projection possibility. There's one thing for sure, with the film's open-ending, Nolan allows us to imagine the possibilities, just like he did in Inception. Because look at the facts, would a director that pays so much attention to every detail would be satisfied with this banal ending. It could also be because his mainstream status asks of him to create this 'alternative' simple ending. But that actually hides with great subtlety the REAL ending to Interstellar. Nolan used the NDE phenomenon to let us see his imaginary thoughts that he was experiencing when went unconscious. What a masterpiece!!

text: Anyone can take their own thoughts from the movie. Honestly, these "5th dimensional future humans" can be interpreted as God. It is one of my favorite movies ever. A lot better that 2001: A Space Odyssey.
